https://www.oedigital.com/news/543028-cy.text: By Peter McToal, Digital Solutions Architect at ABB Energy Industries Published Sep 17, 2026 5:41 am ET As offshore oil and gas platforms, offshore wind farms and maritime energy assets become increasingly connected, they are also becoming more exposed to sophisticated cyber threats. At the same time, a wave of new cyber security regulations is reshaping how operators protect critical infrastructure, creating an opportunity to strengthen resilience across the offshore energy sector by embedding security, visibility and preparedness into long-life assets and operations. We are reaching a critical juncture in cyber security for industrial and critical infrastructure environments. The frequency, sophistication, and intent behind cyber-attacks are all increasing, becoming more complex, more targeted and more sophisticated. But at the same time, legislation is evolving rapidly to further rise to this challenge. This is not simply a tightening of rules. It represents a fundamental shift in approach. Regulatory frameworks are becoming more preventative than prescriptive, and increasingly punitive where organizations fail to act. In effect, they reflect a strategic shift to prioritizing proactive security measures, continuous visibility, and resilience, over reactive incident response. This legislation can be a blueprint for resilience, not just compliance, across our Critical National Infrastructure (CNI). In the UK, CNI spans 13 sectors, as defined by the National Protective Security Authority (NPSA): chemicals, civil nuclear, communications, defense, emergency services, energy, finance, food, government, health, space, transport, and water. These sectors underpin the functioning of society, and their resilience is essential. Recent years have demonstrated how interconnected our systems can be. From the global disruption caused by COVID-19 to the geopolitical instability we’re witnessing today, the resilience of critical infrastructure has been repeatedly tested and increasingly scrutinized. Physical vulnerabilities have become highly visible while in the digital domain, these vulnerabilities are even more pervasive. For our CNI, this creates a uniquely complex risk environment where physical and digital threats are deeply interconnected.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543027-st.text: Commodity vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled to just three ships on Wednesday, down from 12 a day earlier and well below the 10-day average of about 17, preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday. The figures exclude any vessels that might have passed through the waterway with their Automatic Identification System transponders turned off to avoid detection. Of the three vessels, an empty Supramax dry bulk ship entered the strait via the Iranian route, while an empty petroleum product tanker entered through a dark route, shipping data from Kpler showed at 0445 GMT. A Panamax tanker exited the waterway using a dark route, the data showed. Vessel traffic dropped this week as war in the Gulf intensified. Saudi Arabian warplanes pounded Yemen and Houthi fighters launched drones and missiles at Saudi cities. The Iran-backed Houthis' rapid advance in Yemen along the Red Sea coast, attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to the kingdom's East-West oil pipeline have widened Tehran's reach in the conflict and raised risks to global oil supplies. In the Red Sea, vessel crossings through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait eased to 21 on Wednesday, compared with 24 vessels a day earlier. (Reuters)

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543024-ln.text: Global LNG prices could shoot higher this winter as Europe holds its lowest stocks in years and North Asian buyers face increased competition with the Strait of Hormuz still closed, executives said at an industry conference this week. Europe will enter this winter more vulnerable than usual amid storage levels that are lower than last year, industry executives and analysts said at Gastech in Bangkok. At the same time, the war on Iran has prevented Qatar and the United Arab Emirates from shipping liquefied natural gas through the Strait of Hormuz, leading to a loss of 36 million metric tons of supply this year, according to Shell. "Right now, where we stand in Europe is at a historically low storage level heading into the end of fall," said Shell's President of Integrated Gas Cederic Cremers . European Union natural gas stocks are currently 67% full, a record low for this time of year and far below an EU target of storage at 80% of capacity by December. Executives from Norwegian major Equinor said gas stocks could reach 75% full by November 1. Unlike the Ukraine crisis in 2022, European countries did not rush to build stockpiles during summer to meet winter demand due to a lack of financial incentives in a backwardated market, where prompt prices are higher than those in future months. "Unfortunately, it seems to us that Europe is in a very difficult position going into this winter," Cheniere Energy Chief Commercial Officer Anatol Feygin said. "(It's) not a secret to any of us that inventory levels are low. The prompt depends on how weather plays out." Germany's state-owned energy firm SEFE said on Wednesday it had already started increasing its natural gas storage levels as Europe heads into winter with the lowest inventories in years. Asia's spot prices this year LNG-AS have already nearly tripled to close to $30 per million British thermal units, dampening demand, industry executives said, down from a pre-war range of around $10/mmBtu. "There's a big risk if we have a cold winter because there's very little spare supply available, and it'll really test the market," said Simon Flowers, chairman of consultancy Wood Mackenzie . If it's a colder winter than normal, prices may reach $40/mmBtu, equivalent to about $240 per barrel for Brent, Flowers said, adding that prices that high would probably result in some demand destruction. "If it turns out to be warm ... Prices will still be elevated, but they may not be much higher than they are today," he said, noting that with the Iran war escalating and widening, the Strait of Hormuz will likely remain constrained through the year-end. E quinor's Senior Vice President Marketing and Supply Helle Ostergaard Kristiansen told Reuters a cold winter in Europe and Asia and continued disruption to Hormuz LNG shipmen

https://www.rigzone.com/news/winter_is_c.text: A new analysis by the S&P Global Energy Fuels and Refining team, which was sent to Rigzone recently, warned that “winter is coming for diesel”. The analysis noted that “the big squeeze continues to tighten for refined products - especially diesel”, warning that refined product inventories, which it described as “the buffer against disruptions”, continue to erode. According to the S&P team’s analysis, global gasoline stocks began September at the lowest tracked levels for any month in at least the past 10 years, but stocks for diesel continue to push the lower boundary of historical ranges. “While the end of the summer driving season offers at least something of a respite for gasoline demand, the most challenging time of year for the global diesel market is just beginning,” the analysis warned. The analysis pointed out that, “with fall harvests in the Northern Hemisphere approaching and the winter heating season in the U.S. Northeast, Europe, and North Asia not far behind”, global diesel exports “averaged just 5.85 million barrels per day in August 2026”. This was a 25 percent decline compared to August 2025, the analysis highlighted. Looking at the U.S., the analysis noted that diesel prices have hit all-time highs and said inventories had fallen below five-year seasonal lows despite record refinery runs.

https://safety4sea.com/hazardous-chemica.text: A hazardous substance leak aboard a Ro-Pax ferry at Germany’s Port of Rostock has forced the evacuation of around 160 passengers and most of the crew, highlighting the risks posed by dangerous goods carried on ships operating mixed passenger and freight services. T he Stena Line-operated Mecklenburg-Vorpommern was berthed at Rostock on 16 September, preparing to depart for Trelleborg, Sweden, when an unidentified liquid chemical reportedly leaked from a rail car carried onboard. Emergency services were called to the vessel and passengers and most crew members were evacuated as a precaution. The captain and a small number of people remained onboard, while local media reported that four people suffered minor injuries. The nature and extent of the leak remained unclear, with some passengers reportedly experiencing respiratory problems. Later on the day, emergency personnel wearing protective equipment boarded the ferry to assess the situation, while the area surrounding the vessel in the port was placed off-limits. The incident also disrupted the ferry’s scheduled operations, with the 15:00 departure for Trelleborg cancelled. The incident underlines the particular challenges of carrying hazardous substances on vessels, where a leak can quickly become a safety concern for passengers, crew, cargo and port personnel.

https://safety4sea.com/cm-infectious-dis.text: Seafarers operate across borders, climates and health environments, often moving between vessels, ports, airports and shore locations within a short period of time. This makes infectious disease prevention a practical part of crew health management, rather than an issue to consider only when an outbreak occurs. T he risk can change from one voyage to another. A new trading area, different port rotation, shore exposure or crew change may introduce health risks that were not relevant when the original voyage or employment arrangements were made. Recent guidance from the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) provides a useful reminder that prevention starts well before symptoms appear. From vaccination and malaria precautions to job-specific exposure and onboard medical arrangements, shipowners should ensure that infectious-disease controls reflect where their vessels are actually operating and what their crews may encounter. A recent Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda also showed why operators should remain alert to evolving public-health risks, even where maritime operations and port calls remain unaffected, as local health requirements can change quickly Infectious-disease risk is not static. Where a vessel trades, how long it remains in port, whether crew members go ashore and how seafarers travel when joining or leaving the ship can all affect their level of exposure. The MCA advises employers to consider factors including the ports visited, duration of calls, potential exposure ashore, countries through which seafarers travel and the nature of their onboard duties.

https://safety4sea.com/imo-80-attacks-on.text: Escalating geopolitical tensions are placing merchant shipping and seafarers under growing threat across several major trading regions, with IMO warning that civilian vessels and crews must not become targets of conflict. S peaking in London at the IMO Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (14–18 September), IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez warned that geopolitical tensions are exacting an increasingly deadly toll on commercial shipping. The warning comes as the IMO has verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz since 28 February, leaving at least 22 seafarers dead and many others injured. We are reaching a point where these conflicts are being used as a pretext to attack merchant vessels and innocent seafarers. Do not use these conflicts to attack innocent seafarers. The threat, however, extends well beyond the Gulf. In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although the IMO said precise figures remain difficult to verify. Meanwhile, attacks on shipping in the Red Sea have resumed, with four fatalities confirmed following a Houthi attack on a merchant vessel on 11 August. Dominguez stressed that the attacks across the different conflict zones cannot be attributed to a single actor. “In the Strait of Hormuz, it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels. In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels,” he said.

https://safety4sea.com/us-contracted-ves.text: A US-contracted vessel has reportedly come under an Iranian drone and missile attack near the Strait of Hormuz, leaving crew members injured and adding to mounting concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through the important waterway. T he reported attack involved four Iranian drones and at least one missile, with one projectile striking the vessel US media reported on 16 September. Several US personnel were reportedly onboard, while those injured, including crew members affected by smoke inhalation, are receiving medical treatment in an unidentified Gulf country. The vessel’s identity has not been disclosed, and neither Washington nor Tehran has officially confirmed the incident. The reported strike comes as shipping activity through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, highlighting the growing security dilemma facing operators navigating the waterway. Only three commercial vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on 16 September, down from 12 the previous day and well below the 10-day average of around 17, according to preliminary vessel-tracking data reported by Reuters. The figures exclude vessels that may have switched off their AIS transponders to avoid detection, meaning actual traffic could be higher. The vessels identified included an empty Supramax bulk carrier entering through the Iranian route, an empty petroleum product tanker entering via a so-called dark route and a Panamax tanker exiting through a dark route. The steep decline comes despite US claims that the waterway remains open to commercial traffic. US Central Command has said its forces are helping commercial vessels navigate the strait and facilitate the movement of hundreds of millions of barrels of oil to global markets.

https://safety4sea.com/us-house-moves-to.text: The US House of Representatives has voted to disapprove a federal decision authorising California’s emissions requirements for ocean-going vessels at berth, introducing fresh uncertainty over the regulatory framework applying to ships calling at the state’s ports. A ccording to the official US House Clerk record, H.J. Res. 210 passed the House on 15 September by 216 votes to 211. The resolution targets the US Environmental Protection Agency’s 2023 decision relating to California’s Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth regulation. If enacted, the resolution would disapprove the EPA action under the Congressional Review Act. The measure would still need to complete the remaining legislative process before taking effect. The California Air Resources Board (CARB) says its 2020 At-Berth Regulation is intended to reduce emissions from ocean-going vessels while they are docked at California ports. The requirements do not mandate shore power as the only compliance option. According to CARB, regulated vessel visits must use a CARB Approved Emission Control Strategy, which can include shore power or approved emissions capture and control technologies, unless an exception or alternative compliance pathway applies. EPA originally granted California authorisation for the updated At-Berth Regulation in October 2023.

https://safety4sea.com/ibia-issues-biofu.text: A new checklist designed to help shipowners and crews manage the operational risks of FAME-based biofuel blends has been formally issued by the International Maritime Organization (IMO), as the use of biofuels in shipping continues to expand. A s biofuel blends move from trials towards wider use onboard, shipowners and crews are getting a new practical tool to help manage the risks that can emerge when bunkering and consuming FAME-based fuels. The International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) has issued its Shipboard Biofuel Blend Checklist for FAME-based biofuels as an annex to IMO document MEPC 85/INF.10, bringing the guidance into the IMO’s formal documentation. Developed by IBIA’s Technical Working Group as part of the ongoing update of the IBIA/BIMCO Shipmaster’s Bunkering Manual, the checklist is designed to help vessel operators navigate the practical challenges associated with biofuel blends, particularly when a ship is using them for the first time. The checklist covers the key stages of managing FAME-based biofuels onboard, including fuel assessment, compatibility checks, tank preparation, water management, bunkering operations, storage and machinery performance monitoring. IBIA noted that the growing use of biofuel blends can bring different or additional operational risks, particularly for operators with limited experience handling the fuels. These risks can be mitigated through robust fuel-management practices before delivery and throughout the fuel’s use onboard. The checklist is based on CIMAC Guideline 04|2024, Marine fuels containing FAME: A guideline for shipowners & operators, and is intended to serve as a practical reference for crews and operators.

https://safety4sea.com/south-korea-moves.text: South Korea is expanding financial support for ice-capable vessels as part of its wider push to develop commercial shipping along the Northern Sea Route. T he Korea Ocean Business Corporation (KOBC) has introduced a new investment programme providing KRW 120 billion annually to support South Korean shipping companies acquiring icebreakers and ice-class vessels for Arctic operations. The move adds to South Korea’s broader efforts to build an Arctic-capable fleet and gain operational experience in polar waters. Earlier this year, the country launched its first container ship trial voyage through the Northern Sea Route. T he 2,758-TEU PanStar Acro departed Busan in August on a government-backed voyage designed to assess the technical, environmental and commercial feasibility of Arctic container shipping. According to South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, the trial is intended to gather data on voyage duration, fuel consumption, operating costs and cargo demand. The Master and navigation officers received specialist polar-navigation training, while additional emergency-response and communications arrangements were put in place for the voyage. The latest financing initiative is significant because access to suitable tonnage remains a key practical barrier to expanding Arctic shipping. Ice-class vessels require additional investment, while operators must also manage the safety, environmental and operational challenges associated with polar navigation.

https://safety4sea.com/todays-engine-cho.text: Engine decisions made by shipowners over the next decade could lock in much of the fleet’s fuel-consuming capacity through 2050, but whether those vessels actually use alternative fuels will ultimately depend on economics and regulation, according to a new analysis by the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) and Boston Consulting Group (BCG). T he report, Navigating the maritime fuel transition: How fuel economics, regulations, and fleet decisions shape the future bunkering landscape , puts a long-term spotlight on decisions being made in shipyards today. With vessels typically staying in service for 25–30 years and only around 4% of the global fleet replaced each year, the engines ordered now could help shape shipping’s fuel demand well into 2050. However, having the technical capability to consume a new fuel does not guarantee its uptake. Dual-fuel engines provide shipowners with flexibility to switch between conventional and alternative fuels as costs and regulations evolve. The analysis identifies a global pricing mechanism as one of the most important levers for driving the maritime fuel transition at scale. Under the report’s base scenario, new fuels remain more expensive than conventional fuels through 2050. They become cost-competitive when the International Maritime Organization (IMO)’s Net-Zero Framework (NZF) Tier-2 remedial unit (RU) penalty reaches USD 700/tCO2e, as modelled in the high-penalty scenario. At the time of the analysis, the NZF agreed at the 83rd session of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 83), was the only concrete regulatory proposal available for modelling, and the base scenario assumes its adoption as proposed.

https://safety4sea.com/fragmented-ship-t.text: The shipping industry’s digital transformation could create as many challenges as it solves if shipboard technologies continue to operate in isolation, with fragmented cloud, satellite, IoT and cybersecurity systems leaving data disconnected and potentially expanding the cyberattack surface. T he new “Innovation in the Digital Ship Market” white paper from Rakuten Maritime and ClassNK argues that the growing number of digital solutions being deployed onboard needs to be matched by greater integration, allowing data, operational systems and cybersecurity measures to work together rather than in separate silos. The push comes as shipping faces a changing operating environment, including population decline and improvements in onboard working conditions, while smart-ship and autonomous-ship technologies continue to advance. The scale of the digital transformation is also expanding rapidly. According to Allied Market Research, the global maritime digitalization market is projected to reach $423.4 billion by 2031, representing a compound annual growth rate of 10.7% between 2022 and 2031. The autonomous ship market is also expected to reach $217.6 billion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 9.5% from 2024 to 2033. The growing adoption of maritime IoT, AI-based data analytics, cloud computing and smart-ship technologies is generating increasing amounts of operational data. However, the white paper argues that many ship-specific digital solutions remain fragmented, limiting their ability to work together effectively.

https://www.marinelog.com/news/qa-why-re.text: As vessel operators extend the working lives of existing fleets, manage growing demands on crews and prepare for the use of alternative fuels, the way they monitor critical machinery is evolving as well. Traditional used oil analysis remains an important maintenance tool, but the time between collecting a sample and receiving laboratory results can limit its usefulness when equipment conditions change quickly. Marine Log spoke with Barry Sullivan, senior technical services engineer at Castrol, about the role real-time oil condition monitoring can play alongside traditional analysis, where the technology is already being put to use and what could drive broader adoption across the maritime industry. Marine Log (ML): The maritime industry has been using oil analysis to monitor the health of business-critical equipment for decades. Why is that approach under pressure now? Barry Sullivan (BS): Used oil analysis has served the industry well and continues to do so, especially in two-stroke engines. But evolving operating conditions are giving shipowners and operators pause for thought. That pressure stems from business-critical equipment, specifically the assets that either earn revenue directly or are expensive enough that a failure could mean a significant time out of action for the vessel. That’s not always the main engine; it depends on the owner and the vessel type. To begin, it’s clear that it’s a mixed bag for the industry. While some are heading to the yards, many are put off by the long lead times, costs, and ultimately securing financing. As a result, the working lives of fleets are being extended, with the average age in some sectors approaching 25 years and more. That trend shows no sign of reversing. With newbuild prices elevated and shipyards running at sustained capacity, new tonnage is expensive, and vessel values in sectors are falling. Therefore, existing vessels are working longer. This means we need vessels to stay commercially operational for an extended period beyond their initial lifetime.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/sto.text: The Secretary-General of the International Maritime Organization, Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, has called on Member States to refrain from actions that endanger merchant ships and put seafarers’ lives at risk. Addressing the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers, the Secretary-General warned of the severe impacts of geopolitical tensions on the shipping industry. Secretary-General Dominguez said: “We are reaching a point where these conflicts are being used as a pretext to attack merchant vessels and innocent seafarers. Do not use these conflicts to attack innocent seafarers.” Since the current conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February, IMO has verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in the deaths of at least 22 seafarers and injuries to many others. In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although precise numbers are difficult to verify. Attacks in the Red Sea have also resumed, with four fatalities confirmed in the latest attack by the Houthis on a merchant vessel on 11 August.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/dea.text: China to US East coast is close to 11000 USD , 7% below the covid peak, China to US West coast is scratching 8000 USD? China Europe rising 250% and then down 30%. So what’s going on? Let us start with a bold statement. Nobody predicted the freight market of 2026. Not even us; although we did try! Coming into the year, analysts broadly agreed that oversupply and weak demand would keep prices flat or falling. And indeed, at the beginning of the year, this forecast was realized. Transpacific dropped by 30% or so and transpacific spot prices stabilized at around 2000 USD. Even the geopolitical disruptions in the Middle East barely moved the market: rates rose from USD 2,000 per FEU in January to just USD 2,400 by April. Carriers introduced the familiar roster of surcharges (EFS, EBF, EBR), but to no avail. They were able to increase prices, but were struggling to recover all of the cost increases. Demand was simply not there and supply was aplenty, so shippers had the leverage to push back. Is it the oil? From the beginning of June 2026, prices started climbing much faster. So what happened? The simple narrative is, the prices climbed due to increased bunker costs. But prices of VLSFO in Singapore were approx. 400 USD in January, before the war, and 900 USD in September. The near-doubling of costs absolutely contributed to increased freight prices. But it cannot explain the 300%+ price increase we are currently witnessing. Is it Network rerouting? Whenever there is a geopolitical disruption there is a network change. And indeed, there has been a significant network change, but the Middle East represents less than 20% of the global volume and essentially no transpacific service passes through it. Is it the demand side? Against most expectations, volumes were very high in July – China to Europe volumes were 12% YoY. China – US July numbers were also up, but only by a modest 4%. Not a record high, but a clear signal of normal peak season nevertheless. This might be part of the price increase explanation, but unlikely to be the whole story either, particularly on the transpacific. If demand was the main driver then, by definition, the price increases into northern Europe would be higher than the ones towards the US West Coast. This, however, is simply not the case.

https://splash247.com/exmar-lands-10-yea.text: Belgium’s Exmar has secured a 10-year floating LNG infrastructure deal in Ivory Coast, reviving plans for an import terminal at Abidjan that have been on the drawing board for a decade. The Antwerp-based gas shipping and infrastructure group has entered into agreements with state-owned CI-Energies and Petroci covering the lease of a 152,000 cu m FSRU at the Port of Abidjan. The project will give Ivory Coast its long-planned floating LNG import capability as the country looks to supplement domestic gas supplies used heavily in electricity generation. Plans for an Abidjan FSRU date back to early 2016, when the government approved the PACI-GNL project in response to what it described as a growing shortage of natural gas for the power sector. Petroci and CI-Energies were tasked with creating a joint venture with private investors to import LNG, lease an FSRU and develop the associated terminal and pipelines. Later that year, a consortium led by Total signed up to develop a 3m tonnes per annum facility at Vridi. Total held 34%, alongside Socar, Shell, Petroci, Golar, CI-Energies and Endeavor Energy, with startup initially targeted for mid-2018. The project never reached operation. The FSRU scheme has nevertheless remained part of the government’s energy plans and appears again in Ivory Coast’s 2026-2030 pipeline of public-private partnership projects.

https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/20.text: Viatura da Polícia Militar do Estado de São Paulo — Foto: Divulgação/Polícia Militar Os estados brasileiros gastaram R$ 103,5 bilhões com as polícias em 2025, mas a maior parte dos recursos foi destinada ao policiamento ostensivo. Do total, R$ 60,7 bilhões (58,6%) foram destinados às Polícias Militares, responsáveis pelo policiamento ostensivo. Já as Polícias Civis, encarregadas das investigações, receberam R$ 22,2 bilhões (21,5%), enquanto as Polícias Técnico-Científicas, que atuam em áreas como perícia e produção de provas, receberam R$ 2,8 bilhões (2,7%). Na outra ponta do sistema de justiça criminal, os investimentos em políticas exclusivas para pessoas egressas do sistema prisional representaram, em média, apenas 0,001% dos gastos estaduais. O levantamento nacional analisou orçamentos das polícias, sistema prisional e políticas para egressos no ano passado em 26 unidades da federação Os dados fazem parte da nova edição do estudo “O Funil de Investimentos da Segurança Pública nos Estados Brasileiros”, elaborado pelo JUSTA e lançado no 20º Encontro do Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública. O levantamento analisou os orçamentos de 26 unidades federativas em 2025. O Acre foi o único estado que não forneceu dados para o estudo. Segundo o JUSTA, a distribuição dos recursos prioriza o policiamento ostensivo em detrimento das ações de investigação, inteligência e produção de provas. Para a organização, isso pode ampliar a capacidade de prender sem necessariamente aumentar a capacidade de esclarecer crimes e desarticular organizações criminosas.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543045-ar.text: Argentina's government has presented a bill to crack down on companies operating in the Falkland Islands, potentially escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the territory that is controlled by Britain but claimed by Argentina. The proposal introduced on Thursday toughens sanctions on companies and people who unlawfully participate in activities in the Falklands and in Argentina's maritime spaces and continental shelf in "any type of activity aimed at the utilization of renewable or non-renewable natural resources" without authorization from Argentine authorities. It also creates a National Security Council, led by Argentina's president, to oversee national security policy and safeguard critical infrastructure and national sovereignty. Its seven members will include the president's cabinet chief, foreign minister, defence minister, economy minister, secretary of national intelligence and the president's legal secretary. The bill seeks to "punish those who exploit our natural resources illegally, create incentives for them to cease such conduct, and provide the national government with tools to protect itself against external threats," the president's office said in a statement on Thursday. The new bill aims to revamp 2011 legislation with a tougher regime and stronger sanctions aimed at companies and their shareholders and suppliers, the statement added.

https://safety4sea.com/lessons-learned-s.text: A near miss during preparations to connect a tow wire illustrates how quickly a routine vessel-to-vessel operation can become hazardous when agreed arrangements are not followed. T he International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has published a safety flash reporting that a tanker crew unexpectedly discharged a Line Throwing Apparatus (LTA) while another vessel was manoeuvring astern to receive a heaving line. The incident caused no injuries or damage, but it exposed weaknesses in communication, operational interface controls and equipment assurance. The vessel was preparing to connect a tow wire to pull back a tanker. It was manoeuvring astern and was approximately 10 metres from the tanker’s stern, ready to receive a heaving line and messenger line. The tanker was stopped on dynamic positioning, with its bow facing the prevailing current and weather. The agreed arrangement was straightforward: the bridge crew of the vessel would communicate by VHF when it was ready to receive the heaving line. The heaving line was also the approved method for passing the messenger rope. That agreed sequence was not followed. Without prior warning or agreement from the other vessel, the tanker’s deck crew discharged an LTA. The apparatus split into two parts during firing. One part of the rocket struck the upper spooling winch, while the line detached and returned to the tanker’s deck. Nobody was injured and neither vessel was damaged. However, the event occurred while the vessels were in close proximity and during an operation involving lines, winches and personnel on deck. The absence of an actual injury should therefore not obscure the significance of the near miss.

https://safety4sea.com/cyberattacks-on-t.text: Two energy tankers bound for Texas were hit by cyberattacks last month while underway, prompting US Coast Guard and FBI teams to board both vessels for multi-day investigations. O ne of the ships, the VL Prosperity, is a 1,093-foot Liberian-flagged crude carrier that was heading for Galveston. Iranian state media named the vessel shortly after the incident and claimed hackers had penetrated its propulsion, navigation and cargo systems, cutting off communications for roughly 30 hours. US authorities have stopped short of publicly attributing the attacks to Iran, but Rear Admiral Amy Grable, who commands US Coast Guard Cyber Command, confirmed to CBS News that responders uncovered signs of malicious cyber activity once they began examining the ship’s IT and onboard systems. The VL Prosperity is a supertanker with capacity for about 2.3 million barrels of crude. Vessel-tracking data shows it left Egypt’s Sidi Kerir terminal on August 1 en route to Galveston. According to US officials, the ship slowed near the Strait of Gibraltar around the time of the reported attack before resuming its crossing to the United States. Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported on August 20 that the vessel had been targeted on August 7 while transiting the Strait. Citing an unnamed crew member, Mehr claimed hackers had breached the engine room, disrupted cooling flow, pushed up engine speed and tampered with fuel systems. Rob Lee, CEO of industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos, said the technical details in the Iranian account were plausible and consistent with how such systems could realistically be manipulated — while cautioning that attribution has not been established.

https://safety4sea.com/new-smart-ship-pl.text: China Merchants Group has rolled out a new vessel operating system built to tackle one of shipping’s most persistent digital headaches: onboard equipment from different manufacturers that struggles to talk to one another. T he platform was developed by CM Marine Intelligence, a subsidiary of CM Energy, and is designed to give ships a common digital foundation rather than a patchwork of incompatible systems. Its central aim is to resolve the mismatched communication protocols, isolated data silos and hardware-software compatibility gaps that have long made it difficult to get a unified view of what’s happening across a vessel’s systems. Rather than a single piece of software, the offering brings together an operating system, IoT networking, digital infrastructure and cloud-based training tools into one architecture. That architecture is built around four pillars: standardised data models, reliable communications even in complex operating environments, security, and the flexibility to adapt as new technologies emerge. The practical goal is interoperability, letting equipment from different suppliers exchange data freely and giving shipowners a foundation on which to run applications for intelligent navigation, energy efficiency and broader vessel operations, without being locked into a single vendor’s ecosystem. China Merchants Group Chairman Miao Jianmin framed the platform as a full-stack technology architecture, spanning everything from chips to operating systems to applications, aimed at delivering strong performance across navigation, energy efficiency and operational maintenance.

https://safety4sea.com/general-average-d.text: General average has now been declared for the CMA CGM Petra, the container vessel that suffered a cargo hold fire in the Strait of Malacca in August, a move that means cargo interests will need to post financial security before their containers can be released. T he declaration follows the blaze that broke out on August 23 aboard the 8,000-TEU ship while it was en route from Singapore to Lamu, Kenya. Albatross Adjusters has been brought in to administer the general average process, which will apportion the costs of the incident among all parties with cargo on board, in line with standard maritime practice for casualties of this kind. With firefighting and salvage operations now complete, the vessel has made its way to Port Klang, where roughly 450 containers are due to be discharged and inspected — a process that will help determine the extent of the damage and shape how the wider cargo recovery proceeds. The fire was first reported on August 23, while the French-flagged Petra was transiting the Strait of Malacca on its way to Lamu. According to tracking data, the salvage team succeeded in containing the blaze relatively quickly, and no injuries or pollution were reported in its immediate aftermath, though salvage work continued for some time afterward. In the days that followed, the vessel held position in waters off Penang, Malaysia, rather than continuing on its scheduled rotation. By September 1, the ship had missed its planned call at Colombo, underscoring how significantly the incident had disrupted its voyage. The Petra had been operating on the KILIMA service, which links Qingdao, Nansha and Singapore with East African ports including Colombo, Lamu, Mombasa and Dar es Salaam. Cargo loaded at those Asian ports bound for East Africa is among the shipments now affected by the delay and by the general average process.

https://safety4sea.com/a-second-gateway-.text: The world’s shipping network is facing pressure from two of its most critical maritime gateways, with Qatar warning that a closure of Bab el-Mandeb could deepen the disruption already gripping the Strait of Hormuz. Q atar has sounded the alarm over a second vital artery of global shipping, urging the international community to keep the Bab el-Mandeb Strait open as disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues to reverberate through trade and energy markets. The warning is stark – with one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints already under pressure, the loss of another could turn a regional shipping crisis into a far broader disruption. “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandeb into that equation,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told a briefing in Doha on 15 September. “The whole world is going to suffer and it’s going to be catastrophic for the entire world,” he said. Al Hashmi warned that repeated disruption to international waterways must not become the “new normal”, urging countries to work collectively to safeguard freedom of navigation and push for a diplomatic resolution.

https://www.gov.br/antaq/pt-br/noticias/.text: Brasília, 17/09/2026 – A Agência Nacional de Transportes Aquaviários (ANTAQ) abriu a Tomada de Subsídios Pública SRG nº 2/2026, destinada a receber contribuições, subsídios e sugestões sobre o Relatório de Análise de Impacto Regulatório (AIR) Preliminar referente ao Tema 1.3 – “Operações de transbordo de granel sólido (b arge to ship )”, integrante da Agenda Regulatória 2025/2028. A participação estará aberta até as 23h59 do dia 15/10 e será realizada exclusivamente por meio de formulário eletrônico disponibilizado pela Agência. Usuários e agentes do setor aquaviário nacional, além dos demais interessados, poderão encaminhar suas contribuições durante o período. A tomada de subsídios é um mecanismo de participação que permite reunir informações e contribuições para subsidiar a construção de conhecimento e o desenvolvimento de propostas sobre determinada matéria. Na ANTAQ, o instrumento possibilita que os interessados colaborem por escrito. As contribuições deverão ser encaminhadas exclusivamente pelo formulário eletrônico da Tomada de Subsídios SRG nº 2/2026 , até as 23h59 de 15/10. Não serão aceitas manifestações enviadas por outros meios. É possível encaminhar imagens digitais, como mapas, plantas e fotos, pelo e-mail srg@antaq.gov.br, desde que o participante esteja identificado e respeite o prazo. O conteúdo da contribuição, no entanto, deverá ser obrigatoriamente preenchido nos campos específicos do formulário eletrônico. As contribuições recebidas serão disponibilizadas no site da ANTAQ. Como parte das ações relacionadas ao tema, a ANTAQ realizará um webinário no dia 23/09, a partir das 10h, para apresentar e debater o assunto com os interessados. O encontro será uma oportunidade para ampliar o conhecimento sobre o tema e esclarecer aspectos relacionados ao relatório de AIR preliminar, tornando-se uma etapa importante que antecede o período de finalização da participação pública.

https://www.offshore-energy.biz/petrobra.text: Petrobras Netherlands B.V. (PNBV), a subsidiary of Brazil’s state-owned energy giant Petrobras, has expanded its offshore footprint with exploration blocks located in the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire. Petrobras’ subsidiary has signed production sharing contracts (PSCs) for eight offshore exploration blocks with the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire and Petroci. These PSCs cover the CI-513 , CI-600 , CI-601 , CI-602 , CI-603 , CI-605 , CI-701 , and CI-702 blocks off the African country’s coast. The Brazilian giant, through PNBV, will have a 90% stake in the blocks as operator, while Petroci will hold the remaining 10% interest. The company highlights that these deals secure its participation in high-potential exploration areas along the African equatorial margin. These PSCs build on Petrobras’ recent expansion in West Africa’s oil and gas frontier, as it entered negotiations for four-block exploration contracts in Ghana’s Keta Basin.

https://www.offshore-energy.biz/technip-.text: French-based engineering player Technip Energies has been hired to work on a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export terminal in Guaymas, Sonora, on Mexico’s West Coast. Technip Energies has been selected by Amigo LNG , a Mexican joint venture between Texas-based Epcilon LNG and Singapore’s LNG Alliance, for an enhanced project management consultant (ePMC) role on the Amigo LNG project in Mexico. “We will provide overall project management, engineering interface management, construction management, and independent project oversight across the development, and act as the key technical and integration partner across the project’s stakeholders, contractors and execution entities,” the French player emphasized. The company explains that this ePMC role covers the complete 6 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) LNG liquefaction facility, comprising two floating process barges: a pre-treatment barge and a liquefaction barge. The European engineering firm will provide overall PMC oversight for both barges and their integration. This award marks Technip Energies’ first project with LNG Alliance and its second global ePMC contract for an FLNG development. The Amigo LNG project’s scope includes overseeing the associated marine facilities, including a quad berth designed to accommodate two LNG carriers and two floating storage units (FSUs), together with the related berthing, mooring, utilities and export infrastructure.

https://petronoticias.com.br/cacas-da-ar.text: Uma manhã de avanços dos terroristas houthis, do Iêmen, no Estreito de Bab al-Mandab, expõe a crise marítima não resolvida de Israel no Porto de Eilat. Mesmo antes da ameaça às rotas petrolíferas sauditas, os houthis já haviam alcançado uma importante conquista estratégica contra Israel, ao interromper o tráfego marítimo comercial regular para Eilat. A tomada pelos houthis de pontos estratégicos ao longo da costa oeste do Iêmen e da Ilha de Perim, no coração do Estreito de Bab al-Mandab, trouxe à tona uma ameaça que Israel conhece bem e pela qual vem pagando um preço há quase três anos, já que os avanços mais recentes do grupo transformam a ameaça à navegação no Mar Vermelho em um problema estratégico cada vez mais urgente também para a Arábia Saudita. Mesmo antes de a ameaça às rotas petrolíferas sauditas levar o Príncipe Mohammed Bin Salman a buscar ajuda dos Estados Unidos, os terroristas já haviam alcançado uma conquista contra Israel, interrompendo quase completamente o tráfego marítimo comercial regular para o porto de Eilat. Quase três anos se passaram desde que o problema surgiu e nenhuma solução foi encontrada. As Forças de Defesa de Israel atacaram repetidamente alvos dos houthis no Iêmen, o Estado prestou assistência ao porto e uma rota alternativa de importação foi estabelecida através de Aqaba. Nada disso, porém, fez com que as companhias de navegação interacionais retomassem as viagens regulares e diretas do leste para Eilat. Com base nas informações disponíveis publicamente, nenhuma decisão do gabinete definiu a restauração da liberdade de navegação comercial em Eilat como um objetivo de segurança e diplomático, nem o governo apresentou um plano aprovado para trazer os navios de volta ao porto. Os recentes acontecimentos alteraram as circunstâncias em que Israel enfrenta o problema. A ameaça dos Houthis a Bab al-Mandab tornou-se também uma questão estratégica urgente para a Arábia Saudita, e o príncipe herdeiro saudita já solicitou assistência militar dos EUA. Israel e Arábia Saudita agora têm interesses diplomáticos e estratégicos paralelos em relação à mesma rota marítima. Da perspectiva de Israel, a situação da Arábia Saudita cria uma oportunidade que antes não existia na mesma medida: aproveitar um esforço regional em torno do Estreito de Bab el-Mandab para também restabelecer a navegação até Eilat. Os houthis capturaram Mocha, avançaram ao longo da costa e tomaram o controle de Perim, a ilha localizada no estreito de Bab el-Mandab. Eles também conquistaram as ilhas de Hanish Maior e Hanish Menor, fortalecendo seu domínio em torno de um dos pontos de estrangulamento marítimo mais importantes do mundo. O tráfego pelo estreito continua, e os houthis atualmente não controlam a passagem de forma a interromper completamente a navegação.

https://petronoticias.com.br/subsea7-apr.text: A Subsea7 também participará da ROG.e 2026 e vai aproveitar o evento para destacar suas soluções técnicas destinadas ao desenvolvimento de campos em águas profundas, além de promover debates sobre os desafios e as oportunidades relacionados à expansão da atividade offshore no Brasil. “ O futuro dos projetos offshore no Brasil dependerá da capacidade da indústria de combinar tecnologia, competitividade e colaboração. Soluções inovadoras, associadas a uma cadeia de suprimentos forte e integrada, serão fundamentais para viabilizar desenvolvimentos cada vez mais complexos e maximizar o potencial dos recursos do pré-sal. Tecnologias como o aquecimento ativo permitem aumentar a previsibilidade operacional, reduzir riscos e contribuir para acelerar investimentos estratégicos para o país ”, afirma Yann Cottart, Vice-Presidente Sênior Brazil & GPC West. Durante o evento, a Subsea7 apresentará experiências acumuladas em projetos offshore de alta complexidade realizados em diferentes partes do mundo e demonstrará tecnologias destinadas a ampliar a confiabilidade das operações e aperfeiçoar o desenvolvimento de campos submarinos. A companhia também estará presente em discussões sobre planejamento de longo prazo, inovação e desenvolvimento da cadeia de fornecedores, considerados aspectos relevantes para responder à futura demanda do mercado brasileiro. Entre os destaques da programação está a apresentação do sistema Electrically Heat-Traced Flowline (EHTF), desenvolvido em parceria com a ITP Interpipe. A tecnologia reúne aquecimento elétrico ativo, isolamento térmico e monitoramento permanente por fibra óptica para preservar a temperatura das linhas de produção em projetos com long tie-backs. A solução ajuda a prevenir a formação de hidratos e parafinas, ampliando as alternativas para o desenvolvimento de reservatórios remotos e proporcionando maior previsibilidade operacional. A empresa também ressaltará a relevância da cooperação entre operadoras, fornecedores, companhias de tecnologia e prestadores de serviços para acelerar a implantação de projetos e superar os desafios técnicos relacionados ao desenvolvimento de recursos em águas profundas. A participação da Subsea7 na ROG.e 2026 será realizada entre os dias 21 e 23 de setembro, com a presença da companhia em painéis e sessões técnicas voltados à inovação, à competitividade e ao desenvolvimento da indústria offshore brasileira.

https://splash247.com/transito-launches-.text: Dutch chartering company Transito has launched a new service combining sea freight and inland shipping under one contract, as low water levels and other disruptions put more pressure on cargo movements between European seaports and the hinterland. The service, named Total Freight, covers the sea voyage, port handling, transhipment and onward transport by inland vessel. Shippers receive one price per tonne, one contract, and one invoice for the entire movement. Within an agreed range, Transito also takes waiting time between the seagoing vessel and the inland vessel on its own account. When low water, port congestion, vessel delays, or missing documentation disrupt the connection between the sea and inland legs, the cargo owner may bear the resulting waiting time. “A seagoing vessel waits for an inland vessel, an inland vessel waits at the quay, and the terminal waits for paperwork. Those days end up with the cargo owner. We arrange both vessels ourselves, so if one runs late, we move the other with it,” said Bas Weinberg of Transito. Total Freight targets industrial buyers and mid-sized traders without an in-house freight department, particularly companies shipping agribulk, building materials, fertilisers, minerals, recycling cargo, and project cargo.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/j.text: In a rare example of maritime cooperation among unlikely participants, three North Korean seafarers were rescued from their sinking boat while a search is ongoing for a fourth missing individual. South Korea helped to organize the search, asking for the assistance of Japan and Russia. As with anything involving North Korea, the details are scarce. The reports indicate that a North Korean cargo ship was towing a smaller boat which got into trouble in international waters approximately 65 miles southwest of Japan’s Oki islands and 125 miles from Pohang City, Korea. The South Korean Navy reported the incident, saying that four people were believed to have been aboard the boat. The South Korean Coast Guard dispatched two patrol boats and an aircraft, aided by naval ships. It also alerted the fishing community. At the same time, the East Sea Region of the South Korean Coast Guard requested search and rescue cooperation from Japan and Russia’s rescue authorities. The regional office of the Japan Coast Guard reported that it joined the search with patrol vessels and aircraft. The Japan Coast Guard located three of the missing people on Thursday, September 17. It reports that two of the victims were conscious when recovered, but the third was not. A fourth person remains missing, and the search was continuing. The Acting Chief of the East Sea Korea Coast Guard, Lee Jong-wook, told reporters that they had acted swiftly. He said they responded “in accordance with international and humanitarian principles that prioritize saving lives.”

https://maritime-executive.com/article/p.text: Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected India’s version of the incident on Wednesday when the two nations’ warships made contact at sea and accused India of “belligerent action.” Each nation has issued strong protests to the other while analysts fear it represents a rising of tensions among the two nuclear nations that fought a little over a year ago. Pakistan asserts that the collision between its warship and the Indian vessels took place in Pakistan’s EEZ while India only referred to the area as international waters. Unconfirmed reports in the media said the incident took place approximately 220 km (approximately 118 nautical miles) east of the Oman coast in the North Arabian Sea. The Ministry said it had lodged a strong protest “over a highly provocative and unacceptable action by a vessel of the Indian Navy.” It went on to say it “strongly rejects this belligerent Indian action,” while calling for the international community to urge India to “abandon its belligerent posture.” Pakistan said the international community should call on India to “refrain from irresponsible actions that could further destabilize South Asia.” Pakistan asserts the incident took place during its biennial SEASPARK-26 exercise. It asserts the Indian vessel carried out “aggressive maneuvers in dangerously close proximity,” resulting in the two vessels making contact. Reports in the media say the Indian vessel maneuvered, causing the incident, while in the Indian version the Pakistani ship was seen approaching at a fast speed and attempting to maneuver. The only thing both sides agree on is that the incident was a violation of a 1991 agreement that called for vessels from the two nations to remain at least three nautical miles apart at all times. Pakistani officials told the media that the Indian vessel, identified as the guided-missile destroyer INS Kolkata, had “repeatedly tried to enter the exercise area since Pakistan launched the training on September 7.

https://g1.globo.com/rj/rio-de-janeiro/n.text: A recém-nascida morreu nesta quinta-feira (17) por infecção, 4 dias após sua mãe falecer no Rio de Janeiro. A Polícia Civil investiga suspeita de negligência no parto. Jéssica deu entrada no Hospital da Mulher Mariska Ribeiro no dia 8 de setembro para o parto normal de sua filha. A bebê nasceu saudável. Após o parto, Jéssica sentiu fortes dores abdominais, mas recebeu alta médica. Ela piorou, foi internada novamente, passou por cirurgia e morreu no domingo (13). O marido de Jéssica questiona a falta de exames de imagem na unidade. O hospital afirma que a paciente passou por todas as avaliações pós-parto indicadas.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/a.text: A number of geospatial intelligence firms have tracked the departure of a Russian convoy from the Baltiysk naval base in the Kaliningrad, and its subsequent movement through the Strait of Gibraltar to the port of Tobruk in Eastern Libya. The Maritime Executive reported the movement of the convoy, the Ropucha Class Aleksandr Shabalin (L110), escorting the cargo vessels Anastasiia (IMO 9349291) and Yuriy Arshenevskiy (IMO 8406705) cruising between Sicily and Tunisia on September 10. Both the cargo vessels are sanctioned and have well-established histories of moving military cargos. Ural trucks and armored vehicles were seen on the quayside in Baltiysk and being loaded onto the two cargo vessels, and as a landing ship the Aleksandr Shabalin would have had a capacity to transport heavy armored vehicles as well. Just who the final end-users of this military equipment will be is uncertain. It could be Libyan National Army forces led by US citizen (lately a resident of Virginia) Field Marshall Khalifa Haftar, whose faction controls Tobruk and Eastern Libya, facing off against the Islamist-inclined recognized government based in the capital Tripoli, whose principal foreign backer is Turkey. The equipment might be destined instead for the rebel Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, who are backed by the Emirati government and supplied through southeast Libya and from eastern Chad. Or the equipment could be for Russia’s Africa Corps, who are currently supporting government forces in six Central African countries on a mercenary basis, albeit for the strategic benefit of Russia. This Russian activity, in particular its maritime element, is an obvious target for Ukraine, which seeks to harry and weaken Russia wherever it can. A recent report in the Libyan Observer denied reports that the Ukraine is maintaining a drone detachment at the Misrata Air Base, where Turkey also has a presence, but both CNN and French broadcaster RFI have substantiated the presence by interviewing Ukrainian members of the detachment. The Ukrainian SBU detachment in Misrata, which in effect is a semi-independent city state loosely aligned with the government in Tripoli, would most likely have been responsible for attacks on Russian and dark fleet shipping in the Mediterranean. These Ukrainian-acknowledged attacks have included that on the Omani-flagged dark fleet Aframax Qendil (IMO 9310525) in December last year, and on the Russian military cargo vessel Lady Mariia (IMO 9220641), more recently on September 7. These two attacks both employed bomb-dropping hexacopter drones, at too great a range to be launched and controlled directly from Misrata. The Ukrainian Volyniaka hexacopter for example has a range of about 15nm, so would need to be launched from a nearby vessel based out of Misrata.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/t.text: A Turkish shipowner, along with the family of a crewmember who was killed in a Ukrainian attack and the surviving crewmembers, took the unusual step of filing a war crimes complaint. According to Turkey Today, the filing was made in The Hague with the International Criminal Court, an intergovernmental organization established in 2002 to investigate and potentially prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. The filing relates to the July 22 attack on the Turkish-flagged bulker Reyhan Sari (36,075 dwt), which was struck in the Black Sea near the Russian port of Novorossiysk. According to the complaint, seen by the Turkish media outlet Haber Denzde, a 54-year-old sailor working in the engine room, Savas Cakar, was killed. Several others among the 15 crewmembers were also injured in the attack. The ship, however, was able to proceed to Turkey. The vessel, built in 2011, had been acquired by the Turkish company T&O Denizcilik in 2023. They report the ship had loaded coal in the Russian port of Taman and was transporting the cargo to Turkey when it was struck by an aerial drone. They are alleging that Ukraine deliberately struck the ship specifically in the accommodation area with the intent to kill civilians. Furthermore, the complaint alleges that the attack constitutes crimes against humanity and also asserts that illegal cluster munitions were used with armor-piercing capabilities. The court has an established process for handling these types of complaints. Prosecutors will examine the filing and the supporting evidence to determine if there is enough information to proceed. They will also consider if the alleged crimes meet the defined thresholds of the court’s mandate and if the complaint falls within the jurisdiction of the court. If it meets all these requirements, prosecutors would decide if they want to begin a formal investigation and if there is sufficient evidence of the crimes. They could then elect to move it forward to judicial proceedings at the court based in the Hague. Turkey has been calling for a de-escalation of hostilities and specifically the targeting of merchant ships by both Russia and Ukraine. It has also put forward several proposals for a truce to protect Black Sea shipping. While the previous efforts have not been accepted, a Turkish official told the French AFP news agency that they have sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine that would end attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/f.text: FFrance’s fishermen have taken to the waters in a protest over fuel prices that was reported to be growing and disrupting Mediterranean ferry service. Ports from Sète to Nice have been blocked while the fishermen demanded action on fuel and other financial promises from the government. One fisherman told the French AFP news agency the price of diesel fuel was the “last straw.” Another fisherman also cited the increased European regulations and the lack of government action. As a result, they took to their small boats and began blocking harbors at the beginning of the week. At Nice, reports said a ferry was being forced to wait offshore, while at Sète, Corsica Ferries announced service was canceled for the Tuesday night and Wednesday sailings. Corsica Ferries said it was unable to complete the crossing from L’Ile-Rousse and had been forced to cancel service. It was offering passengers alternatives to Nice and Toulon. A spokesperson told the media, “As for what happens next, we have no news.” The protesters were also setting tires on fire and placing signs showing their dissatisfaction to block the entrances to the ports. They also targeted the oil depot at Fos-sur-Mer, near Sète. The government has been blaming the U.S. war with Iran for the rising fuel prices. AFP reports the price of diesel fuel has skyrocketed to an all-time high in France, running between approximately $10 and $12 per gallon. The fishermen have been complaining for months about the financial strain while saying theirs was a dying way of life. The mayor of Nice, Eric Ciotti, visited the fishermen and told the media that they are an “endangered species” in the Mediterranean.

https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: Extended U.S. Navy deployments have periodically drawn public attention to what accumulated months at sea can do to a crew. Reporting on one recent deployment — an aircraft carrier at sea for more than eight months with no announced return date — described sailors reaching a breaking point under the sustained strain of the assignment, and a family member who received a single call from the ship's family-support liaison after a serious incident, then heard nothing further from the Navy in the weeks that followed. The sailor involved, described as repeatedly overextended and burned out, worried the incident might end a career built over more than a decade. The specific episode will fade from the news cycle; the condition behind it will not. It is a familiar one to anyone who has worked in, or around, the cruise industry: what happens in workplaces where people cannot leave the room and cannot leave the people in it. A warship makes headlines because it's a warship. But the underlying condition — thousands of people living where they work, for months at a time, inside a hierarchy that also shapes how and whether they can ask for help — describes a cruise ship as accurately as it describes an aircraft carrier. Researchers studying isolated, confined and extreme — or ICE — environments offer a useful framework for the problem. NASA treats isolation and confinement as one of the five major hazards of human spaceflight, and Antarctic research stations are routinely used as ICE analogues in that literature. Cruise ships are not spacecraft or Antarctic stations. But they share one feature that matters greatly for workplace conflict: work and life occur inside the same bounded social system for extended periods. The cruise industry shares several of the characteristics that ICE research identifies as significant — multinational crews working across language and cultural lines, pronounced rank and departmental hierarchy, shared accommodation, contracts running months at a time, hospitality's own layer of emotional labor on top of it all, and a workforce in which employees may perceive supervisors and department heads as influential to future assignments or contract renewal. Ordinary friction — a difficult supervisor, a conflict with a cabin mate, an unresolved grievance — doesn't dissipate the way it does for someone who goes home at the end of a shift. It accumulates. Cruise-specific research exists, although thinner than the broader maritime literature. https://maritime-executive.com/article/d.text: Overnight Wednesday, Russian and Ukrainian forces traded drone strikes against each others' shipping in the Black Sea. On one Ukraine-bound vessel, the master was killed and at least three crewmembers were injured when a Russian drone damaged the deck and superstrucure. It is the latest in a long series of Russian strikes on shipping near Odesa. Drone operators on both sides of the conflict preferentially target the superstructure and the bridge: wheelhouse windows are vulnerable to blast damage or penetration, it is easy to hit, and a successful strike is likely to disable the vessel. As a manned space, a strike on the bridge is also likely to cause casualties. Video footage released by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday showed that Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Force continues to aim for the bridge deck when targeting Russia-linked vessels; the imagery shows three examples of this practice from Wednesday's operations. "There have . . . been good results in the Black Sea. Every day, we respond to aggression. Russia must choose peace," Zelensky said, congratulating Ukraine's intelligence services and drone forces. I thank our warriors, who make Russia feel the war every day. Last night, in a joint operation by the Security Service of Ukraine, the Unmanned Systems Forces, the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine, and the Foreign Intelligence Service, the Yaroslavl oil refinery was hit. The… pic.twitter.com/lQM7MrpBA3 The IMO is growing concerned at a widening pattern of attacks on shipping, not just in the Black Sea, but also in the Red Sea, Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Gulf. At various times and locations in the past year, at least five militaries or organized groups have used kinetic antiship strikes at scale as a means to advance their broader strategic objectives. In a recent address at IMO, Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez called on member states to apply pressure where possible to push back against attacks on civilian shipping.

https://g1.globo.com/rj/rio-de-janeiro/e.text: O candidato ao governo do Rio Eduardo Paes (PSD) propôs nesta quinta-feira (17) a atuação conjunta da Polícia Militar com forças municipais contra roubos e furtos. https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/20.text: O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou nesta quinta-feira (17) que os casos envolvendo os ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça deveriam ser analisados conjuntamente pela Corte. "Se quiser fazer justiça na votação, tem que colocar todo mundo no mesmo dia. Vamos saber se telefonema é verdade, se [Luiz] Fux está envolvido, se [André] Mendonça está envolvido, se o presidente do TSE [Tribunal Superior Eleitoral] está envolvido. O que não pode é julgar uma pessoa antes das eleições e o restante depois. Todo mundo agora já tem material, é só tornar público", declarou. Lula também disse que a Suprema Corte "tem que ser respeitada" e afirmou que os fatos em apuração devem ser esclarecidos de forma transparente. A declaração, durante entrevista à rádio Itatiaia, foi feita ao comentar os desdobramentos das investigações relacionadas ao Banco Master e o debate sobre a conduta dos dois magistrados ( leia mais abaixo ).

O presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, retirou de pauta nesta quinta-feira (17) o julgamento de André Mendonça no caso Banco Master. A sessão ocorreria em 23 de setembro. A decisão ocorreu após embates no tribunal nesta quarta-feira (15). A corte debatia investigações envolvendo Alexandre de Moraes, suspensas por pedido de vista de Flávio Dino. No despacho, Fachin justificou que há discussões pendentes com impacto no caso. Entre elas estão a tramitação conjunta de processos e questionamentos sobre a relatoria das ações. O julgamento foi adiado para uma data futura indefinida. Juristas avaliavam ser difícil manter a data de 23 de setembro sem resolver as divergências da corte. Fachin também cancelou uma sessão extraordinária do plenário nesta quinta-feira (17). A medida ocorreu após novos atritos públicos entre Gilmar Mendes e André Mendonça.

Por Alexandro Martello , Kellen Barreto , Márcio Falcão , Luiz Felipe Barbiéri , g1 e TV Globo — Brasília O governo federal anunciou nesta quinta-feira (17) um reajuste de 15,04% no Bolsa Família. A gestão afirma que a reposição inflacionária não viola a lei eleitoral. O valor mínimo do benefício subirá de R$ 600 para R$ 691 a partir de outubro. O anúncio ocorre em meio à campanha eleitoral de 2026. Segundo a AGU e especialistas, a correção do Bolsa Família pela inflação está fora do alcance de proibições eleitorais. O ministro Bruno Moretti informou que o reajuste custará R$ 5,8 bilhões neste ano. Ele garantiu que há espaço fiscal seguro para custear a medida.

https://www.tecnologistica.com.br/notici.text: A Águia Sistemas , apresentou soluções para armazéns automatizados durante a INTRA-LOG Expo South America 2026 , que acontece de 15 a 17 de setembro, no Expo Center Norte, em São Paulo (SP). Visitantes do evento puderam ver em ação robôs de triagem com as soluções T-Sort e 3D Sort, desenvolvidas pela Libiao Robotics e disponibilizadas no Brasil pela Águia. Os equipamentos realizam a classificação de pedidos em operações de alto volume, cenário típico de centros de distribuição de e-commerce e varejo. O T-Sort é um sistema flexível e modular que alcança 99,9% de precisão, separa até 10.000 destinos e tem implantação em 1 a 2 semanas, de acordo com a fabricante Libiao. Já o 3D Sorting System expande a classificação para o espaço tridimensional, reduzindo em até um terço o espaço necessário e oferecendo rápida instalação. De acordo com a Águia, o mercado de intralogística passa por uma transformação, impulsionada pela necessidade das empresas de aumentar produtividade, aproveitar melhor os espaços de armazenagem e responder a operações cada vez mais complexas. "Os desafios de armazenagem e movimentação mudaram. Hoje, as empresas precisam pensar não apenas em capacidade, mas em produtividade, flexibilidade e possibilidade de expansão. A tecnologia precisa estar conectada à realidade de cada operação e gerar resultado de forma sustentável", afirma Rogério Scheffer, diretor-presidente da Águia Sistemas . Além de robôs de triagem, a Águia trouxe para a feira soluções robóticas de movimentação de paletes na categoria 4-Way Shuttle, como o SkyCube, da Geek+, que serão detalhadas em breve. A Geek+ também oferece robôs AMR para movimentação de estantes, com o conceito Goods-to-Person. A empresa apresenta ainda soluções que compõem o restante do fluxo interno. Na armazenagem, estruturas como porta-paletes, autoportante, dinâmico e mezaninos, que ampliam a capacidade de estocagem sem exigir novas áreas. Na separação de pedidos, sistemas de flow rack e pick to light, que reduzem deslocamento e erro na operação manual. E, na armazenagem robotizada, o AirRob, que opera na movimentação de caixas com os itens, dentro das próprias estruturas e pode ser implantado em racks já existentes.

A Ativa Logística inaugurou uma filial em Varginha (MG) , ampliando para seis o número de unidades próprias da empresa no estado. Especializada em operações para os segmentos de saúde, beleza e bem-estar, a companhia investiu em uma estrutura de quase 4 mil m² de área construída , com dez docas , ambientes de armazenagem e frota equipada para o controle de temperatura. A unidade é voltada ao transporte, armazenagem e distribuição de medicamentos, correlatos e produtos de beleza. Localizada no Distrito Industrial Cláudio Galvão Nogueira, a filial conta com veículos com baús isotérmicos e refrigerados e áreas climatizadas no complexo. Segundo a empresa, as operações seguem os requisitos da Anvisa para o manuseio e a movimentação de produtos regulados. A nova unidade deverá ter como principal foco o mercado farmacêutico. De acordo com Flávio Damásio, gerente regional da Ativa Logística em Minas Gerais, a expectativa é que 80% das operações sejam destinadas ao canal farmacêutico e 20% a itens de beleza e correlatos. “O planejamento inicial é alcançar um fluxo de 300 mil volumes por mês nesta unidade, somando aproximadamente 1,2 milhão de volumes movimentados até o final de 2026”, afirma. A escolha de Varginha considera, segundo a companhia, a expansão da indústria de saúde e bem-estar na cidade e a infraestrutura logística da região, que conta com o Porto Seco Sul de Minas. Nos últimos anos, a chegada de empresas desses segmentos teria movimentado cerca de R$ 400 milhões em investimentos no município. Com a nova filial, a Ativa passa a contar com unidades em Montes Claros, Uberlândia, Pouso Alegre, Juiz de Fora, Belo Horizonte e Varginha. A companhia também mantém mais de 25 unidades próprias no país e 50 postos avançados em instalações de clientes e destinatários. No total, a empresa dispõe de mais de 350 mil m² de infraestrutura logística e 51 mil posições-palete, atendendo mais de 5.300 cidades. A operação conta com mais de 4 mil colaboradores e frota superior a 1.900 veículos, incluindo modelos com padrão Euro 6. A movimentação anual supera 150 milhões de volumes, equivalentes a mais de 900 mil toneladas.

A Brookfield concluiu a aquisição de um portfólio de oito ativos logísticos da Marq Logistics , pertencentes a fundos imobiliários da Ares, em uma transação de aproximadamente R$ 1,4 bilhão . Os empreendimentos estão distribuídos entre São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro e somam cerca de 560 mil m² de área bruta locável (ABL) . A operação também inclui 128 mil m² de potencial construtivo no Rio de Janeiro e amplia em aproximadamente 55% o portfólio logístico da Brookfield no país. São quatro empreendimentos em cada estado. Em São Paulo, foram adquiridos os ativos Imigrantes, Vinhedo, Dutra I e Dutra II. No Rio de Janeiro, o portfólio inclui Itatiaia, Campo Grande, Pavuna e Irajá. Majoritariamente formados por galpões logísticos Classe A, os empreendimentos apresentam aproximadamente 80% de ocupação e uma base diversificada de locatários. Segundo a Brookfield, a estratégia para os ativos inclui aumento da ocupação e gestão ativa dos empreendimentos. “O mercado logístico brasileiro segue aquecido, com forte demanda por ativos de alta qualidade. Nosso portfólio atual opera com 99% de ocupação, e vemos nos ativos adquiridos uma oportunidade relevante de criação de valor por meio do aumento da ocupação e da gestão ativa dos empreendimentos”, afirma Roberto Perroni, Chair da Brookfield no Brasil e Managing Partner responsável pelos investimentos em Real Estate no país. A aquisição também marca a entrada da Brookfield no segmento logístico no Rio de Janeiro. Segundo Perroni, a operação complementa os investimentos da companhia em edifícios corporativos e residenciais multifamily no estado e amplia a oferta de infraestrutura de distribuição próxima aos principais centros de consumo. Com a conclusão da transação, o portfólio logístico da Brookfield no Brasil passa a reunir 22 ativos e cerca de 1,9 milhão de m² de ABL, considerando empreendimentos em operação e em desenvolvimento.

A especialista em sistemas de armazenagem intralogística ISMA comemora 56 anos de atividade durante um dos maiores ciclos de investimento de sua história. Desde 2022, a companhia já aplicou mais de R$ 50 milhões na modernização de sua unidade industrial em Mogi Mirim (SP). Este ano, a empresa está somando mais R$ 5 milhões na fábrica, para melhorar sua infraestrutura de movimentação interna, implantar uma nova linha de pintura e incorporar novos robôs de solda. Os novos equipamentos incluem uma linha automática de pintura capaz de processar estruturas de até 14 metros , uma linha adicional dedicada à produção de peças de geometrias diversas, perfiladeiras para a fabricação de colunas e longarinas, robôs de solda e a modernização da linha de manufatura de porta-paletes e ações de retrofit na própria planta. A companhia anuncia estar trabalhatando também no desenvolvimento de novos produtos, que devem demandar investimentos adicionais nos próximos anos. Aumento de capacidade produtiva foca em projetos de armazenagem de alta densidade De acordo com a ISMA, os investimentos ocorrem em um momento de aumento da complexidade dos projetos de armazenagem no país, com empresas buscando maior verticalização, alta densidade, retrofit, melhor aproveitamento dos espaços e estruturas preparadas para integração com diferentes níveis de automação. Atualmente, a fábrica possui capacidade produtiva de aproximadamente 2,5 mil toneladas por mês. Os novos investimentos estão sendo direcionados à estabilização dos processos e ao ganho de eficiência operacional, e permitirão ampliar a produção por meio da expansão dos turnos de trabalho, com potencial para dobrar a capacidade atualmente instalada.

https://www.marinelog.com/news/fincantie.text: Chesapeake, Va.-based Fincantieri Marine Systems (FMS) says that it has signed an agreement with Italian high-performance marine engine manufacturer Seatek S.p.A. that will see the two companies jointly assess commercial and naval marine opportunities and market Seatek propulsion systems in the United States, Canada, Central America, and South America. The memorandum of understanding establishes a joint market assessment to evaluate a potential Seatek dealer distribution and service agreement. FMS will showcase Seatek’s high-performance propulsion systems—including a 12-cylinder (1,500 bhp) mock-up and a six-cylinder inline (900 bhp) production engine—at upcoming maritime exhibitions, including the International WorkBoat Show in December and the U.S. Navy League’s annual Sea-Air-Space exhibition in April 2027. “This MOU is a first step toward pairing FMS’s North American service infrastructure with Seatek’s advanced engine technologies,” said Ryan W. Smith , CEO of Fincantieri Marine Systems. “Together, we will assess regional demand to guide potential future distribution.” “FMS offers a strong platform to introduce our technologies to naval and defense stakeholders across the Americas,” said Guglielmo Tummarello, CEO of Seatek. “Our shared goal is to support future customers with the technical expertise and service they need.”
