https://www.marinelog.com/news/corps-com.text: The Buffalo Engineer District is dredging Conneaut Harbor to maintain safe and navigable waterways that are critical to the safety and economic vitality of Conneaut Harbor and the Nation, Conneaut, Ohio, September 08, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Andre' M. Hampton) The Buffalo Engineer District has completed a $4.1 million dredging project at Conneaut Harbor on Lake Erie, removing approximately 75,000 cubic yards of sediment from the federal navigation channel. Dredging began September 1 and was completed September 10, about five days ahead of the planned schedule. The contract was awarded in June to Michigan-based Walsh Service Solutions. Crews mechanically dredged sediment from the federal navigation channel at the harbor entrance and upriver to the Canadian National docks. The material was transported to a local sediment recycling facility for beneficial use through the city of Conneaut and Conneaut Port Authority. Conneaut Harbor was last dredged in 2025, when approximately 70,000 cubic yards of material was removed. The harbor is dredged annually depending on shoaling conditions, available funding and federal navigation priorities. A deep-draft commercial harbor, Conneaut handled 3.7 million tons of cargo in 2023, according to the Corps. Iron ore accounted for approximately 95% of the total, with limestone, sand and gravel making up most of the remaining cargo.

https://gcaptain.com/imo-sounds-alarm-as.text: IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez addresses delegates at the International Maritime Organization in London. Photo: IMO The head of the International Maritime Organization is calling on governments to stop attacks on merchant shipping as conflicts increasingly spill into some of the world’s most important trade routes. IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez issued the warning Wednesday as the organization reported 80 verified attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the Middle East conflict began on February 28, killing at least 22 seafarers and injuring many others. “We are reaching a point where these conflicts are being used as a pretext to attack merchant vessels and innocent seafarers,” Dominguez told delegates at the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers in London. “Do not use these conflicts to attack innocent seafarers.” The warning extends well beyond the Strait of Hormuz. In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, the IMO said dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although the organization said precise casualty figures remain difficult to verify. Violence has also returned to the Red Sea, where four seafarers were killed in the latest Houthi attack on a merchant vessel on August 11.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/i.text: The Indonesian Navy is giving new life to Italy's first aircraft carrier, the 1985-built ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, which arrived in Jakarta on Friday to begin a career as KRI Gajah Mada. The vessel served Italy in multiple conflicts over the span of 40 years, but has been out of commission since 2024; she has been gifted to the Indonesian government and will be revived as a helicopter carrier. Garibaldi was envisioned as a cruiser-carrier, capable of combat in her own right, and was fitted with torpedo tubes and missile launchers for self-defense against surface and aerial threats. In her prime, an air wing of up to 16 AV-8B Harrier jump-jets - a design also used by the U.S. Marine Corps and the Royal Navy - provided reach. She contributed to air support during the war in Kosovo, participated in the early stages of the U.S. occupation of Afghanistan after September 11, and joined the Italian contribution to the no-fly zone mission over Libya in 2011. Garibaldi's position as the Italian Navy's flagship came to an end in 2009 with the delivery of the Cavour, a larger carrier equipped for the modern F-35B stealth fighter. An even larger helicopter carrier, the Trieste - an amphib with a well deck as well as a flight deck - delivered in 2024; with Trieste's arrival, Garibaldi retired from service. Seeing an opportunity to acquire a carrier at a favorable cost, the Indonesian Navy expressed its interest in buying Garibaldi in early 2025. After study, the Italian Navy determined that the most economical course of action would be to gift the carrier to Indonesia, thereby avoiding the expense of upkeep and an approved demolition plan. Despite political opposition, the Italian Senate signed off on the transfer, and the Indonesian government became the owner of a carrier overnight. Indonesia paid for the long-distance delivery voyage at a cost of approximately $60 million, but the vessel itself was free of charge. She departed in late August and arrived Friday, in ample time for her formal renaming and commissioning ceremony. Indonesia still has to invest in the support infrastructure and upkeep that a carrier requires. Its navy is building out a pier and other support facilities at the naval base in Ratai Bay, Sumatra. It also plans to spend significant sums on modernization and refurbishment for the vessel's long-term use. Indonesia's plan is to use the vessel as a helicopter carrier - though she could also be adapted for use as a drone carrier, taking advantage of long-range drone aircraft that Indonesia already owns, as noted by The War Zone. Disaster response is a likely mission set: This week, President Prabowo Subianto called for a large investment in the nation's helicopter fleet for that purpose.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/r.text: In a new review of federal records and port call data, Bloomberg discovered that at least a dozen foreign-flag tankers have engaged in U.S. coastwise trade without registering their activity with the Maritime Administration, as required for using the Trump administration's ongoing Jones Act waiver. Under the national-defense waiver, energy cargoes can be moved between U.S. points by foreign-flag ships. The waiver is renewable and has been extended out until November 15. It is among the longest and broadest exemptions from Jones Act in modern memory, and is strongly opposed by U.S. domestic shipping interests and by Congressional leaders. Bloomberg's review of AIS and port call data turned up at least 12 foreign ships that have operated in coastwise trade during the waiver period without notifying MARAD of their cargo and their voyage. All operated on voyages out of the Gulf Coast refining region, the hub for most of the waivered activity. Under 46 U.S.C. § 501(c), vessel owners and operators are required to report any waivered activity to MARAD within 10 days after a voyage. The reported information includes the vessel name and flag, owner and operator, ports of call, cargo carried, and an explanation of why the waivered voyage was in the interest of national defense. These reports are compiled and posted on MARAD's public website . "It’s outrageous that foreign operators are not reporting their movements under the waiver. Reporting is specifically required by law, which was emphasized in the U.S. Customs and Border Protection notice of the waiver. It begs the question of what other U.S. laws – like immigration, taxation, and labor – are not being followed by foreign vessels using the waiver," sad Jennifer Carpenter, president of the pro-Jones Act American Maritime Partnership. "It’s time for the administration to end the waiver, and it’s also time for Congress to conduct vigorous oversight of the waiver process." Supporters of the Jones Act say that the waiver is undermining the domestic-shipping business model and weakening sentiment for investing in new, made-in-America ships. Without the cabotage market created by Jones Act protection, low-wage foreign operators can compete on price with high-wage American operators in domestic U.S. trade - a situation not found in trucking, rail or aviation, only in maritime shipping.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/s.text: The Scottish government announced in Parliament that it has a new stopgap plan to keep the financially troubled Ferguson Marine shipyard in Glasgow operational and to save a workforce that was facing layoffs in the coming months. The yard, which went into receivership in 2019 and is owned by the government, is finishing its last commercial assignment and said a month ago that it would start voluntary layoffs as it begins a period of transition and seeks future work. The shipyard is the last of a long tradition of building on the Clyde and in Glasgow, but like so many yards has fallen on to hard times. The size of the facility limits its ability to compete for work, including many of the contracts to build replacement ferries for the government-owned CalMac. The yard’s troubles were further compounded by the disastrous project to build the LNG-fueled ferries Glen Sannox and Glen Rosa for CalMac. The project is years behind schedule and incurred large cost overruns. Glen Sannox finally got into service, but there are persistent reports of problems. Last week it was reported that the vessel had experienced a gas leak and that it is still operating on conventional fuel. Her sister, Glen Rosa , recently left the yard, preparing for her delivery before the end of 2026, a decade behind the originally anticipated schedule. Scotland’s Transport Secretary Stephen Flynn announced the newest plan to keep the yard going and maintain employment during this transition period. He spoke out in Parliament, reporting that the government has authorized an unspecified amount of working capital as part of a plan to build tugboats on speculation. Media reports say Flynn told the lawmakers the yard will build an unspecified number of tugboats using a prepackaged design. It is suggested the yard might partner with Damen, or another company, and then would use its design to build the tugs. The tugs would also be offered for sale, as they do not have any firm orders or buyers at this time. The plan immediately came in for a new round of political criticism. Opposition party members cited the lack of detail and noted it follows an announcement in March promising four contracts for Ferguson. The prior plan called for the yard to be given no-bid contracts to build two small ferries for CalMac and, for the government, a Marine Protection Vessel (MPV) and a Marine Research Vessel (MRV). The yard currently has no further commercial work after the delivery of Glen Rosa . In August, management said it would ask for up to 70 employees to agree to a voluntary separation from the yard, which is about a quarter or more of the workforce.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/g.text: The state-owned Deutsche Energy Terminal GmbH (DET) highlighted the return of its fourth FSRU (Floating Storage and Regasification Unit) as it gears up for increased LNG import capacity. Germany launched the FSRU program in 2022 after the Russian invasion of Ukraine to replace supplies of Russian gas, and now as the EU moves to a total ban on the importation of Russian gas. The Energos Force (94,361 dwt) docked at the end LNG terminal in the Stade-Bützfleth industrial port, near Hamburg on the Elbe River. The FSRU will have an injection capacity of up to 3.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas per year by 2027, making Stade, they said, an important component of Germany’s security of supply. It is expected to complete commissioning and begin operations by November. “As promised, the return of the regasification vessel to the Stade jetty marks the start of preparations for the terminal’s commissioning," said Dr. Peter Röttgen, CEO of DET. “The road to this point has not always been easy. Shortly after assuming responsibility for completion, we brought all necessary partners on board, who are working together with full commitment toward this common goal.” DET highlights that extensive technical and safety-related assessments, along with preparatory measures, were carried out, as well as the construction of the jetty and onshore terminal. The terminal is still being completed. While the new facility was being developed, the state-owned company sub-chartered the FSRU Energos Force —the regasification vessel designated for operation in Stade—and deployed it in Jordan. Energos Force is on the Elbe near Hamburg as the fourth FSRU managed by the state-owned company (DET) The FSRU Energos Force was built in 2021 and will operate under a long-term charter to DET. The vessel can regasify up to 500 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (MMSCFD) using steam boilers in a closed-loop system. In summer, it can ideally regasify up to 750 million standard cubic feet per day using Elbe River water in an open-loop system.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/f.text: Commanders from the Finnish and Swedish navies met on Thursday, September 17, reaching key agreements about efforts to enhance security measures in the Baltic. It came as the Finnish Border Guard completed a three-day Marsec exercise co-funded by the European Union as part of the EU Maritime Security Strategy. The commander of the Finnish Navy, Tuomas Tiilikanen, described to reporters the scope of the agreements reached with his Swedish counterparts, reports the Finnish news outlet Yle. The two countries agreed to a series of steps and sharing of resources. Among the immediate efforts, Sweden will deploy one of its Visby-class maritime corvettes into the Gulf of Finland, and it will operate under the command of the Finnish Defence Forces. The commanders said that would permit Finland to concentrate its navy in the eastern Gulf of Finland, where they perceive the greatest threat, including from drones. They are also exploring jointly procuring unmanned surveillance vessels that would be used for monitoring, intelligence, and inspections. Yle reports Tiilikanen said Finland and Sweden would temporarily share resources so that both nations could benefit from the vessels, which he described as surface drones that look like a sailboat. He said the first patrols could start before the end of the year. The forces practiced the boarding and seizure of a vessel suspected of dragging its anchor using the icebreaker Polaris as the target (Finnish Border Guard) Thursday was the third and final day of the Marsec EU26 exercise. It was the third such exercise but the first staged in the Baltic. The Finnish Border Guard was leading key parts of the program, which involved the Helsinki Police Department, Finnish defense forces, and the Coast Guard. There were also international observers, participation from the Polish Border Guard that included a vessel from Poland, and the French Navy joining in the preparatory training.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/a.text: More than 120 people disappeared when the lost ferry Virgo Transport 8 capsized on September 13 in the Java Sea, and an investigation into the circumstances of the casualty is well under way. Early lines of inquiry include a review of its registration status: the ship had been flagged into the domestic Indonesian fleet very recently, and was of an advanced age for approval for the country's coastwise ferry routes. Virgo Transport 8 (IMO 8625179) was built in 1987 and served in Japanese trade under a previous name. Before-and-after photos provided by VesselFinder show that she underwent significant hull modifications on the starboard side when she transferred to Indonesian service, including the addition of two side-mounted ro/ro ramps near the bow and the stern. Deeply indented hull cutaways allowed for installation of two more ro/ro ramps (Courtesy VesselFinder ) Indonesia's ministry of trade used to have a standing regulation that restricted importation of passenger vessels to hulls that were 15 years of age or less, lawmaker Sofwan Dedy Ardyanto noted in a social media post this week. Virgo Transport 8 was more than twice as old as this limit - but the limit might not have applied by the time she arrived. The strict age regulation took effect in 2021 but was superseded by a new, looser set of rules in March 2024. Based on public PSC records, Virgo Transport 8 took on her current name in June 2025 and entered the Indonesian flag registry in March 2026, well after the local regulations changed. Ardyanto encouraged the authorities to determine whether the rules were followed at the time that the vessel was brought into the country. As a practical matter, it is not yet known if age played any role in the casualty, officials told Antara. Early reports indicate that the vessel was hit by a large wave and capsized.

https://g1.globo.com/politica/noticia/20.text: O candidato à Presidência Renan Santos (Missão) entrou com uma representação no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) contra o reajuste do Bolsa Família anunciado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nesta quinta-feira (15) . Mais cedo, o ministro André Mendonça rejeitou uma ação em que o deputado federal e candidato à reeleição Zé Trovão (PL-SC) , aliado do senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), questionava o reajuste. Mendonça, sorteado relator do caso no TSE, mencionou decisões anteriores segundo as quais um candidato a deputado federal não tem legitimidade para apresentar uma ação contra um candidato à Presidência da República, uma vez que os dois cargos são disputados em circunscrições eleitorais diferentes.

https://petronoticias.com.br/petrobras-a.text: Novos movimentos da Petrobrás no continente africano. A empresa assinou nesta quinta-feira (17) Contratos de Partilha de Produção (PSCs) com a República da Costa do Marfim e a PETROCI Holding para oito blocos exploratórios offshore no país africano. A cerimônia ocorreu em Abidjan, capital econômica e sede do governo marfinense, e contou com a participação da diretora executiva de Exploração e Produção da Petrobrás, Sylvia Anjos. Os contratos abrangem os blocos CI-513, CI-600, CI-601, CI-602, CI-603, CI-605, CI-701 e CI-702. A Petrobrás terá uma participação de 90% nos ativos, por meio de sua subsidiária Petrobras Netherlands B.V, e será responsável pela operação. A estatal local PETROCI Holding deterá os 10% restantes. “ Com essa aquisição, a Petrobrás assume presença relevante na Costa do Marfim, país localizado numa região de alto potencial exploratório, com características geológicas semelhantes às de nossas bacias sedimentares. Vamos aplicar nesses blocos nossa experiência e capacidade técnica e estamos confiantes de que poderemos, com elas, descortinar todas as possibilidades que acreditamos existir na margem atlântica africana ”, afirmou a presidente da Petrobras, Magda Chambriard. A entrada nos blocos marfinenses está alinhada à estratégia da Petrobras de recompor suas reservas de petróleo e gás por meio da exploração de novas fronteiras, tanto no Brasil quanto no exterior, conforme estabelecido em seu Plano de Negócios. Segundo a companhia, a avaliação de novas oportunidades busca diversificar o portfólio exploratório da companhia, promovendo a geração de valor e a sustentabilidade de longo prazo de seus negócios. © 2026 Petronotícias. https://maritime-executive.com/article/t.text: The Turkish government has formulated a draft peace plan that proposes to bring an end to the Russian and Ukrainian maritime strikes in the Black Sea - and relieve the pressure on Turkish shipping interests. A Turkish diplomat told AFP that Ankara has forwarded the draft MOU to Moscow and Kyiv for consideration; Wednesday's intense strikes suggest that the two sides have not yet adopted the recommendation. Russia has attacked civilian shipping on and off throughout the war, with the exception of a temporary and partial maritime ceasefire for bulkers carrying Ukrainian grain (the Black Sea Grain Initiative, or "grain corridor"). That Turkish-brokered deal lasted from late 2022 through mid-2023, when Russia unilaterally withdrew from the agreement. Ukraine's mass attacks on Russian-linked civilian vessels are a new development beginning this year, enabled by its "middle strike" drone program and its growing willingness to strike industrial and commercial targets. Turkish shipping companies are involved in both Russian and Ukrainian trade routes, and Turkish ships and seafarers have suffered disproportionately from the escalating attacks from both sides. In early August, Ankara called for a pause on strikes on merchant vessels in the Black Sea, but the proposal did not gain traction amidst ongoing hostilities. The new Turkish draft MOU has something to offer to both Russia and Ukraine: an expanded grain corridor, building off the structure of the initial 2022 maritime ceasefire for bulkers. This version would provide safe passage up the western side of the Black Sea, like last time; in addition, it would have a safety corridor for Russian shipping along the southern and eastern edges. This would include a designated route through Turkish and Georgian territorial seas, the diplomat told AFP. The independent Turkish Agricultural Diplomacy Group (TTDG) has come up with a more expansive proposal, extending beyond a navigation corridor. It would include a ban on attacks on grain silos and terminals, which are priority targets for Russian long-range strikes; a safe-navigation guarantee for ships carrying agricultural cargoes, enabled with a ship registration and verification program; and a strong Turkish coordinating role for the program, including government-backed war risk insurance for participating vessels.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Asset Control has identified and sanctioned an Iranian bitcoin exchange linked to the "Hormuz Safe Marine Services Authority," a front company that enables the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' fee-for-transit scheme for the Strait of Hormuz. In March, just weeks after the U.S.-Israeli strikes began, Iranian forces began an informal practice of charging safe-passage fees for the Strait of Hormuz at a rumored rate of up to $2 million per transit. This was later formalized as an "insurance" fee payment, handled by "Hormuz Safe" and the similar "Persian Gulf Marine Insurance Company." Both of these organizations were sanctioned by OFAC in July for facilitating the IRGC's finances. "Hormuz Safe generates revenue on behalf of the IRGC in an attempt to give the regime tighter control over shipping activity," warned the Treasury at the time. HormuzSafe advertises itself as a modern "digital insurance" company, purporting to offer legitimate services for transits through the strait - for example, salvage towing in the event of an emergency. It offers owners the opportunity to "sail through with complete confidence" with a "99.9 percent safe transit rate." It accepted payments in Bitcoin, various dollar-linked stablecoins, credit cards and wire transfers. In a follow-up action announced Thursday, the Treasury said that it was also sanctioning BitBank, a cryptocurrency handling service used by HormuzSafe to process payments. BitBank is part of the ecosystem of financial-services companies tied to Babak Zanjani, a regime insider who was sentenced to death in 2016 for stealing from the National Iranian Oil Company. He was later released and allowed to build front companies and money-laundering tools to move funds for the regime, according to the Treasury. Per OFAC, "Zanjani’s enterprises have served as both public?facing commercial ventures and covert financial platforms enabling sanctions evasion and support to Iranian state?linked entities." One such Zanjani enterprise, the agency says, is BitBank. He has personally promoted it on social media, giving it a public face as a currency exchange. In private, according to OFAC, BitBank moved hundreds of millions of dollars in Bitcoin to the IRGC at Zanjani's instruction.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543076-oi.text: Oil prices fell 2% on Friday, extending losses for a third straight session as easing concerns over Saudi supply disruptions outweighed anxiety about a widening of conflict across the Middle East. Brent crude futures LCOc1 fell by $2.14, or 2%, to $102.68 a barrel by 0806 GMT. U.S. West Texas Intermediate CLc1 futures fell $1.83, or 1.8%, to $100.08. Immediate concerns over supply tightness have been eased by a combination of Saudi Arabia loading more crude via Oman, a build in oil product inventories in the U.S., Singapore and Europe, plus increased fuel exports from China, said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga. "While continuous pre-weekend profit-taking cannot be ruled out, the current fundamental outlook would not justify a prolonged fall below $100 (a barrel) basis Brent," Varga added. Markets largely shrugged off concerns even as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis exchanged fresh strikes across their border on Thursday, expanding the Middle East war front. Prices climbed to close to four-month highs earlier in the week after sources said crude loadings at Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export hub of Yanbu had been suspended and Riyadh cancelled some deliveries to Europe after its East-West pipeline was damaged in an attack last week.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543077-in.text: INEOS Energy has started commercial operations at the Greensand project in the Danish North Sea, opening what it describes as the European Union's first full-scale carbon dioxide storage site, with initial capacity of up to 400,000 tonnes per year. Denmark's King Frederik X officially opened the facility on September 18 at the Port of Esbjerg. The project is led by INEOS Energy alongside Harbour Energy and the Danish North Sea Fund, or Nordsøfonden. Greensand is designed to scale up to between 4 million and 8 million tonnes of CO2 storage annually as demand grows. In the first commercial phase, CO2 will come primarily from Danish biomethane plants. After capture, the CO2 is liquefied and transported by truck to a dedicated terminal at the Port of Esbjerg before being shipped offshore aboard Carbon Destroyer 1, described as the EU's first purpose-built CO2 carrier. The CO2 is injected for permanent storage into the depleted Nini West oil reservoir, about 250 kilometers offshore and approximately 1,800 meters beneath the seabed. “For years, CCS in Europe has been defined by plans, targets and ambitions. Today, Greensand brings the EU’s first full-scale CO2 storage site and value chain into operation. It provides a foundation on which future Carbon Capture projects across Europe can now build,” said David Bucknall, INEOS Energy’s CEO.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543075-ap.text: Apollo Global Management is exploring strategic options for Energos Infrastructure, in a deal that could value the floating liquefied natural gas infrastructure provider at more than $3 billion, people familiar with the matter said. The investment giant has been holding talks in recent weeks with prospective bidders, communicating it would be open to either a full or partial sale of Energos, the sources said. XRG, the international investment arm of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, is among the potential bidders, with an offer that would see it take a stake of up to 50% in Energos, the sources said. The sources cautioned that no deal involving Energos was a possible outcome, and spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations. Apollo and XRG declined to comment. Energos did not respond to a comment request. Floating LNG infrastructure allows natural gas to be imported for power generation and other commercial uses without the need for large-scale onshore facilities, which can be costly to build, take years to construct, and require significant amounts of land. Stamford, Connecticut-based Energos operates 13 floating LNG vessels, including nine which allow for the storage and regasification of LNG, two storage units, and two LNG carriers. Its assets are currently deployed globally under long-term commercial arrangements, including in Brazil, Egypt, Indonesia, Mexico and the Netherlands, according to its website.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543073-in.text: Indonesia has awarded six oil and gas working areas to companies including Eni and Sinopec and opened a second 2026 tender round covering eight more areas as it seeks to expand upstream exploration. Eni Indonesia Limited was selected for the Sapukala working area, where its initial three-year program includes geological and geophysical studies and the acquisition and processing of 1,500 square kilometers of 3D seismic data. Sinopec International Energy Investment (HK) Holdings Limited won Bengara II, with a program covering three geological and geophysical study packages, 100 square kilometers of 3D seismic and an exploration well. PT Nations Petroleum was selected for Natuna D-Alpha, where planned work includes 591 square kilometers of 3D seismic, an appraisal well and an exploration well, alongside integrated carbon dioxide studies, engineering and other technical work. PT Timur Hijau Investama won both Pesut Mahakam and Puri. Its program includes 235.1 square kilometers of 3D seismic at Pesut Mahakam and 200 kilometers of 2D seismic at Puri. Cinda Energy (Hong Kong) Limited was selected for Rupat, where the initial program includes geological and geophysical studies and an exploration well. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources simultaneously opened the Phase II 2026 tender covering Jago, Mahesa, Rafflesia, Belibis, Talu, Manta, Palu and South Leti.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543071-os.text: Osaka Gas has agreed to acquire a 5% interest in the Browse gas project offshore Western Australia from BP Developments Australia, adding an expected 550,000 tonnes per year of LNG to its procurement portfolio. The Japanese company entered into a sale and purchase agreement through Osaka Gas Browse, an investee of its wholly owned subsidiary Osaka Gas Australia. Osaka Gas Australia and the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security plan to jointly invest in Osaka Gas Browse. Completion of the acquisition remains subject to regulatory approvals, consent from Browse Joint Venture partners and other conditions. The acquired interest covers the Brecknock, Calliance and Torosa gas fields in the Browse Basin, where the project is currently at the pre-front-end engineering and design stage. The project is envisaged to produce about 11 million tonnes of LNG annually using existing liquefaction facilities owned by the North West Shelf Joint Venture. Osaka Gas Browse's 5% interest is expected to provide about 550,000 tonnes per year. The development concept also includes carbon capture and storage to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, while part of the produced gas is planned to be supplied to Australia's domestic market.

https://www.rigzone.com/news/wire/hormuz.text: At least two liquefied natural gas shipments transited the Strait of Hormuz this week as producers look for ways to increase flows to a market struggling with a lack of supply and surging prices. A tanker that loaded at Qatar's Ras Laffan export plant in late August appeared in the Gulf of Oman earlier this week, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg, indicating it had passed through the contested waterway. The vessel wasn't sending a signal when it traversed Hormuz, but jamming and interference is common in the area, complicating efforts to ascertain the exact location of ships. Separately, another two LNG carriers were spotted doing ship-to-ship transfers off the coast of Oman this week, according to satellite images published by Copernicus Sentinel-2 that are only available after a delay. The trickle of shipments indicate that Persian Gulf LNG producers are trying to get more fuel through Hormuz, to provide some relief to Asian and European buyers. Exports from the gulf have been at a virtual standstill since a Qatari tanker was attacked by Iran in early July. The lack of supply has sent spot prices to the highest level in more than three years, and they are at risk of rising further as the Northern Hemisphere winter approaches. Satellite images show that there have been at least three LNG ship-to-ship transfers off the coast of Oman since the middle of August. Such transfers have become common for oil tankers over the last few months, but they are far more rare for LNG, due to the technical challenges involved in keeping the fuel super-chilled during any switch. Continued hostilities in the Middle East are pressuring LNG producers to test alternatives. Buyers in Pakistan and Bangladesh - dependent on gas via Hormuz - are closely monitoring the situation, as every shipment that gets through means they may not need to purchase a replacement from the expensive spot market.

https://safety4sea.com/ics-warns-un-secu.text: The International Chamber of Shipping has taken the industry’s concerns over maritime security directly to the UN Security Council, warning that commercial vessels and seafarers cannot become collateral damage in escalating geopolitical tensions. I nternational Chamber of Shipping (ICS) Secretary General Thomas A. Kazakos addressed the UN Security Council in New York on 17 September, highlighting the importance of freedom of navigation, the protection of maritime trade and respect for the established international legal framework governing the world’s oceans. Kazakos was invited to brief an Arria-Formula meeting convened by the Kingdom of Bahrain and chaired by Bahrain’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr Abdullatif Al Zayani. The meeting brought together UN representatives and invited guests to discuss the deteriorating maritime security environment amid heightened geopolitical tensions, with particular attention on the security situation in the Persian Gulf. For the shipping industry, the discussion comes against a backdrop in which insecurity at sea is increasingly affecting not only vessels and cargoes, but also the people who operate them. Addressing the Security Council, Kazakos put freedom of navigation at the heart of the industry’s concerns. The ability of commercial ships to navigate international waterways safely, predictably and without unnecessary impediment, is crucial to international maritime law and to the global trade system… Shipping must not be held to ransom.

https://safety4sea.com/fresh-tanker-stri.text: Tankers are being struck, vessels are being pursued and commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily suppressed as a string of maritime security incidents adds to the risks facing ships operating in the region. F our incidents reported by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) between 16 and 18 September include two tankers hit by unknown projectiles, a separate security incident in the Strait and an attempted interception of a tanker by a skiff east of Aden. Hormuz Shipping Faces Fresh Strikes as Seafarer Toll Rises The latest reports point to a security environment that remains highly unsettled for merchant shipping, with authorities continuing to investigate the incidents and UKMTO advising vessels to proceed with caution. On 17 September, a westbound tanker reported being pursued by a skiff approximately 75 nautical miles east of Aden, Yemen. The skiff attempted to intercept the vessel, according to UKMTO. Later that day, UKMTO reported another security incident in the Strait of Hormuz, 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The crew were reported safe and no environmental impact had been confirmed. In an incident reported on 18 September, a tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire onboard. The fire was extinguished and all crew were reported safe. The environmental impact remained unconfirmed. UKMTO also issued a verified, time-late report of an incident that occurred on 16 September, in which a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound from the Strait of Hormuz. Again, the crew were reported safe, although no assessment of damage or environmental impact had yet been reported.

https://safety4sea.com/better-sire-2-0-r.text: For tanker crews preparing for a SIRE 2.0 inspection, finding more problems before the inspector arrives may actually be a sign that the vessel is better prepared. T hat is one of the key findings from an analysis by Kaiko Systems, which reviewed around 1,300 SIRE 2.0 inspection reports from 25 fleets, covering inspections from late 2024 to August 2026. The analysis found that vessels achieving the strongest inspection results were not necessarily those with the fewest findings before inspection. Instead, better outcomes were associated with crews that conducted more comprehensive preparation, worked through more of the SIRE 2.0 question set and closed the issues they identified. The wider implication for tanker operators is that inspection readiness should be measured less by how few problems are found and more by how effectively the vessel’s own systems find and resolve them before the inspector arrives. Vessels that completed thorough preparation averaged 2.9 observations per inspection, compared with an industry benchmark of 5.2. The analysis found that crews raising 60 or more findings before inspection recorded 22% fewer observations than crews raising fewer findings, and 30% fewer than vessels carrying out no preparation.

https://safety4sea.com/world-first-ship-.text: The first ship-to-ship bunkering of ammonia to an ammonia-fuelled vessel has been completed in Japan, providing a practical test of one of the operations that will be essential if ammonia is to move from alternative-fuel trials into wider commercial shipping. T he timing is significant, as the industry begins testing how ammonia can be supplied to ships in practice, the IMO is simultaneously developing the safety framework needed to support its wider use. In May, the IMO Maritime Safety Committee approved interim guidelines for ships using ammonia as fuel, alongside interim training guidelines for seafarers working aboard ammonia-fuelled vessels. That work continued on 17 September with an IMO technical seminar addressing ammonia production and supply, bunkering, onboard technologies, spill response, safety and ammonia effluents. Against that backdrop, the world-first STS operation was completed on the same day at a quay within Japan Marine United Corporation’s Ariake Shipyard. Ammonia was transferred from the ammonia carrier Shoei Maru to an ammonia-fuelled medium gas carrier (AFMGC), scheduled for delivery in November 2026, ahead of the vessel’s sea trials using fuel ammonia. The operation involved NYK Line, Japan Marine United Corporation, Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd., Mitsubishi Gas Chemical Company, Inc. and Kokuka Sangyo Co., Ltd. Ammonia is increasingly being considered as a potential marine fuel because it produces no CO₂ during combustion. That gives it a potential role in efforts to reduce emissions from international shipping. But its potential as a fuel comes with a major operational challenge. Ammonia is toxic, making its handling and transfer considerably more demanding than conventional marine fuels. Developing reliable procedures for moving it between vessels will therefore be an important part of building the infrastructure needed to support ammonia-fuelled shipping.

https://safety4sea.com/lng-carrier-emiss.text: A new industry project will test whether direct, independently verified onboard CO₂ measurements can strengthen the accuracy and credibility of emissions reporting from LNG-fuelled ships. T he maritime industry has long relied on fuel consumption, standard emissions factors and engine test-bed data to calculate vessel emissions. But as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) moves towards finalising its Net-Zero Framework, a new industry project is examining whether those estimates accurately reflect emissions measured directly from ships in operation — and whether real-time monitoring could have a role in future emissions regulation. The project, led by Lloyd’s Register (LR), Seapeak, Kongsberg Maritime and Tunable will install a continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) on a newly built LNG carrier due for delivery in early 2027. The system will collect emissions data for a year, allowing the partners to compare directly measured CO₂ emissions with figures calculated from engine test-bed data and established emissions factors. Furthermore, the project will also examine how emissions vary under real operating conditions and whether independently verified measurements could play a role in future emissions reporting under IMO and EU frameworks. Lloyd’s Register, which will act as independent verifier, will assess the monitoring system’s technical performance and regulatory relevance. Seapeak’s James Cruickshank said the project could provide more detailed emissions data for operational decision-making and help identify opportunities to reduce greenhouse gas emissions across a fleet.

https://safety4sea.com/captain-killed-in.text: A merchant vessel heading for a Ukrainian port became the latest casualty of the war at sea on 17 September, when a Russian drone struck the Tanzania-flagged ship in the Black Sea, killing its captain and injuring three crew members. T he Tanzania-flagged vessel was en route to a Ukrainian port when it was attacked on 17 September, according to Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry. The ministry did not identify the destination port, while the condition of the vessel was still being assessed. The attack adds to a series of incidents involving civilian shipping in the Black Sea, where commercial vessels and port infrastructure have increasingly been exposed to the wider conflict. Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry said Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukrainian ports, port infrastructure and civilian commercial vessels, posing a threat to international shipping and logistics routes. Kyiv has called for an international response and coordinated measures to strengthen the protection of civilian shipping in the Black Sea. The latest incident comes as attacks by Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea have intensified through the spring and summer. To remind, in July, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, targeting Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov as part of efforts to tighten pressure around Russian-occupied Crimea.

https://safety4sea.com/eleven-years-late.text: A calcium hypochlorite cargo that violently decomposed aboard the Maersk Seoul in the Strait of Hormuz in 2015 has resulted in a US$13.3 million judgment against the shipper, after an eleven-year legal battle that crossed three jurisdictions. M ore than a decade after a calcium hypochlorite cargo triggered a major fire aboard the Maersk Seoul , an English Commercial Court judgment has put the spotlight on how dangerous goods were packed before they ever reached the ship, explains Clyde & Co. Handed down on 28 July 2026, the judgment in Maersk A/S v Sree Rayalaseema Hi-Strength Hypo Limited (MV Maersk Seoul) [2026] EWHC 2005 (Comm) provides the first detailed public account of the 2015 casualty and finds the Indian chemical manufacturer, referred to as the Defendant, liable for the resulting losses. The Court awarded Maersk US$13,178,280.51 for losses arising from the explosion and fire, along with a further US$168,064.48 and £16,296 for breach of an exclusive English jurisdiction clause. It also granted a permanent mandatory anti-suit injunction. Clyde & Co notes that the ruling carries a wider message for the container industry: dangerous goods compliance goes beyond declaring what is in a box. The way hazardous cargo is packed can be critical to whether it can safely withstand an ocean voyage. The Maersk Seoul, a fully cellular, gearless container vessel built in 2006, was 332 metres long, 42.2 metres wide and capable of carrying 8,411 TEU. On 19 July 2015, roughly nine hours after leaving Jebel Ali in the UAE for Jeddah, the vessel suffered a major explosion and fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tan.text: A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, causing a fire that was extinguished, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). “The CSO of a vessel has reported a tanker being hit by an unknown projectile, causing a fire onboard which has since been extinguished,” the maritime monitor said, adding that the crew were safe, although the environmental impact of the attack was “unconfirmed”. Source: AFP

https://splash247.com/iran-claims-fresh-.text: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Friday they had struck the Togo-flagged product tanker Trend after what Tehran described as an “illegal” attempt to transit Hormuz outside its approved passage system. The 7,119 dwt vessel was hit and stopped after a fire broke out onboard, according to the IRGC. The claims have not been independently verified. UK Maritime Trade Operations separately reported a security incident around 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, although it has not confirmed whether the report relates to the Trend. The International Maritime Organization has now verified 80 attacks on merchant vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz since February 28. Secretary-general of the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Thomas Kazakos, addressed the United Nations Security Council yesterday, noting: “Straits cannot become a place where commercial shipping is required to obtain permission, negotiate passage, or accept arbitrary restrictions, simply because geopolitical tensions have escalated. This is not a privilege to be granted or withdrawn according to the political circumstances of the day.” Meanwhile, Italy has revealed it is preparing to act independently to get nationally linked merchant ships through Bab el-Mandeb in the wake of the Houthis gaining advances in southern Yemen in recent days. Defence minister Guido Crosetto said Rome would not wait for the EU’s Aspides mission to decide when ships could pass, with military planners instructed to prepare a framework for protecting Italian merchant vessels. At least 10 Italian-flagged or Italian-owned ships are reported to be waiting in the region for protected passage.

https://splash247.com/turkey-pushes-blac.text: Turkey has presented Russia and Ukraine with a draft proposal aimed at ending attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, the latest attempt to contain a maritime conflict that is taking an increasingly heavy toll on merchant shipping. Ankara has shared the text of a memorandum with both Moscow and Kyiv designed to find a solution to the growing number of strikes on ships. Turkey was instrumental in an earlier grain corridor agreement from a couple of years ago. Recent US efforts to cool the maritime conflict have failed to produce a broader pause. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that a Russian-Ukrainian ban on attacks against ships carrying civilian cargoes would be impossible to monitor. Yesterday a Tanzanian-flagged merchant vessel heading towards a Ukrainian port was struck by what Kyiv said was a Russian drone. The captain was killed and three other crewmembers injured. Ukraine’s infrastructure ministry said the condition of the vessel was still being assessed. Turkey has its own growing list of casualties to contend with. The owner of the Turkish-flagged bulker Reyhan Sari, surviving crewmembers and the family of a sailor killed in a July attack near Novorossiysk have filed a complaint with the International Criminal Court in The Hague seeking an investigation into the strike. The 36,075 dwt ship had loaded coal at Taman and was heading for Turkey when it was hit. One seafarer was killed and several others injured.

https://splash247.com/splash-wrap-when-t.text: The most extraordinary numbers this week came from tankers, where the Baltic Exchange’s Middle East Gulf-China VLCC benchmark broke through the equivalent of $1m a day for the first time . VLCCs loading outside the Gulf are earning close to a million a day too, suezmax and aframax markets are flying and 10-year-old VLCCs are now being valued above newbuildings. Across shipping as a whole, Clarksons Research’s ClarkSea Index climbed to an all-time nominal high of above $56,000 a day. Martin Stopford told Capital Link in London this week that shipping has generated around $3.1trn in cash since 2021, with roughly a quarter already finding its way into new ships. The difficulty is knowing what to build. Research featured by Splash this week showed just how uncertain shipping’s fuel transition remains . Carbon pricing, hydrogen costs and feedstock availability can all radically alter the economics of methanol, ammonia and conventional fuels over a ship’s lifetime. More than half the vessels operating in 2050 will come from orders placed before 2035. Owners therefore have extraordinary amounts of cash precisely when some of their biggest long-term investment decisions are hardest to make. Money is flowing into existing companies too. Hafnia spent another $145.1m increasing its stake in Torm to 18.22%, taking its total investment in the Danish product tanker owner beyond $456m and cementing its position as Torm’s largest disclosed shareholder. In terms of maritime infrastructure news, the week’s biggest development came from southwest China and the opening of the 134 km Pinglu Canal , a $10.2bn waterway giving many inland provinces a much shorter route to the Beibu Gulf. Construction required excavation of more than 300m cu m of earth and rock, roughly three times the excavation volume of the Three Gorges project. This week’s Maritime CEO featured Aristos Philis of KeelX , who argued that shipping technology needs to become easier to buy, faster to implement and less painful to abandon. His message is particularly relevant in a market where owners have money to spend but no shortage of vendors competing for it: technology has to solve something tangible rather than simply add another dashboard. The same practical approach came through in this week’s Splash Ports CEO interview. PortMiami boss Jonathan Daniels is preparing for substantial further growth from an island facility that cannot expand horizontally. His answer is to stack higher, squeeze more from existing infrastructure and deploy technology against specific bottlenecks as the port updates its 2050 masterplan.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/c.text: China has recently enhanced the signals communication array at its base for the People’s Liberation Army (Navy) in Djibouti. An in-depth report produced by CSIS (the Center for Strategic and International Studies, based in Washington, D.C.) described the enhancements made at the base. The PLAN’s Overseas Support Base at Doraleh in Djibouti is the only acknowledged Chinese external base, but was supposed to be the first of several such bases to be constructed worldwide under the classified Project 141. Ream in Cambodia was the second such base to come into use, but its status, along with that of a Chinese facility at Hambantota in Sri Lanka, has since appeared more akin to a facility for use by visiting ships. Plans for a base in Abu Dhabi’s KIZAD port look likely to have been scrapped under pressure from the United States. The PLAN now appears to have scaled back its plans for further Project 141 sites, preferring instead to utilize commercial facilities operated overseas by the likes of COSCO. The improvements to communications facilities at the base in Doraleh described in the CSIS report cover aerials and satellite dishes across the full electromagnetic spectrum, from High Frequency, Very/Ultra High Frequency, SATCOM and 5G. CSIS cannot be sure whether these aerials are for transmission or reception. However, it seems likely that these new arrays are for passive interception, as the PLAN would not have been operating Naval Escort Groups in the area without adequate secure communications since 2008, and the full-spectrum frequency profile of the new aerial farm is more akin to that needed for a signals collection site. From Doraleh, the PLAN could have an interest in covering the activity of the many other foreign naval bases in Djibouti, but it will also want to keep abreast of ongoing conflicts in Yemen, Sudan and Somalia. The PLAN will have a particular interest in the substantial US Navy presence in the Arabian Sea, and in monitoring merchant traffic in the Red Sea. Militaries in this region tend to rely on rudimentary long-distance HF communications, interception of which from Doraleh is practical, but as an interception site Doraleh perhaps lacks the height to intercept VHF communications at longer ranges. China has well-established means for sharing timely and high-resolution satellite imagery with Iran and, hence, through IRGC liaison officers, forward to the Houthis in Yemen. If this is the case, similar channels could be used to pass signals intelligence as well. The PLAN maintains a three-ship flotilla in Djibouti, which rotates about every 10 months , the ships coming from the North, East, and South Sea Fleet in turn. https://maritime-executive.com/article/m.text: Scotland’s plan for the modernization and improvement of its vital ferries continues to encounter problems, with more reports of delays and cost overruns. The BBC says the next ferry will finally be delivered nearly two years behind schedule, while two others are being delayed until 2027. Costs for these newbuilds have also risen by approximately $27 million, or nearly a 10 percent increase for a project originally valued at approximately £200 million. This comes even after the state-owned Caledonian Maritime Assets Limited (CMAL) took the unusual step in June 2026 of taking ownership of three incomplete ferries being built at Turkey’s Cemre Shipyard. The company said it was taking the steps because of the precarious financial situation of the yard. It cited economic challenges, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran and disruptions in the Red Sea, along with, the BBC says, falling currency exchange rates, supply chain difficulties, and labor shortages. CMAL paid a reported £23 million for full ownership of the three incomplete vessels. “Taking ownership of the vessels at this stage is a precautionary move to reduce risk, protect the investment already made, and support our objective of bringing these vessels into service as quickly and efficiently as possible,” said Kevin Hobbs, the current chief executive of CMAL. The Scottish government was fully supporting the move, with reports noting that if the yard collapsed financially, CMAL owned the ships and could tow them out for completion elsewhere. Despite taking these steps, the BBC reports the problems persist in the program, which is nearly a decade in the making. The Scottish government announced plans for new vessels in April 2018, and by 2019, CMAL began design work for what has ultimately become a construction order for four passenger-car ferries to serve routes including to Islay, the southernmost of the Inner Hebrides islands, off the west coast of Scotland. The construction plan was part of a broad 10-year program of investment by CMAL, backed by the Scottish government, which committed £580 million for the five years between 2021 and 2026. They highlighted plans to deliver 21 new vessels to the fleet, along with upgrades to harbor infrastructure.

https://g1.globo.com/rj/rio-de-janeiro/n.text: Ricardo Couto recebe Lula na Superintendência da PRF, em Irajá — Foto: Rafael Nascimento/g1 O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) anunciou nesta sexta-feira (18) uma força-tarefa entre os governos federal, estadual e municipal para reforçar o combate ao roubo de cargas nos principais corredores rodoviários do Rio de Janeiro . https://g1.globo.com/mg/minas-gerais/ele.text: Cleitinho Azevedo (Republicanos) em entrevista ao MG1 — Foto: TV Globo/ Reprodução O candidato do Republicanos ao governo de Minas, Cleitinho Azevedo, defendeu, em entrevista ao MG1 desta sexta-feira (18), a renegociação das parcelas da dívida com a União por meio do Programa de Pleno Pagamento de Dívidas dos Estados (Propag). https://www.tecnologistica.com.br/notici.text: A Associação dos Produtores de Biocombustíveis do Brasil (APROBIO) , a Associação Brasileira das Indústrias de Óleos Vegetais (ABIOVE) , o Serviço Nacional de Aprendizagem Rural do Rio Grande do Sul (SENAR-RS) e o SULPETRO assinaram , em 3 de setembro, durante a Expointer, em Esteio (RS), um Protocolo de Intenções para a iniciativa “Tanque em Dia” , voltada à disseminação de boas práticas no recebimento, armazenamento, manuseio e uso de combustíveis e biocombustíveis em propriedades rurais. A proposta busca ampliar o acesso dos produtores gaúchos a informações técnicas sobre a conservação dos produtos até o abastecimento de máquinas agrícolas. A iniciativa reunirá a expertise técnica da APROBIO e da ABIOVE, que atuam conjuntamente por meio da AliançaBiodiesel, a experiência do SENAR-RS em formação e assistência técnica e a atuação do SULPETRO junto à rede de revendedores varejistas de combustíveis. Entre as ações previstas estão a capacitação de multiplicadores, participação em eventos técnicos, disponibilização de especialistas e produção de materiais de orientação. O trabalho deverá abordar aspectos como limpeza e conservação dos tanques, prevenção da presença de água e impurezas e procedimentos adequados de armazenamento. Os cuidados são especialmente relevantes para o diesel B, que contém biodiesel em sua composição. Segundo o material da iniciativa, condições inadequadas de armazenamento podem favorecer a formação de depósitos, crescimento microbiológico, corrosão e obstrução de filtros, comprometendo a qualidade do combustível e o funcionamento dos equipamentos. “O tema ganha especial importância em um momento de avanço dos biocombustíveis na matriz brasileira. Com a ampliação de seu uso, cresce também a necessidade de disseminar informações sobre os cuidados necessários em todas as etapas da cadeia, inclusive depois que o combustível chega ao consumidor”, afirma Jerônimo Goergen, presidente da APROBIO. Para André Nassar, presidente da ABIOVE, a parceria permitirá levar conhecimento técnico diretamente às propriedades. “Nosso objetivo é levar conhecimento técnico e as melhores práticas de armazenamento de combustíveis diretamente aos produtores rurais gaúchos, garantindo mais segurança, qualidade e eficiência para as operações no campo”, afirma.

https://g1.globo.com/tecnologia/noticia/.text: Anatel deu 30 dias para elas rastrearem a origem de outras milhões de ligaçõadulteradas — Foto: Priscilla Du Preez/ Unsplash A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações ( Anatel ) exigiu o bloqueio de ligações de duas empresas que somaram mais de 4,3 milhões de chamadas adulteradas, uma prática conhecida como spoofing, entre setembro de 2025 e junho de 2026. Em comunicado divulgado na última quarta-feira (16), a Anatel informou que as ligações fazem parte de um volume maior, que passa de 203 milhões de chamadas adulteradas. A agência não conseguiu identificar a origem de todo tráfego e exigiu que ele seja rastreado por operadoras. (saiba mais abaixo) As chamadas identificadas pela agência foram realizadas pela Voros Telecomunicações , que atende empresas que fazem grandes volume de chamadas, e a ELO Contact Center , que presta serviços de telemarketing para a TIM.

https://www.tecnologistica.com.br/notici.text: A especialista em sistemas de armazenagem intralogística ISMA comemora 56 anos de atividade durante um dos maiores ciclos de investimento de sua história. Desde 2022, a companhia já aplicou mais de R$ 50 milhões na modernização de sua unidade industrial em Mogi Mirim (SP). Este ano, a empresa está somando mais R$ 5 milhões na fábrica, para melhorar sua infraestrutura de movimentação interna, implantar uma nova linha de pintura e incorporar novos robôs de solda. Os novos equipamentos incluem uma linha automática de pintura capaz de processar estruturas de até 14 metros , uma linha adicional dedicada à produção de peças de geometrias diversas, perfiladeiras para a fabricação de colunas e longarinas, robôs de solda e a modernização da linha de manufatura de porta-paletes e ações de retrofit na própria planta. A companhia anuncia estar trabalhatando também no desenvolvimento de novos produtos, que devem demandar investimentos adicionais nos próximos anos. Aumento de capacidade produtiva foca em projetos de armazenagem de alta densidade De acordo com a ISMA, os investimentos ocorrem em um momento de aumento da complexidade dos projetos de armazenagem no país, com empresas buscando maior verticalização, alta densidade, retrofit, melhor aproveitamento dos espaços e estruturas preparadas para integração com diferentes níveis de automação. Atualmente, a fábrica possui capacidade produtiva de aproximadamente 2,5 mil toneladas por mês. Os novos investimentos estão sendo direcionados à estabilização dos processos e ao ganho de eficiência operacional, e permitirão ampliar a produção por meio da expansão dos turnos de trabalho, com potencial para dobrar a capacidade atualmente instalada.

A OceanPact concluiu a combinação de negócios com a CBO , após a aprovação final do Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) e o cumprimento das demais condições previstas para a operação. Anunciado no início deste ano deste ano (leia mais aqui ), o negócio incorpora a CBO à OceanPact e cria a unidade OceanPact CBO , que passa a operar 70 embarcações , com mais de 5 mil colaboradores , receita anual superior a R$ 4 bilhões e backlog contratado acima de R$ 14 bilhões . A combinação amplia a capacidade da companhia para operações marítimas e offshore de maior complexidade, incluindo resposta a emergências ambientais, operações submarinas, descomissionamento, logística integrada e projetos ambientais. A complementaridade das frotas também deverá ampliar a flexibilidade na alocação dos ativos e reduzir a idade média das embarcações. Segundo a OceanPact, a integração está estruturada em quatro frentes: fortalecimento da geração de caixa e do potencial de pagamento de dividendos; ampliação da capacidade de atuação; geração de valor por meio da integração comercial e operacional e captura de sinergias; e complementaridade da frota e diversificação da base de clientes. “A chegada da CBO à OceanPact marca uma nova etapa na história da nossa companhia. Temos uma grande oportunidade pela frente: combinar o melhor das nossas histórias para construir uma operação ainda mais completa, eficiente e preparada para gerar valor para nossos clientes e a sociedade”, afirma Flavio Andrade, presidente da OceanPact. Com a incorporação da CBO, serão emitidas 274.551.446 novas ações ordinárias da OceanPact, que passam a ser negociadas na B3 a partir de 17 de setembro. A diretoria da companhia também passa a contar com Marcos Tinti e Marcelo Martins, executivos provenientes da CBO, além de Flavio Andrade, Haroldo Solberg, Eduardo de Toledo, Erik Cunha, Adriano Ranieri e Fernando Borensztein. A nova estrutura acionária é composta por Vinci Compass, com 21,8%; fundos geridos pelo Pátria, também com 21,8%; Flavio Andrade, com 13%; BNDESPar, com 10,9%; executivos da OceanPact, com 3,8%; e mercado, com 28,7%. O Conselho de Administração terá sete integrantes e será presidido por Luís Araujo.

A DHL Supply Chain firmou acordo para adquirir a Open Market , operadora de logística e transporte na Colômbia pertencente à brasileira AGV . A operação amplia a capacidade da companhia na logística de life sciences, saúde e bens de consumo no país e adiciona à estrutura da DHL uma rede de 21 armazéns, com 120 mil m² de área total, 13 plataformas de cross-docking e frota própria , além de aproximadamente 4.100 funcionários. A aquisição está alinhada à estratégia global do Grupo DHL para 2030, que prevê expansão em mercados e setores de crescimento, incluindo logística para ciências da vida e saúde. A integração da Open Market também acrescentará ao portfólio da DHL competências em transporte, embalagem e operações com controle de temperatura. Segundo Hendrik Venter, CEO da DHL Supply Chain, a Colômbia é considerada um mercado de crescimento para o grupo em razão da demanda por serviços integrados de logística e transporte. O executivo destaca ainda a experiência da Open Market na gestão de cadeias de suprimentos de produtos farmacêuticos, médicos e de cuidados pessoais. Para Agustín Croche, CEO da DHL Supply Chain para a América Latina, a rede de transporte, as plataformas de cross-docking e os armazéns com controle de temperatura da Open Market complementam a estrutura já existente da companhia na região. A empresa também atende aos segmentos de bens de consumo, engenharia e manufatura. A DHL também já vinha ampliando sua infraestrutura na Colômbia. Entre os investimentos recentes está a expansão do Constellation Distribution Center, em Cota, próximo a Bogotá, que reforça a capacidade da empresa para operações de cadeias de suprimentos especializadas. Com a incorporação dos profissionais da Open Market, a DHL Supply Chain Colombia também amplia sua equipe e incorpora experiência no mercado local. Robinson Vasquez, CEO da operação colombiana da DHL Supply Chain, afirma que a integração permitirá ampliar a oferta de soluções especializadas aos clientes.

A Scheffer Logística e Automação apresentou novas tecnologias exclusivas de automação da armazenagem e movimentação de paletes durante a Intra-Log Expo South America 2026. A feira aconteceu entre os dias 15 e 17 de setembro, em São Paulo (SP). Entre as novidades estão as tecnologias 4-Way , voltada à armazenagem automatizada de alta densidade, e VRF , composta por robôs autônomos para movimentação de paletes. As novas tecnologias passam a integrar o portfólio da Scheffer e ampliam as possibilidades de desenvolvimento de projetos automatizados para diferentes perfis de operação. O sistema 4-Way usa carros automatizados que podem movimentar paletes em quatro direções dentro da estrutura de armazenagem, permitindo acessar diferentes posições e aumentar o aproveitamento do espaço disponível. De acordo com a empresa, a tecnologia é indicada para operações que buscam aumentar a capacidade de armazenagem, otimizar áreas existentes e criar sistemas escaláveis, nos quais capacidade e desempenho podem acompanhar a evolução da operação. Para a solução apresentada durante a feira, a Scheffer trabalha em parceria com a Longa Industrial , responsável pela engenharia e fabricação das estruturas de armazenagem, integradas ao sistema automatizado desenvolvido para a aplicação. Outra novidade apresentada pela Scheffer foi a tecnologia VRF , formada por robôs autônomos desenvolvidos para movimentar paletes entre diferentes pontos da operação. A solução amplia as possibilidades de automação de fluxos internos e pode ser aplicada na conexão entre áreas como recebimento, armazenagem, produção, separação e expedição.

https://www.rigzone.com/news/wire/house_.text: Congress gave final approval to a bill to give President Donald Trump new powers to impose tariffs on countries that purchase Russian petroleum products, a setback for a coalition of business lobbyists concerned the legislation creates a legal underpinning for a broad new tariff regime against US trading partners. The legislation, which the House passed Wednesday in a 262-159 vote, has been celebrated by Ukrainian officials eager for a tangible sign of US support in its fight against a Russian invasion. The war, now in its fifth year, is in a critical phase of escalation. The measure now goes to Trump’s desk for his signature, after easily passing the Senate last month. The president plans to sign the bill in the coming days, a White House official said. The top five purchasers of Russian petroleum products — a list that includes China, India and US allies like Turkey — could be hit with broad new tariffs, if Trump chooses to use the new powers. Democrats offered an amendment to clarify that the European Union would not be considered as one country under the bill, but the effort to preemptively limit the scope of the bill was rejected. “This legislation strengthens economic sanctions against the Russian government, its financial institutions, and the foreign governments that aid Russian aggression against Ukraine by purchasing cheap Russian oil and gas and helping the Kremlin evade other sanctions,” House Speaker Mike Johnson said in a statement after the vote. The Kremlin on Thursday called passage of the measure an “unfriendly” move and warned it could affect negotiations to end the war. “The introduction of some additional sanctions from the US will certainly complicate efforts to reach a peaceful settlement in Ukraine,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, according to the Interfax news service.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543087-ae.text: Aesen introduced the Aesen 116H, a next-generation hybrid crew boat developed to support the evolving operational requirements of offshore personnel transportation and infield logistics operations. This vessel combines hybrid propulsion technology, intelligent energy management and enhanced operational resilience to support safer, more efficient and lower-emission offshore operations. By integrating hybrid propulsion and energy storage systems, Aesen 116H is engineered to optimise engine loading and power utilization, enabling an estimated 30 to 40 percent reduction in fuel consumption compared with conventionally powered crew boats operating under similar duty cycles. The design contributes to lower emissions while maintaining the performance, reliability and responsiveness required for demanding offshore environments. In addition to its hybrid capabilities, Aesen 116H incorporates a multi-layered redundancy philosophy to enhance operational continuity and reliability. The vessel is designed to maintain essential functions across a range of operational contingencies, supporting safer and more resilient offshore transportation services. A key feature onboard is Smart Window technology , which enhances situational awareness on the bridge by improving visibility of critical operating areas around the vessel. The system complements conventional navigation and monitoring technologies, supporting informed decision-making in complex offshore operating conditions.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543080-tr.text: Transocean has been awarded a two-well contract for its Deepwater Conqueror ultra-deepwater drillship in Equatorial Guinea, adding about $80 million to the offshore driller's backlog. The approximately 170-day campaign with an undisclosed operator is expected to begin in 2027, directly following the rig's current contract in the U.S. Gulf. The estimated backlog excludes additional services and compensation for mobilization and demobilization. Built in 2016, the DSME 12000-design Deepwater Conqueror can operate in water depths of up to 12,000 feet and drill to a maximum depth of 40,000 feet.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543085-ex.text: Exmar has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore for a concept to convert an existing membrane-type LNG carrier into a floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) unit for offshore gas developments. The FLNG concept would use a membrane-type LNG carrier with an effective LNG storage capacity of about 170,000 cubic meters and a design life of 25 years. Designed for operation in mild environments, the converted vessel would provide offshore gas processing, liquefaction and LNG storage and is intended for the development of stranded gas resources. The concept is aimed at projects seeking lower initial capital requirements and shorter timelines between final investment decision and production by converting an existing LNG carrier rather than constructing a new vessel. Bureau Veritas assessed the concept against applicable requirements for offshore production gas units, liquefied gas carriers and position-keeping systems. The review at this stage covered the hull structure and stability, existing LNG cargo containment system and FLNG mooring arrangement. “Floating liquefaction solutions already play an important role in unlocking offshore gas resources and supporting the development of energy projects in a flexible and cost-effective manner. We are pleased to grant Approval in Principle (AiP) to Exmar’s FLNG conversion concept, which demonstrates how existing LNG carrier assets can be repurposed to support future offshore developments,” said David Barrow, SVP for Western Europe and Americas at Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543078-pe.text: Petrobras, through its wholly owned subsidiary Petrobras Netherlands (PNBV), the Republic of Côte d’Ivoire and PETROCI Holding signed Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) for eight offshore exploration blocks located in Côte d’Ivoire. The PSCs cover offshore blocks CI-513, CI-600, CI-601, CI-602, CI-603, CI-605, CI-701 and CI-702. Petrobras, through PNBV, will hold a 90% interest and serve as operator, while local state-owned company PETROCI Holding will hold the remaining 10% interest. The signing ceremony was held on September 17 and was attended by Petrobras Executive Director of Exploration and Production Sylvia Anjos. “With this acquisition, Petrobras establishes a significant presence in Côte d’Ivoire, a country located in a region with high exploration potential and geological characteristics similar to those of our sedimentary basins. We will apply our experience and technical capabilities to these blocks, and we are confident that, with them, we will be able to unlock all the possibilities we believe exist along the African Atlantic margin,” said Magda Chambriard, Petrobras’ CEO. The initiative is aligned with Petrobras’ strategy of replenishing its oil and gas reserves through exploration in new frontier areas, both in Brazil and abroad, as set out in its Business Plan. The assessment of new opportunities is intended to diversify the company’s exploration portfolio, generate value and support the long-term sustainability of its business.

https://safety4sea.com/lessons-learned-i.text: A maintenance task involving a known leak on a main hydraulic pressure line resulted in a technician suffering a shoulder injury after residual hydraulic fluid was released and a pipe unexpectedly resisted movement. T he incident, highlighted by IMCA, shows a familiar but important safety problem: equipment may be isolated without necessarily being in a safe condition to open. The case also shows how a task classified as routine can quickly become an intrusive, physically demanding operation when residual energy, restricted access and manual handling come together. The technician was carrying out maintenance on a small leak in a main hydraulic pressure line. The hydraulic system had been shut down and locally isolated before the work began. However, hydraulic oil remained inside the pipework. When the technician loosened the flange connection, residual fluid escaped. The technician then attempted to control the escaping oil while simultaneously repositioning the pipe within a restricted workspace at shoulder height. Resistance was encountered while force was being applied to align the pipe. The load then transferred suddenly through the technician’s shoulder, causing the injury. The incident did not involve a failure to shut down the system in the conventional sense. The system had been isolated. The critical weakness was that isolation was treated as sufficient without formally verifying that the section being opened was free of pressure and residual fluid.

https://safety4sea.com/plastic-pellets-f.text: Plastic pellets released after the sinking of the container ship MSC ELSA-3 off India’s Kerala coast in May 2025 are continuing to wash up along the shoreline, with researchers finding pellets buried deep in beach sediments and evidence that the material is changing chemically and biologically in the marine environment. A one-year study by the Suganthi Devadason Marine Research Institute (SDMRI), Thoothukudi, tracked the spill across 93 coastal sites along India’s southwest and southeast coasts. The findings, published in Marine Pollution Bulletin, indicate that the environmental footprint of the casualty has persisted well beyond the initial shoreline clean-up. The MSC ELSA-3, a Liberian-flagged container ship, sank carrying around 640 containers containing plastic resin pellets, industrial materials and hazardous cargo, including calcium carbide, as well as substantial quantities of diesel and furnace oil. The incident resulted in what researchers describe as India’s first documented large-scale marine resin pellet spill. According to the study, the scale of the initial contamination was significant. Shoreline surveys recorded concentrations of up to 31,230 pellets per square metre at affected sites. Although abundance fell by more than 80% within three months, the contamination did not simply disappear. New nurdle hotspots emerged by October 2025, including concentrations of up to 10,875 pellets per square metre on the mainland of the Gulf of Mannar and 2,960 pellets per square metre on islands.

https://safety4sea.com/upcoming-igc-code.text: The next generation of LNG carriers is already being designed with an eye on safety requirements that have yet to formally enter into force, as shipbuilders and classification societies prepare for a significant update to the IMO’s rules governing liquefied gas carriers. H D Hyundai Samho and ClassNK signed an MOU at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok on 16 September to jointly develop an LNG carrier design incorporating the forthcoming amendments to the International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases, or IGC Code. The timing is significant as the amendments are expected to be adopted at the 112th session of the IMO Maritime Safety Committee (MSC 112) in December 2026 and are scheduled to enter into force on 1 July 2028. The proposed amendments address a range of technical and operational issues as the design and operation of gas carriers continue to evolve. Among them are: The amendments reflect the increasingly complex technical landscape surrounding gas carriers, where new fuel pathways and technologies are creating new safety considerations alongside the established risks associated with the carriage of liquefied gases. Against that backdrop, the HD Hyundai Samho-ClassNK project will focus on four areas of the forthcoming requirements: emergency shutdown arrangements for valves connected to cargo tanks, material requirements for exposed cargo piping, interlocking and accumulation-pressure requirements for cargo tank pressure-relief valves, and risk-based cargo tank filling limits.
