https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/chi.text: China left its benchmark lending rates unchanged for a 16th consecutive month on Sunday, as policymakers face less room for monetary easing following a more hawkish shift by major global central banks, Reuters reported. The one-year loan prime rate was maintained at 3.00%, with the five-year LPR remaining at 3.50%. The decision matched market expectations, with all 21 participants surveyed by Reuters forecasting no change to either benchmark. China’s decision comes after the Federal Reserve raised U.S. interest rates last week and signaled further increases could follow in coming months as policymakers remain concerned about inflation. The move has widened the divergence between U.S. and Chinese monetary policy. The yield premium on benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasuries over comparable Chinese government bonds has hovered near a record high following the Fed increase. China faces its own constraints on further monetary easing as policymakers contend with weak credit demand and pressure on banks’ profitability.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/fed.text: Following the US Federal Reserve’s decision on 16 September 2026 to raise the federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points from 3.75% to 4%; Jaison Davis, Economic Research Analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, provides his perspective: “This is a credibility move. Headline inflation is stuck at 3.4%, well above the 2% goal, and energy is the driver. Gasoline is up more than 27% over the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and fuel, has fallen to 2.4%, its lowest in over five years. Shelter has eased to 3.0% and food to 2.7%, so the pressure is narrow and energy-led, not broad. The Fed is tightening against an energy-led headline number even as underlying pressure cools. That is a deliberate choice to protect expectations, and it carries the risk of over-tightening into a supply shock. “The market response was measured rather than fearful. Equities held firm and government bond yields eased, with the 10-year slipping below 5%. In plain terms, investors judged the move as credible, and they expect a firmer Fed now to mean lower inflation later. For companies, that matters. An orderly response keeps financing conditions steadier and avoids a sudden jump in borrowing costs. “The path from here points up. The projections signal one more 25 basis point increase this year, taking the range toward 4.25%. This points to higher rates for longer. Companies that had planned around early rate cuts will need to revisit those assumptions. The bar for easing is now much higher, and it rests on clear evidence that inflation is heading back to target. “A firmer Fed and a stronger dollar tighten conditions well beyond the US. Money tends to move toward higher US yields, and that pressures emerging market currencies. The Indian rupee is already near record lows, around 96 to the dollar, and Brent crude near $108 adds to India’s import bill. For companies that import goods, borrow in dollars, or earn overseas, a stronger dollar lifts costs and pressures margins. It also widens the gap with central banks such as the RBI, which are trying to protect growth, so their caution now looks even more sensible.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/xen.text: The Xeneta Weekly Ocean Container Shipping Market Update provides data and intelligence including the latest freight rate and capacity movements across global trades with supporting insight from Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst. Xeneta analyst insight – carriers seize opportunity as freight rates head towards record levels from Far East to US “Spot rates from Far East to US West Coast and US East Coast are up 324% and 325% respectively since pre-Hormuz crisis at the end of February. That leaves freight rates on these critical trades just 18% and 11% short of the all-time high set during the COVID-19 disruption. With bunker prices pushing fuel surcharges higher, surpassing the pandemic peak cannot be ruled out, which would be an extraordinary market development. “If a freight rate record is broken, it is most likely to occur on the trade into US East Coast, but even if we do not see a new all-time high, the fact we are even discussing the possibility demonstrates how sensitive critical ocean container shipping trades are to geopolitical forces and how a regional conflict in the Middle East can have major implications at a global level. “Carriers are seizing the opportunity while the market is hot, adding capacity into US East Coast ahead of what could be a turn in the market within the next two to three weeks. Offered capacity on the Far East to US East Coast trade is 6-7% higher in September than in August. “We should expect one more freight rate push at the start of October as shippers rush cargo out of Asia ahead of the Golden Week shutdown, before rates start to soften, or at least the pace of growth will slow.”

But recent leaks underscore the safety concerns as plans move closer to reality. Chinese shipping firm Shenghang Shipping’s converted ammonia carrier has achieved operational readiness as a bunker vessel after receiving certification for ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering from China Classification Society. The 5,500-cbm vessel, Shenghang Yongle, was originally built as a liquefied gas carrier and has been converted to deliver liquid ammonia to other vessels through ship-to-ship bunkering. The companies have not disclosed where the vessel will be deployed or which port will host its first commercial ammonia bunker operation. The Shenghang Yongle, described as the world’s first operational ammonia bunker vessel, has put the fuel back in the spotlight. But the bigger picture is taking shape across several regions, with ports setting dates for bunker pilots, suppliers lining up fuel, and infrastructure being developed. Lotte Fine Chemical has bunkered ammonia to vessels in South Korea’s Port of Ulsan, and signed an agreement with Amogy in September to explore further ammonia bunkering there. A port tugboat was also bunkered with green ammonia at COSCO’s Dalian terminal last year. Pilbara Ports plans to carry out an ammonia bunker pilot this year. Rotterdam, which completed a pilot transfer last year, expects its first ammonia bunker deliveries in 2026-2027.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: Over the weekend, the U.S. Coast Guard arranged a long-range rescue for a boxship crewmember who was suffering from a serious, growing infection. Last week, the 1996-built boxship Kotka (ex names Maersk Kotka, Knud Maersk ) was under way on a long voyage from Colombo, Sri Lanka, bound for New York. On Wednesday night, the master of the Kotka contacted shoreside authorities and reported that a crewmember had developed a "severe, non-ambulatory infection" that was not getting better with onboard medical treatment. At the time, the ship was in the middle of the Atlantic, roughly equidistant between the Windward Islands and Senegal, about 1,300 nautical miles from shore - well beyond the range of existing U.S. medevac assets. The Coast Guard's San Juan station took responsibility for the case and instructed the master to divert towards St. Maarten to close the distance. The Kotka changed course and headed due west, making 17 knots. On Friday, as the ship got closer, Air Station Borinquen dispatched a Jayhawk helicopter to St. Maarten in preparation for a medevac flight, and Air Station Miami sent an HC-144 Ocean Sentry aircraft to provide a communications relay. On Saturday, the helicopter aircrew rendezvoused with Kotka at a position about 100 nautical miles to the east of St. Maarten. The vessel's crew helped bring the patient out on deck, using a wheeled office chair to move him to a clear area, and loaded him into a basket for hoisting. The aircrew winched him safely aboard and flew him to San Juan for transfer to the hospital for specialized higher care. “Our team was at its best throughout the complex execution of this multi-day rescue,” said Capt. Robert E. Stiles, Coast Guard search and rescue mission coordinator for the case. “We commend our aircrew for getting the aircraft on scene to rescue a ship’s crew member and get him to a shoreside medical facility for the higher level of care he required. We are hopeful he will make a full recovery."

https://maritime-executive.com/article/v.text: On Thursday, a bulker made contact with the stern of a Chinese fishing vessel during a complex traffic situation off the coast of Singapore - but the smaller vessel appears to have miraculously escaped. At about 0800 hours GMT on Thursday, the bulker First Margaux got underway from a busy anchorage on the east side of Singapore, headed westbound (per AIS data provided by Pole Star Global ). Fishing vessel Luqing Yuanyu 108 got under way at about the same time from a different anchorage just off Sentosa and headed south. There was heavy traffic in the vicinity, with limited room for maneuver. Both vessels reached the westbound lane of the TSS and set a typical course towards the Strait of Malacca. Luqing Yuanyu entered the TSS in front of First Margaux, and the bulker was moving about 2-3 knots faster. Slowly overtaking Luqing Yuanyu from the smaller vessel's port side, First Margaux passed astern of the fishing vessel and continued to close the distance as the crew watched and shouted. Sometime around 0900, First Margaux's bow made contact with Luqing Yuanyu 108 on the starboard quarter, then pushed the smaller fishing vessel sideways, turning her and forcing her to heel hard to port. Water flooded in over the low gunwales of the Luqing Yuanyu's main deck. The Chinese-flagged ship Luqing Yuanyu 108 has been involved in a collision with the cargo ship Panama near Singapore pic.twitter.com/kPfpuwbDxO The video ended shortly after the moment of contact. The fishing vessel continued to transmit an AIS signal and was still visible on tracking as of Sunday, indicating that it survived the encounter and reached a nearby berth. No injuries or fatalities have been reported. First Margaux continued westbound at a steady 10 knots for another two hours after the collision before stopping, circling back and then going to anchor.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/r.text: Saudi Arabia has traditionally been the beacon of stability within OPEC. It is the Middle East's largest producer, reliably supplying markets in Asia and Europe through long-term contracts. Unlike most OPEC members and other oil producers, Saudi Arabia would maintain significant spare production capacity. This enabled the leaders in Riyadh to manage global oil markets as its main "swing producer." Saudi Arabia's size, reserves and political stability made it the natural leader of the OPEC cartel. However, much has changed in recent months. The Kingdom has entered a severe geopolitical and economic crisis as a result of the U.S. war against Iran and the closure of critical oil export infrastructure. In this Tanker Opinion, we'll discuss recent events and the impact they have on the tanker market. A few statistics will put the importance of Saudi Arabia in context. Prior to the Iran war, Saudi Arabia was the third largest crude oil producer in the world, behind only the United States and Russia. It has the planet's second largest proven oil reserves (after Venezuela). The Saudis also made a significant push into refining. The country has dramatically grown its refinery throughput over the last 25 years. It is now the 6th largest refiner in the world with a domestic capacity of 3.3 Mb/d. In addition, Saudi Arabia owns significant stakes in international joint-venture refineries in countries like China, South Korea and Malaysia. The Saudis also control one of the largest oil tanker companies in the world. Bahri, the national shipping company of Saudi Arabia, is one of the largest owners/operators of VLCCs. The conflict between the U.S. and Iran has severely impacted the Kingdom's oil sector and economy. Although Saudi Arabia is not a direct combatant, it is deemed to be a U.S. ally, and its energy infrastructure and military bases are being systematically targeted by Iran and Iran-aligned groups. After the start of the conflict, Iran targeted transits through the Strait of Hormuz and seaborne exports from countries inside the Arabian Gulf were severely restricted. While Saudi Arabia's exports suffered, it had another option to bring its oil to market. It was able to divert a significant portion of its crude oil exports (around 5.0 Mb/d) through the East-West pipeline to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. However, this alternative route was not without risks. To export crude from Yanbu to Asia, tankers needed to pass through the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which is controlled by the Houthis, an Iran-backed rebel group in Yemen that has a long-running feud with Saudi Arabia. On July 20, Houthi rebels launched a Red Sea blockade targeting all vessels carrying Saudi export barrels. As a result, tankers loaded with Saudi crude were forced north toward Egypt's Suez C

https://maritime-executive.com/article/a.text: Preceding the recent Chinese Coast Guard attempt to ram the Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources vessel BRP Datu Magat Salamat off Palawan on September 18, China attempted to silence the Defense Secretary of the Philippines as he was midway through giving a speech at the Defense Dialogue conference in Seoul on September 8. Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, Jr. was halfway through a speech discussing the 2016 ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, which found that Beijing’s claims to historic rights within the Nine-Dash Line in the South China Sea had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). China has rejected the ruling, although it quoted UNCLOS in its criticism of the Philippines following the BRP Datu Magat Salamat incident off Palawan (below). China CG rams BFAR vessel on fuel subsidy mission for Filipino fishermen — 54 NM off Palawan This morning, 18 September 2026, China Coast Guard vessel CCG-21585 rammed BRP Datu Magat Salamat (MMOV 3015), the same BFAR vessel the Philippine Coast Guard assisted yesterday as it… pic.twitter.com/HgE4FiKpQ7 The note from the military attaché based at the Chinese embassy in Seoul instructed Secretary Gilberto to stop speaking. Secretary Teodoro instead carried on, and read the text of the Chinese message to his audience, saying that "this is actual coercion, bullying and aggression." Secretary Teodoro speech was greeted with enthusiasm by the audience in Seoul, and has prompted calls for him back home to stand in 2028 as President, Vice President or for a seat in the Senate. He has previously attracted the ire of China, and in June the Secretary, his wife and child were sanctioned by China, barred from travel to China or dealings with Chinese organizations. The Filipino approach to its dispute with China over rival claims to disputed islands has not changed significantly in recent years, despite changes in political leadership. It remains a policy of restraint, bolstered by increases in deterrent spending on naval and maritime forces. The Philippine Navy commissioned its second Miguel Malvar Class frigate, BRP Diego Silang (FFG07) in December 2025, and hopes to order two more. Hyundai is building six offshore patrol vessels for the Philippine Navy, two of which are now completed and undergoing sea trials in South Korea. Japan is offering to transfer six Abukuma Class multi-role frigates to the Philippines, as well as additional Beechcraft TC-90 aircraft for maritime surveillance. Two 124-meter landing dock platforms are being built by Indonesian shipbuilder PT PA. All these enhancements are part of the Horizon 2 modernization program initiated by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte in June 2018.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/c.text: Authorities at the port of Quang Ngai, Vietnam are working on a plan to offload a bulker that began taking on water during a transit into the port of Dung Quat. On Friday morning, the bulker Merchant Mariner was inbound for the industrial port of Dung Quat, home of the giant Hoa Phat steel plant. She had a cargo of 174,000 tonnes of Malaysian iron ore on board, and had a draft of about 18.4 meters. At about 1130 hours, the crew contacted local authorities and reported flooding in three ballast tanks, potenially caused by contact with a reef at a position about 15 nm off the port. AIS data (provided by Pole Star Global ) shows that the vessel passed through shallower water with isolated soundings of as little as 18 meters. While transiting this area, she slowed suddenly from 10.5 to five knots, then regained speed (below). Merchant Mariner slows to five knots after transiting over region of shallower water (Pole Star Global) The ship went to anchor and continued to settle lower in the water through the day, her draft increasing to 19.7 meters at the stern by Friday evening, the authority said. The crew were instructed to close off tank valves as a precautionary measure, and a tug was put on standby. Quang Ngai Maritime Port Authority has requested the vessel's master and the Hoa Phat ore terminal to come up with a safe plan to unload the ship despite her damaged condition. All 24 crewmembers are safe and no pollution has been reported, the authority said, and there are no signs of water in her cargo holds.

Chattogram port workers have planned a fresh wave of protests as disagreement with the government over leasing of a container terminal mounts. The workers under the union, Chattogram Port Protection Movement Council, are opposed to the proposed leasing of the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) to the UAE-based port operator DP World. NCT is Chattogram’s largest container terminal, handling nearly half of the port’s container volume. Currently, the terminal is operated by the state-owned Chittagong Dry Dock Limited (CDDL), a corporation under the Bangladesh Navy. As part of the ongoing port privatization drive, DP World has emerged as a front-runner candidate to operate NCT. The port workers are concerned that the government has not carried out proper public consultation on the concession deal. In February, the Chattogram port workers’ union called for a strike, which impacted port operations for almost two weeks. At the time, the union claimed that its negotiations with the government had failed as its key demands concerning the lease were not met. The strike was called off mid-February when current Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took over from the interim government led by the Nobel Peace prize laureate Muhammad Yunus. In a press conference over the weekend, the Chattogram Port Protection Movement Council said it would begin peaceful protests from September 22. The union is composed of several port-based workers’ organizations, which are pushing for greater transparency in the privatization plans. In addition, the union leaders demanded for the withdrawal of cases filed against fifteen port employees and union leaders for participating in the February strike. Again, the union requested the government (through the finance and shipping ministers) to organize a national dialogue on the NCT deal. In a build-up to these consultations, the union leaders called for trade groups across all sectors to prepare for a day-long sit-in protest on October 5 in front of Chattogram Port headquarters. With Bangladesh working to modernize its port sector, private operators are increasingly being awarded concessions to major terminals in the country. In July, the Saudi port operator RSGT launched operations at the Patenga Container Terminal in Chattogram Port. Last month, APM Terminals began construction of the new Laldia container terminal in Chattogram. Containerized trade at the port is increasing year on year, reaching a throughput of 3.56 million TEU in 2025.

https://splash247.com/paratus-and-vantri.text: Paratus Energy and Vantris Energy joint venture Seagems has moved closer to adding another pipelay support vessel to its Brazilian operation after Petrobras accepted its bid for an unidentified third-party vessel. Paratus said that Petrobras had published partial results from its latest PLSV tender, confirming acceptance of the Seagems bid. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/yan.text: A single attack on a Saudi pipeline in early September has done more than knock out one export route. Three weeks on, it is reshaping crude flows, lifting tanker freight rates, tightening diesel supply into Europe and adding pressure to already-elevated gas and coal prices. The disruption is a useful case study in how quickly a localised infrastructure event can cascade across a plethora of commodity markets. Market context Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, also known as Petroline, links crude and gas fields in the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu. Before the attack, throughput ran at roughly 5.5 million barrels a day, of which around 4.5 million barrels a day of crude was exported through Yanbu — historically one of the kingdom’s main outlets for supplying Mediterranean and northwest European refiners without routing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz or the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait. On 10 September, Houthi forces struck pumping stations across two regions of Saudi Arabia. The damage is materially worse than an April incident that hit a single station and was repaired within three days: this time, multiple pumping stations were disabled, even though the pipeline itself remains largely intact. No crude has loaded from Yanbu since 11 September, and terminal inventories — already thinned by a drawdown in the weeks before the attack — cover only three to five days of loadings at normal rates, or around nine days of refinery runs if no further crude reaches the region. Key insights and analysis Crude: a fragile recovery timeline, but a balanced global market Saudi Aramco is building a bypass around the damaged sections of pipeline, with full repairs estimated at four to six weeks. Unconfirmed reports over the past several days suggest Saudi Arabia is aiming to restore roughly half of Yanbu’s throughput sooner via this bypass — equivalent to around 2 to 2.5 million barrels a day of exports resuming within about a month. Kpler’s base case assigns roughly even odds to that partial-recovery outcome, with the remaining probability split between a faster full-recovery scenario and a slower, more disruptive one in which renewed Houthi attacks on the bypass extend the outage over several months. Given that Saudi Arabia is reportedly prioritising domestic refinery runs during the outage, any resumed exports are likely to arrive gradually rather than all at once. Two effects are already visible in the market: • North Sea crude differentials have widened sharply. Medium and heavier North Sea grades such as Johan Sverdrup have traded at premiums of up to $20 a barrel over North Sea Dated, as refiners scramble to replace medium-density Saudi barrels. Light grades have also firmed on the same demand-driven panic buying. • Saudi crude cargoes int

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tur.text: Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan. The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea. While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University. “The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It’s not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.” Growing attacks In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

https://splash247.com/clarksea-index-sur.text: Clarksons’ cross-sector ClarkSea Index continues to record new all-time highs as strong conditions spread across gas carriers, bulkers, containerships and car carriers to go alongside the extraordinary earnings seen in the crude tanker sector. The ClarkSea Index climbed another 14% on Friday to $64,569 a day, propelled by record crude tanker earnings but with Clarksons stressing that conditions across the VLGC, bulk carrier, containership and car carrier markets are also at “exceptional or strong levels”. The latest reading puts today’s market well beyond the peaks associated with shipping’s celebrated 2007-08 boom. Clarksons data show the old ClarkSea record was $50,714 a day in December 2007, with the 2008 maximum fractionally lower at $50,402 a day. Today’s index is already 27% above the previous high-water mark. Tankers remain the headline act thanks to the ongoing war between the US and Iran. Clarksons put global average VLCC earnings last week at a record $643,000 a day, up another 40% in a week, while suezmaxes were earning around $375,000 and aframaxes $184,000. New Yorker broker Poten & Partners noted in its latest weekly report: “The tanker market is benefiting from the current situation. The escalating conflict has created more risks, uncertainties and dislocations in the market and spiked freight rates to unprecedented levels.” The significance of the latest ClarkSea record is increasingly the breadth of the rally.

https://splash247.com/toro-doubles-mr-fl.text: Nasdaq-listed Toro Corp has doubled its MR tanker fleet with the acquisition of two ships for a combined $83.4m, accelerating its return to the product tanker sector as it prepares to spin off its remaining LPG carriers. The Petros Panagiotidis-led company has paid $45.9m for the 2018 Japanese-built Wonder Alasia , taking delivery on September 17. A second, 2014 Korean-built scrubber-fitted MR was acquired for $37.5m and handed over a day later. The latter is set to be renamed Wonder Atria . Both ships were acquired from unrelated third parties and paid for from cash on hand. The additions take Toro’s current fleet to six ships comprising four MRs and two LPG carriers. Toro had only two product tankers before the latest purchases. The company returned to the sector last year with the $36.25m acquisition of the 2021-built Wonder Altair , followed in September 2025 by the South Korean-built Wonder Maia for $30.3m. The latest expansion comes few days after Toro unveiled plans to carve out its final two LPG carriers, the 2015-built Dream Arrax and Dream Vermax , into another Panagiotidis-controlled Nasdaq vehicle, AI OKTO Corp, together with $45m in cash. If that transaction goes through, Toro would be left with the four-ship MR fleet. Toro emerged from Castor Maritime in 2023 with eight tankers before progressively selling down that fleet and shifting into LPG shipping. It subsequently reversed course, returning to product tankers while moving its LPG tonnage into other Panagiotidis-controlled listed vehicles.

https://splash247.com/pantheon-sells-15-.text: Anna Angelicoussis-led Pantheon Tankers is cashing in again on the booming VLCC secondhand market, with brokers reporting the sale of the 2011-built Sea Leopard for $135m. The 314,000 dwt DSME-built tanker has been committed to undisclosed buyers in what ranks among the largest VLCC secondhand deals reported last week. Pantheon has yet to announce the transaction and still lists the vessel in its online fleet. Clarksons put the benchmark cost of a new VLCC at around $131m at the start of September, meaning Pantheon is reported to be getting more for a 15-year-old ship than the headline price of contracting a new one for delivery several years from now. Signal Ocean has documented the same inversion across the age curve. At the end of August, five-year-old VLCCs were assessed at $151.1m against $130.2m for a newbuilding, while values for 15-year-old ships had risen 61% year on year. The speed of the latest repricing is illustrated by Frontline. The John Fredriksen-controlled owner agreed in July to sell two 2017-built VLCCs for $270m, or the same $135m per ship Pantheon is now reported to have achieved for a vessel six years older. The Sea Leopard also marks another sizeable step up from Pantheon’s previous disposal. The company sold its then-oldest VLCC, the 2009-built, 318,441 dwt Caesar , for about $70m in February.The 2011-built ship subsequently became the oldest VLCC in Pantheon’s operating fleet.

https://splash247.com/yangzijiang-mariti.text: Yangzijiang Maritime Development has put an official stamp on a newbuilding spree Splash has been tracking for months, disclosing 24 firm ship orders across five vessel types along with options on another 16. The Singapore-listed maritime investment group said the latest firm package comprises six 64,500 dwt bulkers, six 49,800 dwt product and chemical tankers, four 28,000 dwt stainless steel chemical tankers, four 29,000 dwt stainless steel chemical tankers and four 319,000 dwt VLCCs. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/asi.text: Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US rose this week on expanded peak season demand and capacity controls from carriers, while liquid tanker rates ex-US Gulf were mixed. CONTAINER RATES Container rates to the US West Coast are between $7,075-$8,330/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between $9,165-$12,000/FEU, at the highest since mid-2022 for both trade lanes. The following image shows rates from global logistics company Freight Right Logistics. Robert Khachatryan, founder and CEO of Freight Right Logistics, said capacity has tightened from earlier in September as carriers maintain firm control over available space with blank sailings and booking rollovers (when a container is not loaded onto its originally scheduled vessel and is instead rescheduled for a later sailing). “Vessel schedules have become increasingly unreliable,” Khachatryan said. “A shipment can secure space and still see its scheduled departure pushed back several days. When a booking rollover is combined with a delayed vessel departure, total delays can approach two weeks.” Rates from online shipping marketplace and platform provider Freightos rose by 3% to the West Coast and by 2% to the East Coast.

https://splash247.com/dong-fang-offshore.text: Taiwanese offshore vessel owner Dong Fang Offshore (DFO) has approved another newbuild at Norway’s Vard, setting aside up to $86m for a service operations vessel aimed at the international offshore energy market. A stock exchange disclosure shows DFO’s board approved construction of one operations and maintenance support vessel with Vard Group or one of its affiliates, including Vard Singapore. The authorised construction budget has been set at $76m to $86m. DFO said the vessel will be broadly similar to a service operation vessel but will use a different design from the three SOV/CSOV units it already has on order. Unlike those ships, which are tied to long-term Taiwanese offshore wind work, the latest investment is being made to provide capacity for potential international projects. The decision extends a sizeable Vard-backed expansion programme. Splash covered DFO’s €113.5m ($134m) subsea construction vessel order at the Norwegian shipbuilder last year, followed by a third Vard-built CSOV scheduled for delivery in 2028. That vessel is already committed to a minimum 15-year charter in Taiwan. DFO has increasingly been pushing beyond its home market. Its Orient Adventurer is working under a multi-year charter with DeepOcean in Europe, while the company last year also teamed up with Australia’s GO Offshore to pursue offshore wind and oil and gas vessel work across Asia-Pacific. The latest fleet decision came as DFO took delivery of the Orient Inspirer from Vard Vung Tau on September 16, two months ahead of schedule. The vessel is expected in Taiwan later this month and is due to start a 12-year operations and maintenance charter on November 1. That fixture, with Vestas for the Changfang-Xidao and Zhong Neng wind farms, was signed in 2024.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/hor.text: Oil and liquefied natural gas shipments navigating the Strait of Hormuz reached a six-month high over the past two weeks, demonstrating that U.S. naval escorts and mine-clearing operations are yielding results despite ongoing regional hostilities, according to U.S. Central Command. “Clearly, momentum is building,” Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), said in a video statement released Saturday. Cooper confirmed that primary transit channels through the strategic waterway have been cleared of naval mines and that regional Gulf allies have successfully exported more than 1 billion barrels of crude through the strait in recent months. The announcement comes as Washington enforces an “ironclad blockade” against Tehran, which Cooper noted has resulted in Iran exporting “zero barrels” of oil. The U.S. military has supported over 2,000 commercial vessel transits in coordination with Gulf Cooperation Council partners, insurers, and maritime shippers to stabilize global energy flows. Riyadh air raid alerts and escalating Houthi attacks The operational milestone in the Persian Gulf unfolds against a backdrop of escalating regional violence. Early Saturday, Saudi Arabian authorities issued two air raid alerts for Riyadh – the first early-morning emergency warnings in the capital since the height of direct U.S.-Iran conflict in the spring. The Saudi Directorate of Civil Defense confirmed the alerts were subsequently lifted. However, reports emerged of two loud explosions in the capital, followed by a visible plume of smoke near King Khalid International Airport that caused operational delays. The security threats follow weeks of intensified drone and missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure and towns, including an attack on Taif on Thursday that resulted in one death and several injuries.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/77-.text: Operational Overview Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority opened in mid-May to oversee transits and toll payments through the Strait of Hormuz. It has since released three tranches of blacklisted vessel names, on August 24, September 2, and September 14. Windward analysis of all 77 vessels finds that every one used the “unauthorized” southern corridor through Omani waters or transited Iran’s northern corridor without paying any tolls. The list is highly targeted and punitive, aimed at ships deemed to have undermined Iran’s control over the Strait by not seeking Iranian permission to transit. Based on the selection criteria, any vessel using the southern corridor could be placed on the list, as could ships using Iran’s northern corridor with marine insurance linked to Western providers. Inclusion on the list does not appear to have prevented ships from continuing to trade in the region. When adding further vessels to the list on September 14, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority directly referenced classification societies and marine insurers, saying they needed to protect against the consequences arising from dealing with these vessels. Nearly all but six of the blacklisted vessels were assessed as having P&I cover with the International Group of 12 P&I Clubs, which are prohibited from insuring ships that pay tolls to Iran. Tankers Dominate the List 85% of blacklisted ships were tankers. This reflects their disproportionate use of the U.S. military-assisted southern corridor to ship oil exports from Gulf energy companies to market. While the average number of reported U.S.-facilitated transits through the corridor brings total transits to 16% of pre-war levels, crude volumes excluding Iran moving through Hormuz over August were assessed by Windward at 45% of pre-war levels. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/mar.text: The Bahamas has been an IMO member state since 1976 and has served continuously on the IMO strategic body the Council, since 1999. Through the BMA, we participate in committees, sub-committees and their subsidiary groups addressing many of the issues that ultimately affect ships operating under our Flag. That involvement gives us the opportunity to bring practical experience into discussions before new requirements reach the fleet. Owners and managers see quickly where regulation works and where implementation becomes difficult. Our technical teams see how requirements affect different vessel types and trades, while seafarers experience their impact directly. That experience should be reflected when international rules are being developed. The Bahamas is a global leader in maritime governance and was the first nation to ratify the ILO Maritime Labour Convention (MLC, 2006). Acting as a vital diplomatic and technical bridge at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the country continuously drives international safety and environmental policy forward, such as passenger ship safety, fire-fighting systems, MARPOL requirements and cargo classification. In the 2026 legislative cycle, The Bahamas has further co-sponsored major safety and casualty-investigation initiatives which include, but are not limited to, leading proposals to mandate enhanced cargo hold fumigation safety measures by 2027, overhaul marine casualty reporting and investigation frameworks, improving survival craft ventilation and resolving safety harness ambiguities in free-fall lifeboats. Furthermore, it intends to spearhead a global mandate for automated external defibrillators (AEDs) on all vessels. These may be technical subjects, but that is where much of the important work happens. Regulation is stronger when operational experience is brought into the discussion rather than considered only after a requirement has been adopted. The process also must work in the opposite direction, with international decisions translated into clear requirements for the fleet. Earlier this year, The Bahamas introduced a modernised suite of Merchant Shipping Regulations covering areas including registration, safety investigations, inspections and seafarer standards. This may not be headline-grabbing work, but it is fundamental to providing owners with clarity and ensuring international requirements are applied consistently. For our clients, there is a practical benefit in having their Flag State closely involved at the IMO. They should expect us to understand what is coming and what it will mean for their operations, while also knowing that experience from the fleet can feed back into future regulatory discussions. That connection is becoming even more important as shipping tackles decarbonisatio

https://splash247.com/transpacific-europ.text: The world’s two great east-west container trades are moving in dramatically different directions, with the gap between transpacific and Asia-Europe spot rates widening to unprecedented levels. Clarksons Research said in its latest Shipping Intelligence Weekly that “geographic divergence” continued in the container freight market, with Shanghai-North Europe rates falling 5% week on week to $2,425 per teu, while transpacific rates continued to climb on resilient demand. Clarksons said the differential between the two trades has now reached “the widest levels ever seen by some margin.” The scale of the split is even clearer in Xeneta’s latest like-for-like feu data. On September 17, Asia-US east coast spot rates stood at $11,259 per feu, compared with $4,103 per feu from Asia to North Europe – a gap of more than $7,100 per feu. The US east coast market is now within touching distance of pandemic records. Xeneta calculates current rates are only 11.2% below the all-time high of $12,683 per feu set in January 2022. Asia-US west coast rates, at $7,960 per feu, are 17.9% below their covid peak. The reasons behind the divergence are increasingly structural. On the Asia-Europe trade, more services are again routing through the Red Sea, restoring capacity and reducing the tonne-mile inflation created by Cape diversions. That is helping push freight lower even as other sectors of shipping continue to benefit from Middle East disruption. The transpacific, by contrast, is being supported by resilient cargo demand and carrier discipline. Xeneta said offered capacity from Asia to the US East Coast is 6-7% higher in September than August, yet rates have continued climbing. Chief analyst Peter Sand said carriers were “seizing the opportunity while the market is hot” with Sand expecting another rate push around the start of October and China’s Golden Week.

https://splash247.com/is-maritime-neglec.text: Olga Boenigk, the founder of AI goes Maritime, has a different take on the whole shipping and artificial intelligence debate. We’re an industry that’s proud of being careful. We take our time. We wait to see what works before we touch it, and most of the time that has served us well. I’d defend it in a lot of things. But careful only works when the ground stays still. And it isn’t standing still. Ask around shipping about AI right now and you’ll get one of two reactions. A polite brush-off, or a slightly panicked silence while someone works out what they’re meant to say about it. Almost nobody says what they actually think, because almost nobody is sure what to think. Meanwhile, look at what’s happening to the big enterprise systems. The ones everybody bought because nobody ever got sacked for buying them. Talk to the people using them now and you hear the same story everywhere: teams building their own workarounds, quietly, because what they’re paying for can’t do what they need it to. And the vendors are working out that they can’t just bolt AI onto what they’ve already built. They have to think again from the ground up. That realisation is arriving late. The small players smelled this a long time ago. No legacy to protect, no twenty-year roadmap, nothing to migrate. They just build. So the Goliaths are losing ground to the Davids, and not because they’re badly run. Because they’re huge. Huge is slow. And slow is expensive right now.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/rhi.text: Water levels on the Rhine fell to 20 centimeters on Sept. 18, with forecasts now predicting the water levels to reach zero by the end of the month, a development that threatens to shut down barge transport across the entirety of one of Europe’s most important fuel supply arteries, with only partial services on some stretches expected to continue. Water levels at Kaub, the shallowest part of the Middle Rhine, stood at 20 cm as of the evening of Sept. 18, after mostly hovering around 30 cm between Sept. 14 and Sept. 17. The levels are now forecast to approach zero by Sept. 28 and then remain at that level for at least three days, according to data from the German water authority WSV. The Rhine’s low-water crisis continued to constrain product logistics across the region, market participants told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The Upper Rhine destinations are nearing a de facto shutdown as water levels remain critically low. A European trader warned that with no meaningful rainfall in sight, severe navigational restrictions may persist for an extended period without a significant change in weather patterns. German weather service DWD forecasts some rain across Rhineland-Palatinate, where Kaub is located, on Sept. 20, but expects mostly dry conditions on Sept. 19 and Sept. 21.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/ira.text: Iran has laid out conditions for restarting talks with the United States as regional fighting intensifies, with Saudi forces intercepting a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh and the Yemeni group claiming attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera that Tehran had conveyed its demands to Washington through Qatari mediators and was waiting for the U.S. to act before negotiations could resume. Rezaei said Iran had seven conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian assets and the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports. He said Washington must implement Tehran’s conditions before negotiations begin. Rezaei also warned that Iran was prepared for further military confrontation and said U.S. bases could face heavier strikes if Washington launched another attack. He said Tehran remained committed to its existing nuclear doctrine but was considering whether to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty depending on U.S. actions. The diplomatic push comes as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalates. A Saudi-led coalition said air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and thwarted attacks targeting Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu. The Houthis claimed attacks on what they called sensitive targets across Saudi Arabia using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. The group also said it targeted Saudi Aramco facilities in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. The Saudi coalition did not report whether the attacks caused damage.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wor.text: NYK Line, with Japan Marine United Corporation, Nihon Shipyard Co., Ltd., Mitsubishi Gas Chemical Company, Inc., and Kokuka Sangyo Co., Ltd., has completed the world’s first ship-to-ship (STS) ammonia bunkering operation to an ammonia-fueled vessel on September 17. At a quay within Japan Marine United Corporation’s Ariake Shipyard, ammonia fuel was transferred from the ammonia carrier Shoei Maru* via the STS method to an ammonia-fueled medium gas carrier (AFMGC)*** scheduled for delivery in November 2026. The operation was conducted in preparation for sea trials of the AFMGC using fuel ammonia. This achievement represents an important initiative that has put into practice an operation essential for the future practical deployment of ammonia-fueled vessels. Ammonia is expected to play an important role as a next-generation marine fuel because it emits no carbon dioxide (CO₂) during combustion and can contribute to the decarbonization of international shipping. At the same time, its toxicity makes it difficult to handle, and establishing highly safe and reliable operations remains a challenge for practical use. The bunkering operation was conducted following extensive discussions among the companies involved. Safe operating procedures and work processes were established prior to the operation, enabling the transfer to be completed safely. Through this initiative, we have accumulated practical insights regarding safe fuel supply operations. This operation serves as a pioneering example of the fuel-supply framework that will be required for the widespread adoption of ammonia-fueled vessels. The AFMGC is currently in the final stage of construction and is scheduled for delivery in November 2026. The successful completion of this operation marks a significant milestone toward the broader commercial use of fuel ammonia and the practical deployment of ammonia-fueled vessels. It also represents an important step forward in establishing an ammonia supply chain. Source: Nippon Yusen Kaisha

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: On Saturday, U.S. forces in the Caribbean destroyed another suspected drug-running vessel with an airstrike, killing four people. It is the 70th publicized instance of use of lethal force against a drug boat in the region, and highlights the dual-mode structure of U.S. counternarcotics operations in the region: lethal when aerial assets are the sole means of engagement, nonlethal when Coast Guard or Marine Corps boarding teams are involved. The strike targeted a small vessel operating on "established narco-trafficking routes" in the Caribbean. The boat had a cluttered top deck level or canopy, unlike most stripped-down "go-fast" boats or pangas, and it was operating at moderate speed. A large secondary explosion bloomed from the wreckage after the strike. Southcom said that confirmed intelligence indicated that the vessel had involvement in smuggling narcotics. On September 19, under the direction of #SOUTHCOM , Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in… pic.twitter.com/LPNJ5ec3GU U.S. Southern Command is not solely invested in kinetic attack as the only means of conducting interdictions. Within the last two weeks, Marine Corps units under Southcom boarded, cleared and destroyed two different "floating gas station" fuel boats used by drug-runners in the Eastern Pacific. Both boats were blown up after their crews were removed, and the suspects were handed over to Ecuadorian authorities. "We are exerting unrelenting pressure on these narco-terrorists and hurting them where it counts: dismantling their intricate networks, disrupting their sophisticated logistics, and dealing a blow to their finances. https://maritime-executive.com/article/n.text: As the European Union gears to announce its updated list of approved ship recycling facilities, pressure is mounting for the bloc not to include two Indian yards over allegations that they rely on hazardous beaching methods. The European Commission is expected to unveil the 16th edition of its approved list next month, which for the first time is proposing to include yards in South Asia. Indian yards Shree Ram and YSI Recyclers applied to be included in the list; if added, they will be able to pay high South Asian scrap prices to European owners, in fully lawful transactions. Days before the unveiling of the updated list, a group of NGOs, steel companies, recycling yards and unions have teamed up to exert pressure on the Commission not to include the two Indian yards on the list. Through an open letter to Commissioners Jessika Roswall and Stéphane Séjourné, the group said that the yards rely on the beaching method whereby vessels are dismantled directly on the intertidal mudflat, a method that is not only hazardous to the environment but also poses economic and safety risks. In the letter, the group argues that the Alang-Sosiya and other beaching regions in India are known for contamination of soil and marine ecosystems. They cite a case in which a heavy fuel spill occurred in a yard neighboring one of the yards being proposed to be included in the EU list. The spill contaminated parts of the Gujarati coast, spreading easily along the tidal mudflats. The open letter by NGO Shipbreaking Platform, EUROFER, IndustriAll Europe, European Environmental Bureau, Recycling Europe, and Transport & Environment also highlights that governance and environmental monitoring of Indian yards may have limitations. They allege that the regional Gujarat Pollution Control Board has issues with chronic understaffing, inadequate technical capacity, insufficient monitoring and sampling, and weak transparency. “While individual yards can commit to go beyond their national legal framework, it remains unclear how the Commission intends to ensure compliance in third countries without strong public enforcement and environmental governance at national level,” states the letter.

https://g1.globo.com/podcast/o-assunto/n.text: Estamos às vésperas de enfrentar um super El Niño, um fenômeno que pode ser o mais forte em mais de 100 anos. O El Niño é um evento que ocorre de tempos em tempos, mas este tem um agravante: o aquecimento global. A revista Science, uma das mais respeitadas do mundo, publicou um estudo que confirma que a crise climática provocada pela queima de combustíveis fósseis agrava os efeitos desse fenômeno. E o Brasil tem muito a ver com isso. É urgente que o país tenha maior capacidade de lidar com os eventos climáticos extremos – eventos que causam tantos danos, como vimos recentemente na Amazônia e no Rio Grande do Sul. Mas também precisamos reduzir ainda mais o desmatamento de nossas florestas e temos que decidir qual modelo queremos para a extração de petróleo na margem equatorial. Ou seja, a pauta ambiental que vencer esta eleição pode influenciar o futuro de todo o planeta. Neste episódio, Natuza Nery conversa com André Trigueiro, jornalista da TV Globo e editor do programa Cidade e Soluções da GloboNews. Especialista na cobertura ambiental, Trigueiro comenta as propostas (e a falta delas) dos candidatos nesta pauta. Também neste episódio você ouvirá trechos das entrevistas que o produtor Marco Antonio Martins conduziu com os especialistas Suely Araújo, Ricardo Abramovay, Mercedes Bustamante e Natalie Unterstell. Convidado: André Trigueiro, jornalista da TV Globo e editor do programa Cidade e Soluções da GloboNews.

https://g1.globo.com/fantastico/noticia/.text: A polícia investiga esquema de fraude em licitações e suspeita de falsificação de medicamentos para tratamento contra o câncer em vários estados do país. No Rio Grande do Sul, a Operação Placebo cumpriu mandados em junho e prendeu 1 empresário em flagrante com medicamentos que tinham indícios de adulteração. O esquema contava com 1 médico e advogados que indicavam farmácias ligadas ao grupo para vencer licitações e desviar recursos destinados aos pacientes. https://g1.globo.com/mundo/noticia/2026/.text: Um vídeo que viralizou nas redes sociais mostra o momento da colisão em alto mar entre um navio graneleiro de grande porte do Panamá e um barco de pesca da China no Estreito de Singapura . https://www.rigzone.com/news/has_the_oil.text: Has the oil market changed forever following the U.S.-Iran conflict? If so, why? These were the questions Rigzone posed to several oil and gas analysts to try and find out if the oil industry will undergo lasting changes as a result of the recent conflict. In response, Jamie Webster, Partner and Director at Boston Consulting Group’s (BCG) Center for Energy Impact, told Rigzone that the oil market has changed forever, adding that there are “three big macro changes that are underway”. “How energy moves is being rewired and permanent changes will take place,” Webster told Rigzone, outlining one of these changes. “Asia will no longer take ~86 percent of ME oil, we are already seeing significant changes in trade flows and some of these will become permanent (hysteresis to use the economic term),” he added. Outlining another change, Webster said “the energy transition is alive and well and accelerating in various ways with the crisis”.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/vlc.text: Large tankers have steered away from the Bab al-Mandab Strait amid intensifying Houthi military advances and attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, supporting oil shipping rates while other types of commercial ships show more willingness to tolerate Red Sea transit risks. Earlier this month, the militant group’s troops moved southward into the coastal city of Mokha while claiming Perim Island in the strategic waterway, while attacking the East-West pipeline amid an escalation of its conflicts with Saudi Arabia. S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data shows no Very Large Crude Carriers have transited the strait since Sept. 9 after three crossings earlier this week, compared with 24 for the whole of August, and 63 for July. “Mokha and Perim provide the Houthis with their most advantageous position on Bab el-Mandab in years,” said Scarlett Suarez, risk consultancy Dryad Global’s senior intelligence analyst. “The current assessment suggests a significant risk to Saudi-associated tankers and cargoes, [and] an increased likelihood of targeted strikes at the choke point,” Suarez told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. The development came after the Houthis declared a naval blockade on ships sailing to and from Saudi ports July 20 before attacking several tankers operated by Bahri, the Saudi state carrier.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/str.text: A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water. Experts have identified these and many other visual signaturesin the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there’s an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk. One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill. Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills. There are likely several other spills that we don’t know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an “ecological catastrophe” and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems. “People should be concerned,” Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken “a very, very heavy toll on the environment,” she said, with the damage now reaching new scales.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tur.text: Turkey has sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine that would end attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, a Turkish diplomat told AFP. The move follows a sharp uptick in attacks in the Black Sea, which has seen at least 25 Turkish-owned vessels hit since late June, industry figures show. “We have shared a text of a memorandum, a draft text, with the Russians and the Ukrainians to come up with a solution to those strikes taking place in the Black Sea,” the diplomat said. He said the proposal was “inspired by” the grain corridor mechanism – a 2022 deal brokered by Turkey and the UN to grant safe passage for Ukrainian grain to be exported via the Black Sea without risk of attack. Although Russia pulled out a year later, Ukraine set up an alternative path via a shipping route that hugs the coast of Romania and Bulgaria. “In that mechanism, there is maybe a four- or five-mile gap where the Ukrainian ship has to leave the national territorial waters and travel in international waters, which is the risky part,” he explained.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/sau.text: Saudi Arabia found a new route for crude exports after halting operations of its east-west pipeline linking the country due to an attack by Iraq’s Iran-aligned militias. The method is to sail back through the Strait of Hormuz, which had been effectively blocked by Iran’s threat, and then transfer the oil to another vessel off the coast of Oman. On the 17th (local time), the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, “A ‘shuttle service’ through the Strait of Hormuz is now emerging as Saudi Arabia’s best alternative,” adding, “The biggest hope for calming oil prices now depends on crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia’s ability to quickly repair damaged infrastructure.” After the war with Iran broke out and the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blocked, Saudi Arabia continued exports by sending crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast via the east-west pipeline. According to analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA), the rerouted crude exports that avoided the Strait of Hormuz offset about one-fifth of the crude supply decline that occurred in July–August due to the strait’s closure. However, with the east-west pipeline shut down by the attack and the threat from Iran-aligned Houthi rebels growing in the Red Sea, it became difficult to use the existing alternative export route. In response, Saudi Arabia turned to shuttle service through the Strait of Hormuz. In this shuttle operation, tankers typically form a convoy under U.S. military protection at night or switch off their automatic identification system (AIS) transceivers to slip through the Strait of Hormuz, then conduct ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman to load crude onto other vessels waiting there. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is also known to be moving crude through the Strait of Hormuz by deploying its own ships or chartering others. Estimates vary widely for how much crude is exiting the Strait of Hormuz this way. Because ships turn off their transponders, which are location-tracking devices, it is difficult to track actual movements. Commodities traders estimate that about 9 million barrels per day of crude and petroleum products are leaving the strait this way. As Saudi Arabia increased crude supplies to Asian countries via shuttle service, Brent futures, the global benchmark, settled at $104.82 per barrel, down $1.01 from the previous session, signaling steadying international oil prices. Still, the risk of attack remains because ships must pass through the Strait of Hormuz again. According to Al Jazeera, Richard Matthews, head of consulting and research at London-based shipping services firm Gibson Shipbrokers, said, “Vessels are likely to move with AIS transceivers turned off and coordinate with the U.S. Navy,” addi

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/lng.text: The LNG freight market experienced a volatile but generally firmer week, supported by stronger LNG commodity prices, ongoing geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East, and increased market activity. Market sentiment improved as concerns over the Strait of Hormuz and low European gas storage levels boosted LNG price expectations, although this did not translate fully into physical shipping demand due to ample vessel availability. Baltic LNG assessments strengthened significantly through the first half of the week before easing slightly on Thursday. BLNG1 (Australia-Japan) increased from $26,800/day at the start of the week to finish at $27,200/day. BLNG2 (US Gulf-Continent) climbed from $21,500/day to a peak of $26,900/day before ending the week at $23,900/day. BLNG3 (US Gulf-Japan) posted the strongest gains, rising from $40,400/day on Monday to $53,400/day by Friday. Chartering activity was concentrated around Australian and Qalhat requirements in the Pacific, while US Gulf export opportunities dominated Atlantic basin enquiries. Winter cover interest remained evident, with some charterers opting to secure spot tonnage amid still-competitive freight levels. However, it was reported that plentiful vessel availability continued to limit upward momentum in rates. In the period market, the six-month assessment declined to $45,600/day, while one-year and three-year rates remained broadly stable at $52,533/day and $72,350/day respectively. The LPG market continued to strengthen this week, supported by strong arbitrage economics and exceptionally tight vessel availability. VLGC freight ex-US reached fresh highs, with several fixtures concluded above $300/mt HCvP and only a handful of vessels remain available for prompt October requirements. On the BLPG1 Ras Tanura–Chiba route, rates settled at $242.00, with TCE earnings closing at $231,509/day.
