https://safety4sea.com/cm-operating-in-c.text: From the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea to the southern Red Sea, merchant vessels are operating in areas where military activity can directly affect commercial shipping. The nature of the threat differs by region, but the operational challenge is the same: security conditions can change quickly and require continuous reassessment. U nlike traditional piracy or armed robbery, conflict-related threats may include missile and drone attacks, mines, military interception and strikes against nearby ports or infrastructure. Three regions currently illustrate these risks particularly clearly. The security situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz remains highly volatile. As of 15 September 2026, IMO had recorded 80 confirmed incidents involving shipping in the wider Middle East since the current conflict began. Recent incidents have involved vessels damaged in the Strait, Gulf and waters off Oman, with seafarer fatalities and injuries also reported. Commercial traffic through Hormuz has meanwhile fallen sharply from normal levels. For vessels operating in the region, exposure may include missile or drone attacks, mine risks, interception or detention, as well as disruption caused by military activity and changing restrictions on navigation. The key challenge is therefore not only the severity of the threat, but the speed at which the operating picture can change between voyage planning and actual transit . IMO has repeatedly stressed that the situation remains unresolved and that the protection of seafarers must remain the overriding priority. Thousands of seafarers have been affected by the disruption, while vessels have at times been unable to leave the Persian Gulf safely. For operators, the key challenge is that conditions considered acceptable during voyage planning may be substantially different by the time the vessel approaches the area.

https://safety4sea.com/when-one-meal-can.text: A dish that appears perfectly harmless can quickly become a serious health risk if allergens are not identified, information is not communicated clearly, or cross-contact occurs during preparation, highlights Stella Leontiou, Head Nutritionist at BSM Catering. F or most people, sitting down for a meal onboard is simply part of the daily routine. But for a seafarer living with a food allergy, every meal comes with an important question: “Is this safe for me to eat?” Have you ever stopped to think how difficult it can be for someone with a food allergy to eat confidently while living away from home for months at a time? At sea, allergy management presents unique challenges. Seafarers share the same galley, eat from the same menu, have limited access to alternative ingredients, and may be days away from medical assistance. In this environment, preventing problems before they happen is not simply good practice – it is an essential part of protecting crew health and safety. While some allergens are obvious, others can easily be hidden in everyday ingredients such as sauces, marinades, dressings, desserts, baked goods and processed foods. Would you immediately recognise that a stock cube, seasoning mix or ready-made sauce contains soy, sesame or another allergen?

https://safety4sea.com/hydrogen-takes-to.text: A Japanese coastal tanker has completed a two-hour demonstration voyage powered by a hydrogen-fuelled engine, marking what the Nippon Foundation has described as the world’s first carbon-neutral demonstration sailing using the technology. T he 4,500-gt Kikou Maru travelled approximately 33 kilometres through Osaka Bay on 25 September, operating its hydrogen-fired engine throughout the voyage. The demonstration was carried out under the Nippon Foundation’s Zero-Emission Ship Project, an initiative aimed at accelerating the development and adoption of zero-emission technologies for Japan’s domestic shipping sector as the country works towards carbon neutrality by 2050. The voyage represents a test of hydrogen as a potential marine fuel for coastal vessels, particularly in a sector where operators are seeking alternatives to conventional fossil fuels while maintaining the range, reliability and safety required for commercial operations. The engine employs a pilot-ignition system, allowing hydrogen to be used as the primary fuel for propulsion. According to the Nippon Foundation, the demonstration reduced carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 1.2 tonnes compared with operating the tanker on conventional fossil fuels. The result provides an early indication of the potential emissions benefits of hydrogen propulsion in domestic shipping, although wider commercial deployment will depend on factors including fuel availability, bunkering infrastructure, vessel conversion costs and operational safety.

https://safety4sea.com/eu-court-challeng.text: The European Union’s General Court has partially annulled the European Commission’s decision concerning the Taxonomy criteria for shipping, finding that the Commission had failed to properly address methane-slippage emissions from ships. T he ruling means the Commission must revisit the relevant criteria and establish a measurable threshold for methane emissions from vessels. The decision places limits on the Commission’s discretion when setting environmental criteria under the EU Taxonomy Regulation, which defines which economic activities can qualify as environmentally sustainable. The case was brought by a group of NGOs, which challenged the inclusion of fossil-fuelled ships and aircraft under the EU’s sustainable finance rules. The organisations argued that the criteria were too weak and could allow high-emitting transport activities to be classified as sustainable investments. The court’s ruling specifically concerns methane “slippage” from ships. The NGOs which include Dryade, Fossielvrij NL, and Protect our Winters Austria, supported by legal experts Opportunity Green and CLAW, said the European Commission had failed to establish a clear threshold for methane emissions from vessels under the Taxonomy criteria. As a result, the Commission must now set a quantifiable limit for methane slippage emissions from ships. The organisations said the ruling sends a broader signal about the climate impact of fossil gas in shipping, arguing that LNG should not automatically be treated as a clean transition fuel because of methane emissions associated with its use.

https://www.gov.br/antaq/pt-br/noticias/.text: Brasília, 02/10/2026 - A Agência Nacional de Transportes Aquaviários (ANTAQ) realizou, nessa quarta-feira (30), o segundo encontro do workshop Agendas em Sincronia, iniciativa criada para ampliar a integração entre as diferentes áreas da Agência e aproximar seus instrumentos de planejamento. Desta vez, o debate teve como foco os subsídios recebidos durante o processo de revisão da Agenda Regulatória 2025-2028 e as possibilidades de tratamento de temas que também dialogam com outras frentes de atuação da instituição. Conduzido pela Superintendência de Regulação (SRG), o encontro apresentou o processo de revisão da Agenda e o tratamento dado às contribuições recebidas. Ao todo, foram validadas 99 contribuições, provenientes das unidades da ANTAQ, do público externo e do Ministério de Portos e Aeroportos. Desse total, 17 foram consideradas elegíveis no âmbito da Agenda Regulatória. As demais passaram por análise para identificar outras possibilidades de tratamento dentro da Agência. Entre as contribuições classificadas como novos temas, 21 foram selecionadas para discussão no workshop. A proposta foi colocar esses assuntos em diálogo com as áreas que já desenvolvem trabalhos relacionados, permitindo avaliar de que forma cada demanda pode ser aproveitada ou tratada no âmbito das diferentes agendas da ANTAQ. As discussões passaram por questões relacionadas à navegação interior, fiscalização, interoperabilidade e governança de dados, desempenho portuário, transparência de cobranças aos usuários, qualidade dos serviços e capacidade operacional dos portos. Para cada contribuição debatida, foram indicadas áreas para conhecimento e avaliação quanto à pertinência de eventual tratamento, respeitadas as competências de cada unidade. Para o superintendente de Regulação, José Renato Fialho, a integração entre as áreas permite ampliar o olhar sobre os temas discutidos: “Mais do que definir em qual agenda cada contribuição deve entrar, queremos criar conexões entre os trabalhos que já são realizados na Agência. Muitas vezes, um mesmo tema pode ter diferentes dimensões e ser melhor compreendido quando as áreas compartilham informações, experiências e perspectivas", destacou. O workshop Agendas em Sincronia foi criado para aproximar os diferentes instrumentos de planejamento da ANTAQ. A iniciativa parte do entendimento de que, além da atuação especializada de cada unidade, temas comuns podem exigir maior troca de informações e uma visão integrada entre regulação, fiscalização, estudos, agenda ambiental, planejamento e gestão.

https://gcaptain.com/no-lights-no-radio-.text: A sailor observes the oil tanker HELGA, which is moored at one of Iraq's southern offshore oil terminals near Basra, as it prepares to load crude oil, April 24, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty Oct 2, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The tanker captain summoned his years of experience when he saw the blast in front of him. He veered his 300-meter-long ship around the vessel ahead and could see a fire had started. He called the US Navy to tell them of the attack. The maneuver in the Strait of Hormuz with drones and missiles overhead is the sort of quick thinking that’s proving vital to getting oil supplies to the global market as Washington and Tehran fail to reach agreement on reopening the waterway to regular traffic. The account of the incident, told to Bloomberg by a captain in his early 40s who declined to be identified while discussing commercially sensitive journeys, shows how and why those flows from the Middle East are rising largely under the watch of the US military. His vessel is among the ships engaged in shuttle runs through the strait, ferrying barrels often at night and with strict instructions about what equipment can be used — no lights, no phones and with only one radar. They were often just a mile from the coast of Oman, though the depth of the sea there is about 100 meters, more than enough for even the biggest supertankers to sail through. The captain said he and his crew got their bearings by using the coast and lighthouses as a reference.

https://www.marinelink.com/news/dnv-back.text: BW Offshore's blue ammonia floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) concept, jointly developed with McDermott, has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from DNV, advancing the proposed offshore low-carbon ammonia production solution towards further design development. The AiP provides an independent, risk-based assessment of the concept at an early stage and establishes a basis for further design development, certification and classification. Unveiled in February, the FPSO concept is designed to process up to 3 million cubic meters of natural gas per day and produce more than 1 million tonnes of ammonia annually. The unit would convert natural gas supplied from offshore fields into hydrogen and then ammonia, while carbon capture technology is designed to capture and compress up to 99% of the CO2 generated during production. The captured CO2 could then be exported for geological sequestration or other approved uses. The concept has an estimated carbon intensity of around 0.5 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of ammonia, with options to further reduce emissions from onboard power generation systems. Locating the production facility near offshore gas resources and CO2 storage sites is intended to reduce reliance on the land, permitting and infrastructure required for large onshore facilities. Liquefied ammonia would be stored in refrigerated tanks in the FPSO hull and offloaded directly to gas carriers, avoiding the need for pipeline or port infrastructure.

https://gcaptain.com/six-vessels-hit-in-.text: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker has been struck in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the number of vessels reported hit in the strategic waterway since Sunday to at least six. UK Maritime Trade Operations said Friday that the master of a tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile while conducting an outbound transit of the strait at 1122 UTC. The impact caused a small fire and a blackout onboard. The fire was extinguished and the tanker was able to continue underway, UKMTO said. No casualties or environmental impact were reported. Authorities are investigating the incident, designated UKMTO Warning 148-26. UKMTO has not identified the tanker or said who may have been responsible for the attack. The latest strike adds to a growing tally of attacks around the Strait of Hormuz over the past several days.

REUTERS/Stringer RIYADH, Oct 2 (Reuters) – Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters. The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will by led by Yemeni forces on the ground, which are overseen by Riyadh, and supported by Saudi air strikes, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations. While the US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, and some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, the Saudi allies aren’t expected to play a direct role in combat operations, said the people who requested anonymity to discuss security matters. Saudi Arabia entered neighboring Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war. A key objective of the planned Saudi offensive, which hasn’t been previously reported, is aimed at reversing the rapid gains made by the Houthis last month when they advanced down the coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, according to the people with knowledge of the plans who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.

https://petronoticias.com.br/bw-offshore.text: A empresa norte-americana de engenharia e construção offshore McDermott e a norueguesa BW Offshore estão mais próximas de tornar realidade sua solução flutuante de energia de baixo carbono, após receberem a aprovação da DNV para o conceito conjunto de uma unidade flutuante de produção, armazenamento e transferência (FPSO) de amônia azul. O aval é considerado um passo importante para viabilizar a produção flutuante de amônia de baixo carbono em larga escala. A empresa norueguesa explica que a AiP representa uma avaliação independente e baseada em riscos do conceito em uma fase inicial de desenvolvimento. A demanda por combustíveis de baixo carbono está crescendo, impulsionada pelos esforços de descarbonização em setores como transporte marítimo e geração de energia “, disse a BW Offshore. A validação do conceito abre caminho para uma produção offshore de amônia em escala, considerada um avanço importante diante do aumento das pressões por descarbonização nos setores de transporte marítimo e geração de energia. A BW Offshore acrescentou: “ Gostaríamos de agradecer à McDermott pela forte colaboração no desenvolvimento do conceito e à DNV por sua análise criteriosa e construtiva. https://maritime-executive.com/article/i.text: India is making further progress in positioning itself as a global leader in the export of alternative fuels in shipping. Ports Minister Sarbananda Sonowal and Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel recently participated in laying the foundation for an e-methanol plant at Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) in Kandla, Gujarat. This is the first port-based e-methanol production facility in India. The project is part of the government’s wider campaign to promote cleaner maritime transport in the country. The facility is also poised to make India a competitive global supplier of green shipping fuels. The plant is scheduled to produce green methanol at much lower cost compared to other global producers, just $750 per ton, against a global rate of $1,300 per ton. Recent research has highlighted three Indian ports with strategic advantages to support green fuel production. DPA on India’s west coast is one of the mentioned ports, which is already hosting major investments in green hydrogen production. Last year, the port commissioned L&T Energy to build a 1 MW green hydrogen plant as part of a larger 10MW project. Again, DPA in April conducted India’s first methanol bunkering demonstration, which at the time was said to be a lead-up activity to the e-methanol plant. With the facility now launched, India’s role in global maritime decarbonization is firming up. The $240 million plant is expected to produce 150 tons per day of e-methanol once fully built. It will use green hydrogen, water, and biogenic CO2 to produce the e-methanol. DPA is targeting to become a major bunkering hub for methanol-powered vessels plying the Asia-Europe trade corridor. “The long coastline of Gujarat will now power the world’s ships through Kandla. This plant turns our renewable energy strength into an export,” said Bhupendra Patel. The plant is a joint initiative between DPA and Assam Petro-Chemicals Ltd. (APCL), and installation will be done in phases, as scalable modules. Phase 1 will have 50 tons per day capacity at an investment of $125 million. The targeted completion date is January 2027. Phase 2 will add a further 100 tons per day at a cost of $115million, to be completed in March 2027. DPA will contribute 76 percent of the project’s capital while APCL will contribute the remaining 24 percent.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/g.text: Marine investigators in Canada released a report outlining how gaps in situational awareness and a breakdown in communication caused a collision involving a tug, a barge, and a workboat in Squamish Harbor, British Columbia, in December 2024. The incident involved the tug Haisla Northwind, the barge BSG Lubricator, and the workboat Triton 1. It occurred in the marine safety zone of the Woodfibre LNG Project site. The incident on December 18, 2024, occurred while the tug was pushing the barge on a scheduled run carrying provisions to the Isabelle X, a former ferry that was being used as a floating accommodation (floatel) for project workers, which was moored at the site. The barge collided with Triton 1, which was idling on standby, causing the workboat to capsize and sink. The workboat’s operator, who was the only person on board, entered the water before being rescued by the workboat Roe 5 that was nearby and was treated for hypothermia. Only minor pollution was observed following the collision, with spill containment booms being deployed as a precaution. While no damage to the tug or barge was reported, the Triton 1 was not salvaged. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) has released its report on the incident , indicating that gaps in situational awareness and breakdown in communication were the main cause of the collision. The report shows that as Haisla Northwind pushed BSG Lubricator forward, visibility from the wheelhouse was obstructed by structures on board the tug and the barge, which reduced the tug master’s ability to visually detect the Triton 1 as it idled on the water. Due to the obstructed visibility from the wheelhouse, the master of Haisla Northwind was not aware of the workboat directly on his path. The investigators also established that bright lights from the construction site and nearby vessels also reflected off the water, creating glare that made the Triton 1’s navigation light difficult to distinguish from other lights in the area. It was also established that Triton 1’s operator heard no arrival message on the VHF radio, did not expect any vessel to be approaching, and his attention was distracted by a cellphone call. Also, the operator is said to have expected the workboat’s navigation lights to make it visible to other vessels.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/i.text: The issue of fatigue among tug operators at the Panama Canal is again attracting attention after the captain of a tugboat is said to have died due to a grueling work schedule. The International Transport Workers' Federation (ITF) is calling on the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) to take action after a 59-year-old captain died aboard the tug Cerro Santiago. The captain died on September 30 while assisting a northbound Neopanamax vessel. He was said to have been working an extended midnight watch on his sixth consecutive day of duty. While initial reports indicate the captain of the 2013-built tug died due to a possible stroke, ITF wants the cause of death to be established through a thorough, independent, and transparent investigation. The ITF is making reference to the fact that fatigue among tug workers has, over the years, been a major issue of concern. For that reason, the investigation into the captain’s death, it says, must include reviewing the possibility of fatigue and must include mechanisms to enforce workers’ protections in terms of rest, consecutive duties, working hours, and staffing. “Unions in the canal have been warning about safety risks associated with fatigue for years, and those warnings must now be heard,” said Stephen Cotton, ITF General Secretary. He added that the authority must address the issue of fatigue by putting limits on consecutive duties, allowing workers to have proper rest, and hiring more people to have safe staffing levels. While the authority has remained quiet on the captain’s death, the issue of fatigue among tug operators continues to be a concern for the critical waterway that is the maritime trade route handling about 40 percent of U.S. container traffic and approximately five percent of world trade.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/str.text: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October. Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships. These meetings are an important part of how we represent your interests. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators. Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops. Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The continued discussions on the IMO Net-Zero Framework and revisions to the EU ETS also received significant attention. Operational and human factors featured prominently, including enclosed-space fatalities, hydrogen sulphide exposure, fatigue, crew welfare, criminalisation and suicide prevention.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/the.text: Shipping is turning back to one of the oldest tricks in the book as modern sails find their way onto tankers, container ships and LNG carriers. The past couple of months have seen a streak of developments around wind-assisted propulsion, spanning installations, orders, vessel launches, technology approvals and new trials. These are not just small-scale demonstrations, with major shipping companies across multiple ship types now entering the field. Maersk is preparing to fit a rotor sail on a container ship. Odfjell has ordered wind-assisted propulsion for a second tanker. Wallenius Lines is adding it to an LNG-capable dual-fuel vehicle carrier. MOL has launched an LNG carrier equipped with wind-assisted propulsion. Bulkers, tankers, cargo ships and gas carriers are all getting some version of the technology. It is still far too early to call wind-assisted propulsion mainstream. Just 99 vessels are currently equipped with the technology, according to DNV data. Bulkers account for the biggest share with 25 vessels, followed by general cargo ships and oil or chemical tankers with 24 each. There are also 11 ro-ro cargo ships and eight gas tankers fitted with the technology.

The impact on medium-range tanker earnings in particular could be swift and severe, BRS said Sept. 28. US President Donald Trump had floated a diesel export ban in response to record domestic fuel prices ahead of midterm elections. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/wha.text: There Is No Official Shadow Fleet List The shadow fleet, also called the dark fleet, refers to tankers and support vessels that rely on deceptive shipping practices to move sanctioned or high-risk commodities while concealing their true origin, ownership, or destination. That definition is broadly recognized in practice. It has no standing in law, and that is where the difficulty starts. No international convention defines the shadow fleet, no regulator maintains a register of it, and no two organizations use the term identically. A vessel is treated as part of the shadow fleet because of how it operates. Its composition shifts as vessels are sold, reflagged, or designated, but vessels rarely leave it. Once a tanker is trading sanctioned crude with non-Western insurance and opaque ownership, the commercial route back to mainstream trade is largely closed. The practical consequence is a mismatch. Compliance screening is built to verify identity, which means the vessel, its flag, its registered owner, and whether any of them appear on a sanctions list. The shadow fleet is defined by conduct instead. A vessel can return a clean result on every identity check and still be operating entirely inside it. Why Every Published Estimate Is Different Ask five organizations how large the shadow fleet is, and you will get five answers, sometimes differing by a factor of three. Estimates vary widely, and the older ones are now substantially out of date. The European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic service, put the range at 600 to 1,400 vessels.

In third place is Argentina, whose exports typically peak from May onwards, with a 2.8% share so far in 2026, followed by Uruguay with 1.3% and Canada with 1.0%. In Jan-Aug 2026, Argentina exported just 3.4 mln tonnes of soybeans, down -43.1% y-o-y from the 6.0 mln t in Jan-Aug 2025. In terms of imports, the top destination for soybeans so far in 2026 is still Mainland China, accounting for 65.0% of global seaborne imports. Imports to China increased by +2.0% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2025 to 107.6 mln tonnes. In Jan-Aug 2026, Chinese imports increased by +4.0% y-o-y to 75.5 mln tonnes. Imports to the European Union declined by -6.2% y-o-y in Jan-Dec 2025 to 13.5 mln t. In Jan-Aug 2026, however, European imports recovered by +5.2% y-o-y to 9.7 mln tonnes. The EU now accounts for 8.3% of global seaborne soybean imports”, the shipbroker said. It added that “top soybean discharge ports in China in Jan-Dec 2025 were: Rizhao (9.6 mln t in Jan-Dec 2025), Machong (7.4 mln t), Tianjin (7.2 mln t), Zhangjiagang (7.0 mln t), Gaogang (5.4 mln t), Fangcheng (4.2 mln t), Nantong (4.2 mln t), Dongjiakou (4.0 mln t), Ningbo (3.6 mln t). 93.1% of soybean imports into China in 2025 were loaded on Panamaxes (including Kamsarmax), 6.3% on Supramaxes, 0.3% on PostPanamaxes. In Jan-Aug 2026, arrivals of US soybeans into China were broadly stable, down -1.1% y-o-y to 12.3 mln tonnes, following a -10.8% y-o-y decline in Jan-Aug 2025. This was also below the 13.9 mln t delivered from the USA to China in Jan-Aug 2024. The USA now accounts for 16.2% of China’s imports so far this year. Brazil accounted for 75.5% of China’s soybean imports in Jan-Aug 2026, with volumes from Brazil to China essentially flat at +0.4% y-o-y in that period, at 57.0 mln tonnes. It is important to consider the seasonality of soybean crops. Brazilian exports are shipped mostly in the Spring, from February to July, and will appear in China’s import statistics from March to August. USA exports, on the other hand, normally peak in the fourth quarter of the year, and should be the most active trade in the winter months. With the peak Brazilian season now largely reflected in the Jan-Aug 2026 import figures, attention turns to the upcoming US export season in the fourth quarter, which will indicate whether China returns more actively to the US crop this year”, Banchero Costa concluded. https://maritime-executive.com/article/d.text: With the naval blockade preventing any Iranian tankers leaving the Gulf, for the last 10 weeks Iran has been selling oil from the stocks it had built up for just such a contingency which are being held afloat primarily off Malaysia and China. Historically, Iran has sold 90% of its exports of crude to China. Chinese purchasers are still wary of being subject to US sanctions because these sanctions have global effect. To be sanctioned may entail being excluded from global dollar transactions, and thus impinge on wider business activity. So the Iranian brokers collude with the Chinese purchasers to disguise the origin of the oil being sold, and to hide the nature of the transactions which are used to pay for the oil. Chinese purchasers, normally from the independent teapot refineries of Shandong, have been happy to collude, because in exchange for taking on the risk of being sanctioned they receive a discount on the purchase price of the oil. But between the Iranian state entities owning the oil at source, and the final Chinese end-user and his refinery, is a network of middlemen and brokers, organizing the physical shipment of oil and the ship-to-ship transfers which are used to disguise its origin. Often the same middlemen and brokers are then involved in channeling payments for the oil, masking the origin and destination of the payment, structuring and layering transactions through a series of front companies so that it can integrated back into the legitimate financial system without trace of its antecedents, with the nature of what has been paid for disguised. The system for years has depended on a blind eye being turned to these transactions as they pass through the financial system, with certain governments either tolerant or complicit in jurisdictions where those profiting are closely connected to officials or ministers. But for those middlemen and brokers who for years have skimmed profits from this sanctions evasion, times recently have become very hard. Because the product which is being bought and sold – sanctioned Iranian oil – is drying up fast, as stocks afloat are sold and run down. These middlemen and brokers are known in Iran as trustees because they are entrusted with the State’s oil and then are expected to pay for it. They are also trusted because they are closely connected to families in the highest level of the ruling clerical elite, and being privileged can travel and transact with the regime’s protection in a way most other Iranians cannot. Besides not having product to sell, these trustees are now under major attack from two quarters. https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: A review of Poten's Daily Market Report, which monitors spot freight rates on many of the key tanker trade routes, shows eyewatering numbers. The wars in Europe and the Middle East have created significant inefficiencies in the market. On top of that, there is the threat of attacks in areas like the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Black Sea, which have spiked insurance rates and risk premiums. Widespread sanctions have also limited the availability of mainstream vessels that have the flexibility to trade worldwide. Last, but not least, ownership of the large tanker fleet (in particular VLCCs) is more concentrated than in the past, which, in combination with the other factors, has shifted some of the negotiating power from the charterers to the owners. The big question is: How high can it go and how long will it last? It is safe to say that it has already gone higher and lasted longer than most people expected. The follow up question could be: is there a level at which freight rates start to restrict oil demand? In the oil markets, when prices spike (like in the early weeks of the war against Iran), people start talking about which price levels will lead to demand destruction. Obviously, there are no hard and fast numbers, it very much depends on the circumstances and which countries/regions they are talking about. However, oil analysts typically focus on quoted oil prices for Brent, WTI, etc. when discussing this topic. In the current market, that is a mistake. Freight needs to be taken into account. Historically, freight was such a small component of the delivered cost of a barrel of oil that it could be easily ignored. As recently as January of this year, this was still the case. https://maritime-executive.com/article/o.text: Oman’s Maritime Security Centre has issued a series of new instructions regarding the passage and presence of ships transiting its territorial waters. The new regulations are grounded in a Royal Decree (30/2026) published at the beginning of the year, before war broke out, and are based on the interpretation of the Royal Decree made by the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology. The Ministry is responsible for oversight of maritime matters in the Sultanate, and has been known for its commitment to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The new instructions do not apply either to warships, to ships designated for military purposes, or to vessels making their way to Omani ports. In other words, the rules apply to vessels transiting through Omani territorial waters, or those who wish to anchor in Omani territorial waters. Foreign-flagged vessels are required to apply for a formal navigation license through a shipping agent at least three days in advance. Licenses will not be issued unless vessels have valid flag registration and insurance certificates, including Protection and Indemnity (P&I) insurance. - Only enter protected or restricted areas after having obtaining official approval. It is not clear where such areas are, but will presumably be updated in Notices to Mariners. Enforcement of these regulations will pose a considerable challenge to the Omani Coast Guard, given the volume of traffic and that the regulations apply to vessels transiting Omani territorial waters. Many such vessels may enter and exit Omani territorial waters before enforcement action can be taken.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/i.text: On Sunday, Iran hit another tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, extending a fast-paced run of attacks on the "shuttle" shipping trade between Gulf oil producers and the STS transfer zone in the Gulf of Oman. Industry media sources have reported that the vessel sustained engine room damage. U.S. Central Command's Joint Maritime Information Center logged three more Strait of Hormuz incidents on Saturday. During the first tanker's Hormuz transit, a drone flew down the funnel and entered the engine room, causing a small fire and brief loss of power; the second tanker was hit on the port quarter, damaging the engine room and prompting a tow; and the third tanker was struck on the port quarter, causing it to lose propulsion. No injuries were reported in any of Saturday's incidents. Over the past week, the pace of successful Iranian strikes has sped up following weeks of relative security. The attacks put pressure on the steady flow of tanker traffic through the waterway, which had recently rebounded to more than 12 million barrels per day - enough to restore total Gulf export volume to nearly prewar levels. Strait of Hormuz: five tankers struck in four days Iranian forces struck the Kuwaiti VLCC KAZIMAH III in the Strait of Hormuz on 1 October. It is the fifth tanker hit since 28 September and the second Kuwaiti state VLCC in four days. Neither Kuwaiti tanker was on the PGSA NCV list. Most of the recent victims were transiting AIS-dark. Gulf crude flows are holding up through a dark tanker shuttle and ship-to-ship transfers. In the Black Sea, a Turkish-operated bulk carrier was disabled near Novorossiysk with one crew member missing. Off Somalia, Puntland has recovered two hijacked tankers, but the pirate networks remain intact as the monsoon ends. https://gcaptain.com/iraq-shifts-oil-str.text: Drone view of oil tanker HELGA berthed at one of Iraq's southern offshore oil terminals near Basra as it prepares to load crude oil, becoming the second vessel to arrive since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, April 24, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty Oct 4, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Iraq’s state tanker company arranged a very large crude carrier to transport 2 million barrels beyond the Strait of Hormuz, marking a move toward offering oil outside the Persian Gulf . Iraqi Oil Tankers Co. loaded a VLCC and arranged for it to sail through the strait “for the first time in decades,” Director General Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar said in video comments published on the Oil Ministry’s Facebook page. Previously, buyers would have arranged for supertankers to collect Iraqi crude at Basra, near the head of the Persian Gulf. Read Also: Thousands Of Trucks Haul Iraq’s Oil Through Syria In Sign Of Hormuz Legacy The transit marks a shift in how Iraq markets its crude, with the state tanker company taking responsibility for moving a shipment beyond the critical strait. Delivering outside the Gulf could help Iraq reach refiners reluctant to send vessels through Hormuz and secure better prices, reducing the discounts needed to attract buyers to its southern terminals. Oil producers across the Middle East are rushing to secure tankers to underpin their ability restore flows of crude and refined fuels through the strait, following disruptions caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping arm is among those building the capacity of its tanker fleet.

https://petronoticias.com.br/grupo-atem-.text: O Grupo Atem iniciou as operações de uma base fluvial em Itacoatiara (AM), estruturada pela Navemazônia para apoiar a transferência de cargas de navios para balsas durante o período de vazante dos rios. A nova estrutura faz parte do planejamento do grupo para reduzir os impactos de eventuais restrições à navegação e manter o fluxo de petróleo e derivados até Manaus e outras localidades do Amazonas. A estratégia combina o monitoramento dos rios com a antecipação de viagens e formação de estoques, reforço da frota e informações produzidas pelo Laboratório de Modelagem do Sistema Climático Terrestre (Labclim), da Universidade do Estado do Amazonas (UEA). Segundo atualização apresentada pelo Labclim em 17 de setembro, o fenômeno El Niño atingiu a categoria “muito forte” e poderá continuar influenciando as chuvas e os níveis dos rios até março ou abril de 2027. O cenário deste ano, entretanto, permanece diferente das estiagens registradas em 2023 e 2024. Em Manaus, o Rio Negro segue em processo de descida, mas ainda dentro da faixa considerada normal para o período. A maior atenção está concentrada no Alto Rio Negro, onde os volumes de chuva e os níveis dos rios permanecem abaixo do padrão esperado. As projeções climáticas são utilizadas em conjunto com a experiência acumulada pelo Grupo Atem durante as estiagens de 2023 e 2024. A partir desse aprendizado, Refinaria da Amazônia, Atem Distribuidora, Navemazônia, responsável pelo transporte fluvial, e Rodoamazônia, que atua no transporte rodoviário, passaram a trabalhar de forma integrada para adaptar embarcações, estoques, rotas e modais às condições de navegabilidade. O número de balsas-tanque empregadas pelo grupo em 2026 mais do que dobrou em relação a 2024. Segundo a empresa, a ampliação da frota aumenta as possibilidades de remanejamento de estoques e de utilização de embarcações com características adequadas às diferentes condições encontradas durante a vazante. “ Nas estiagens anteriores, aprendemos na prática que não existe uma única solução para enfrentar as restrições de navegabilidade. É preciso combinar antecipação de estoques e viagens, diferentes embarcações, rotas e modais. Hoje, somamos essa experiência às informações produzidas pelo monitoramento climático para tomar decisões com maior antecedência ”, afirma Guilherme Santana , vice-presidente de Distribuição e Operações do Grupo Atem. Um dos pontos de atenção durante o período de vazante é a Costa do Tabocal, na rota de acesso a Manaus. A redução do nível do rio pode limitar a passagem de navios de grande porte responsáveis pelo transporte de petróleo e derivados destinados à Refinaria da Amazônia, que fornece combustíveis para distribuidoras, empresas de navegação e outros setores.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/rhi.text: Water levels on the Rhine river slumped to fresh record lows for the second time in a week, Oct. 1, the German water authority reported, preventing fuel tanker deliveries from making their way inland and dashing hopes for a rapid rebound in traffic ahead of peak winter demand levels. After a summer of record temperatures and droughts across Europe, low water levels have become an increasingly serious threat to the continent’s busiest river, typically a vital conduit for energy, metals and chemicals to reach inland markets. Earlier this week, a car carrier ship was reported to have run aground at Dusseldorf harbor, while elsewhere on the continent, a slump in Danube river levels recently revealed lost WWII-era shipwrecks and forced power plants to shut down. Official readings from the German water authority WSV showed water levels in Kaub, the Rhine’s shallowest point, had dropped 6 centimeters below its 113 cm benchmark level, surpassing a previous all-time low of minus 2 cm against the baseline threshold recorded on Sept. 29. The WSV’s benchmark rate, or “zero” reading, varies in different segments of the river, subject to water depth. Falling water levels at the Kaub pinchpoint in Germany follows reports of record low water levels in parts of the lower Rhine, which runs from near Bonn in Germany to the border with the Netherlands. Readings at the Dutch village of Lobith and Cologne in Western Germany hover only slightly above recent all-time lows, recorded Sept 28-30. The historically low water levels have stopped most tanker traffic from navigating the Upper Rhine, which traverses southern Germany to the neighboring Swiss market, putting extra pressure on already-tight fuel stocks affected by the US-Iran war. Swiss government data showed that heating oil costs hit their highest since 2022 in September, climbing 8% from the previous month’s average. According to data from Spotbarge, a Dutch shipping and bunker monitoring company, only two specialist chemicals barges, Raadsman and Millora managed to transit the Kaub crossing Oct 1, but shipping was otherwise at a standstill. Only a few captains and barge companies are willing to risk the voyage in such extreme conditions, with regular vessels having to wait for WSV levels closer to plus 60-70 cm, or a minimum of 173 cm at Kaub, before attempting to make the voyage.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/fro.text: This year’s IMO theme for World Maritime Day is “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence”. Can you tell us what this actually means from a shipowners’ and managers’ perspective? For owners and managers, it comes down to what happens once new requirements or standards are introduced following the adoption of international regulations. That is the point at which they must assess what those requirements mean for their vessels, their crews and their day-to-day operations. This is where The Bahamas Maritime Authority, as a Flag State, has an important role to play. We must ensure that requirements are clearly communicated and supported by practical guidance to enable effective implementation. Equally important is the feedback we receive from owners, managers and seafarers, who are often the first to identify what works well in practice and where challenges may arise. For me, that is the true meaning of “From Policy to Practice”. Agreeing and adopting regulations is only the first step. The real measure of success is whether those regulations achieve their intended objectives once they are embedded within management systems and applied on board ships. Are we making ships and shipboard systems safer? Are we strengthening security? Are we improving environmental performance? Are we providing appropriate training and safeguarding the health and wellbeing of seafarers? Most importantly, are we giving those responsible for implementation a framework that is practical and workable? Those are the questions that define maritime excellence. As regulation becomes more complex, how can Flag States help owners in understanding the changes? Is BMA actively involved in this process?

https://splash247.com/why-shippings-nich.text: Mark O’Neill discusses the likely shipping impact as the world shifts from globalisation to regionalisation. For decades, global shipping has been built around a simple premise: the more integrated the world economy became – governed and regulated by a sophisticated and universally respected international rules-based order – the more efficient, standardised and global maritime transport would become. Massive fleets, standardised vessels, containerisation, global networks and economies of scale transformed shipping into the indispensable infrastructure and catalyst of globalisation. The big shipping players became bigger and metamorphosed into complex, integrated, global logistics operations, and the small players slowly became more and more uncompetitive and irrelevant. The geopolitical environment has become significantly more complex and multi-layered, while the international maritime framework that underpinned the predictability of global trade is showing increasing signs of strain. Trade tensions, sanctions, regional conflicts, strategic competition between major powers, white/grey/dark fleets, disruptions to established shipping routes and the growing use of economic measures as instruments of foreign policy are making global trade massively less predictable and manageable. The result is not necessarily the end of globalisation. Rather, it is a shift towards regionalisation, towards specialisation, towards niche. Supply chains are being re-considered and are increasingly being designed around resilience, security and proximity as well as pure cost efficiency. Cargo owners are considering nearshoring, friendshoring and multi-regional sourcing. Shipping routes that once appeared permanent can suddenly become commercially or politically unattractive. The ability to change routes, ports, cargo configurations and operating models quickly is therefore becoming a competitive advantage. The companies that benefited most from globalisation were often those able to standardise and commoditise their services at enormous scale. Large operators could deploy vast fleets, optimise networks and spread costs across millions of tonnes or TEUs. Standardisation was the source of their competitive advantage.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/why.text: Around 99% of Australia’s trade by volume and 87% by value is carried by sea, making maritime transport essential to the nation’s economic prosperity and connection to global markets. At the same time, international shipping is beginning a major transition toward zero- and near-zero-emission fuels and technologies, driven by evolving regulation, customer expectations, and supply chain decarbonisation commitments. Australia’s shipping-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from commodity exports are estimated at around 34 million tonnes annually, equivalent to approximately 8% of the country’s total GHG emissions. Although these emissions are not directly captured within Australia’s domestic emissions targets or policy framework, the Australian economy remains highly exposed to shipping’s net-zero transition. Maritime decarbonisation is therefore not simply a climate issue, but an economic, energy security, and strategic opportunity for Australia. As key trading partners such as Japan, South Korea, and China move to reduce emissions across global supply chains, Australia’s competitiveness will increasingly be influenced by the emissions performance of the products it exports and the systems used to transport them. Australia’s resources and energy exports are forecast to generate more than AUD $400 billion in export earnings in 2026-27, with iron ore alone accounting for more than a quarter of those earnings. Supporting the uptake of clean maritime fuels can help ensure Australia remains integrated into the low-emission supply chains being developed by its major trading partners. It will also help maintain the international competitiveness of key export industries, including iron ore, critical minerals, agriculture, aluminium, and other energy-intensive sectors. At the same time, it will reinforce Australia’s reputation as a reliable trading partner in a low-carbon global economy. As these trading partners pursue green steel, low-emissions manufacturing, and broader industrial decarbonisation pathways, demand for lower-emission commodities and supply chains is expected to grow. Shipping could provide one of the earliest sources of demand for alternative fuels such as ammonia, helping unlock investment in fuel production, storage, transport, and bunkering infrastructure. Realising this opportunity will require coordinated policy, investment, and industry action to scale the fuel production and supporting infrastructure needed to provide confidence for private investment. Concentrated export hubs and shipping routes—such as those supporting Australia’s iron ore exports—offer practical opportunities to aggregate demand, demonstrate commercial viability, and support the growth of Australia’s emerging clean fuel industry.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/los.text: The first article in this series examined accidents involving loss of bridge control due to a mechanical or electrical failure in conventional steering systems. However, accidents can also occur when systems are fully functioning. They can be triggered by wrong settings applied by the crew. Amidst the panic when control is lost, crew have only minutes or seconds to properly diagnose the issue and steps taken to try and regain control can make matters worse. Case 1: Full ahead while alongside In the first accident we consider, there was virtually no time to react. The accident also occurred when least expected: when the vessel was moored alongside. The fishing vessel had a controllable pitched propeller, on which the blade angles can be rotated for forward or reverse thrust without changing the direction of the engine’s rotation. On the passage leading up to arrival in port, propulsion control had been transferred from the bridge to the engine room for maintenance. When that was completed the engine room pitch control lever was left in full-ahead position. The vessel berthed under bridge control and when all was secured, propulsion control was transferred back to the engine room for shut down. That transfer was accepted without checking the pitch control lever, which remained in the full ahead position in the engine room. The vessel moved forward, broke her moorings, and rammed into another vessel berthed broadside ahead. This caused serious damage, flooding and pollution. Fortunately, no one was harmed. The investigation found no documented procedure for the changeover between control stations, such as prior confirmation of pitch lever positions. Fatigue after a long shift likely also played some part. Classification society rules were also analysed and unified rules required “means to prevent the propelling thrust from altering significantly when transferring control from one control to another”. However, individual class society interpretation and application of the rules can differ. In this case, class approval was based on a factory acceptance test and a system designed (as per the manufacturer’s manual) without interlocks or synchronised settings. Due to safety concerns, work was postponed until Sunday. “Our immediate priority is to safely assess the condition of all three cranes and determine the steps necessary to restore operations,” Respicio said. “Our gantry crane mechanics, operations personnel and management team are mobilizing early Saturday morning. We will focus our resources on safely returning available equipment to service while developing the operational plan necessary to support the upcoming vessel schedule.” Efforts resumed Sunday, and the team reported some success. They used heavy equipment to roll Crane 5 away from Crane 4, making space for the work to restore Crane 4 to service. So far, the port has not changed its cargo operations scheduled. The next two vessels to call both have ro/ro cargo, which can be offloaded without the gantry cranes.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/a.text: The Asyad Group’s Drydock subsidiary, which operates a substantial facility within the inner harbor at Duqm in Oman, has seen a massive expansion of its workload during the first eight months of 2026. The increase is likely attributable to the inability of regional clients to access ship repair within the Gulf, given the closure of the Strait of Hormuz – but also to the increasing range of services that the Asyad Drydock is now able to offer. The drydocks attracted 56 new international clients, adding to a client base of 900 existing customers, and had completed 119 ship repair and maintenance projects over the eight-month period. By comparison, 230 projects were completed over the 24 months of 2024 and 2025, thus reflecting a 55% increase in workload so far this year. The yard has also expanded into shipbuilding and has two projects underway for undisclosed customers. The addition of a floating dock (supplementing the existing dry dock) has meant that 13 ships could be drydocked during the period, in comparison to two projects undertaken over the same period last year. To deal with demand for its services, the facility had started to moor ships side-by-side for maintenance projects, enabling the yard to increase throughput and complete simultaneous projects. The additional work has had the beneficial effect of increasing workforce skills and experience. There is now an expanding local supply chain network, which has grown as the commercial opportunities have developed, and the value of work let to local sub-contractors and suppliers reached $32.5 million during the eight month period. This type of work is particularly important for expanding the manufacturing segment of the non-oil related segment of Oman’s GDP activity, a key target in Oman’s broader economic reforms.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: The carrier USS George H.W. Bush has arrived at the port of Phuket, Thailand for a one-week R&R call, ending a six-month voyage at sea. Analyst Tom Bike spotted her movements off the coast of Sumatra on Oct. 3, and she was photographed pulling into port at Phuket with tug assistance on October 4. She has about 4,800 crewmembers aboard, not counting the additional personnel aboard the escorts in her strike group. The last carrier to call in Thailand, USS Abraham Lincoln, went to the more frequently-used port of Laem Chabang, a few miles away from the traditional R&R destination of Pattaya. Phuket has similar attractions as a well-known resort town, plus convenient Indian Ocean access for Mideast naval operations. USS George H.W. Bush's departure from the Arabian Sea leaves only one carrier operating within reach of Iran, the USS George Washington. The USS Theodore Roosevelt and her strike group are under way in the Pacific, likely bound for the Mideast to augment or provide relief for Washington. Bush's departure is also part of a broader perceived drawdown in the U.S. presence. Most of the 12-strong force of B-1B bombers staged at RAF Fairford in the UK - a jumping-off point for long-range strikes over Iran - flew home to the continental U.S. over the weekend, reducing the U.S. Air Force's ability to conduct short-notice heavy bombardment in the Mideast. A small gang of UK nationals mounted what local authorities believe to have been an attempted terrorist strike on RAF Fairford - and potentially the U.S. bomber force - on September 27. A British-Iranian dual national was detained in connection with that incident last week. All of the suspects have been released pending further investigation.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/t.text: The Royal Navy's UK Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) has reported an attempted attack on a tanker at a position south of Mokha, Yemen, the latest in a string of strikes widely attributed to Yemen's Houthi rebel group. The militia, which has been advancing rapidly into areas controlled by the internationally-recognized Republic of Yemen government, has not claimed responsibility for the attempted strike. At about 1650 hours UTC, the company security officer for a vessel operator informed UKMTO that a tanker's crew had spotted "multiple explosions in close proximity to the vessel." The crew is unharmed and there was no environmental impact, UKMTO said. An inquiry is under way. UKMTO advises vessels to proceed with caution near Bab el-Mandeb. Recent Houthi strikes have focused narrowly on Saudi-linked vessels, both in the group's rhetoric and in its actual attack patterns, but EOS Risk Group's Martin Kelly warns that Houthi target selection criteria have previously tended to expand when hostilities escalate. The attempted strike followed just hours after the Yemeni government publicly announced the launch of a major military operation targeting Houthi positions, with active support from Saudi forces. The Houthis have been making significant military gains against the IRG in recent weeks, seizing most of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and advancing on key government positions. They have also engaged in a series of effective attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting Aramco's energy infrastructure with significant effects. Over the weekend, a Houthi drone and missile attack reportedly reached a refinery in Riyadh, 500 miles from the border; meanwhile, Saudi forces conducted airstrikes in the vicinity of Taiz, a Yemeni government stronghold that is in increasing danger of encirclement. Houthi fighters have reportedly cut the road between Taiz and the Yemeni seat of government in Aden. The New York Times reports that Saudi advisors are on the ground in Yemen, assisting government troops with tactics and targeting. Two U.S. officials confirmed that a large cohort of U.S. military intelligence analysts are supporting the Saudi side of the effort with target identification and selection - though the Trump administration has reportedly declined to provide direct combat support for Saudi forces.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: The U.S. Coast Guard launched a large-scale search over the weekend following a report that a medical transport jet went down off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts. At about 0200 hours on Saturday morning, the Federal Aviation Administration notified the Coast Guard that the Gulfstream G100 (IAI Astra) air ambulance plane had crashed during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. Six people were aboard the aircraft, four flight crew members from Canada and two passengers from Bermuda. The USCG soon located floating debris in the water near the suspected crash site, and multiple units responded to the scene. In all, three search planes, three helicopter aircrews, one motor lifeboat and the cutter USCGC William Sparling joined the effort at various points over the weekend. Flight tracking data suggests that the incident area was located south of the island over open ocean. As of Sunday, the responders had searched about 4,400 square miles of ocean. There were no further signs of survivors, and the Coast Guard called off the search effort on Sunday. The next of kin have been notified. "Suspending a search is not an easy decision," said Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard's Northeast District. "We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts." An investigation into the cause of the crash is under way. An early review of flight data shows that the plane slowed down and plummeted from its flight altitude of 24,000 feet just after 0100 hours, an hour before the FAA sounded the alarm, according to the New York Times.

https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: For the first time in decades, the United States is being forced to think seriously about naval shipbuilding as an allied industrial problem. Years of delayed programs, strained yards, maintenance backlogs, workforce losses and shortages, and the near-disappearance of commercial shipbuilding have converged with China’s extraordinary maritime-industrial expansion; old assumptions about U.S. defense-industrial sufficiency are untenable. In its May 2026 Shipbuilding Plan, the Navy formally crossed an important conceptual threshold. It describes the failure of American shipbuilding as structural, acknowledging that requirements expanded during execution, mature designs were modified, and cost estimates and construction schedules proved chronically optimistic. More consequentially, the plan embraces stable long-term demand, distributed construction, foreign investment in American yards, selected overseas module fabrication, possible overseas construction of some naval vessels, and maintenance support from allied shipyards. That conceptual shift makes South Korea the first serious test of whether declared American reforms can be translated into industrial practice. The growing role of Hanwha, HD Hyundai, and Samsung in U.S. maritime-industrial discussions, reinforced by the Korea-U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership Initiative (KUSPI), will reveal whether American institutions can adapt their expectations, contracting practices, and production systems sufficiently to employ Korean expertise and industrial depth against the Chinese maritime challenge. The maritime-industrial crisis is broader than the familiar catalog of delayed ships and strained shipyards. The U.S. fleet declined from a Cold War peak of 568 battle force ships in 1987 to a low of 271 in 2015. The May 2026 plan counted 291 battle-force ships against the statutory objective of 355 and acknowledged that the shipbuilding budget had doubled over the preceding two decades without producing a larger fleet than the Navy possessed in 2003. Under the FY2027 projection, the battle force reaches only 299 ships by 2031. The plan instead introduces a broader “Total Naval Vessel Force” of 450 vessels in 2031 by adding 68 auxiliaries and 83 unmanned vessels to those 299 battle-force ships. Virginia-class submarine production, meanwhile, remains roughly 1.1 to 1.2 boats per year against the long-stated two-per-year objective. EUNAVFOR ASPIDES/Handout via REUTERS SINGAPORE, Oct 5 (Reuters) – Crude oil exports from the Middle East rose above pre-war levels in four of the seven days of the final week of September, shipping data showed on Monday, despite attacks on vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to between 19.5 million barrels per day and 22.5 million bpd, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed. Exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February this year beforethe US-Israeli war with Iran began. The 7-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd on October 1, the data showed. These include transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. The overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30, Kpler data showed.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/met.text: HHLA’s subsidiary METRANS has completed the extensive expansion of its terminal in Poznań/Gadki, Poland. Two new remote-controlled railway gantry cranes, extended and additional tracks, as well as expanded storage and service areas, have boosted the site’s capacity. Maximum storage capacity has risen from 8,850 TEU to 11,800 TEU, while the annual handling capacity has increased by almost 80 per cent to around 590,000 TEU. METRANS operates a hub terminal in Gądki, near Poznań, Poland’s fifth-largest city. The subsidiary of Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG (HHLA) handles rail containers at the site and provides temporary storage facilities. Gądki is an important hub in METRANS’ intermodal network, connecting the Polish market with major economic centres across Europe. With real GDP growth of 3.6 per cent in 2025, Poland is one of the fastest-growing economies in the EU. Its GDP recently stood at around 923 billion euros, making Poland the EU’s sixth-largest economy. Peter Kiss, CEO of the METRANS Group: “Gądki demonstrates how modern inland terminals and a strong rail network can improve the connection between seaports and customers across Central Europe. By investing in capacity, technology and efficient rail infrastructure, we are creating the conditions for reliable intermodal transport and the efficient movement of cargo between ports and their hinterland. Poland’s dynamic economic development offers strong potential for further expanding METRANS’ European network.” A key focus of the expansion project was the modernisation and extension of the container terminal. Two new remote-controlled railway gantry cranes, each with a span of 80 metres, now handle the transhipment between modes of transport. The project included the construction of the crane runway with power supply and a remote-control station, as well as two additional tracks. The three existing tracks were extended to over 750 metres. This enables the Gądki terminal to handle even the longest freight trains. To accommodate the simultaneous expansion of the container storage, transhipment and transport areas, 53,000 m² of paved operational areas were newly constructed. Modern camera gate systems now support handling operations and automatically identify containers as they enter the terminal. They also record the condition of containers when they are delivered by rail or road. The technical equipment is complemented by a rail weighbridge for monitoring the axle loads of rail vehicles and a container weighing system.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/nep.text: The Neptune Bunker Information tab has been updated with bunker quality data covering April to September 2026, providing Members with further insight into regional fuel quality trends and areas of elevated risk. Several ports record high levels of technical off-specification results across the residual and low-sulphur fuel sectors. Among HFO samples, the highest technical off-specs were recorded in Antwerp (46.2%), Norfolk (41.4%), Panama Canal (38.0%), and Rotterdam (35.5%). The issues varied by location but commonly included density, viscosity, water content, catalytic fines and ash-related exceedances. These figures remain significantly above those reported at other major bunkering hubs. For VLSFO, sulphur non-compliance requires additional attention in Europe. Rotterdam samples recorded a sulphur off-spec rate of 68.6%, while samples in Antwerp reached 58.9%, the highest levels seen in the current dataset. Although the number of samples involved is substantially smaller than in other major bunkering ports, the results underline the importance of maintaining robust bunker procurement, testing and fuel management procedures, particularly in respect of emission control regulatory requirements. Within the ULSFO category, the highest technical off-spec percentages were reported in Barcelona (70.3%) and Genoa (51.0%). In both ports, the results were primarily associated with pour point non-compliances, highlighting the need for careful consideration of storage and handling requirements, particularly where low ambient temperatures may become operationally significant. Members are encouraged to continue following established bunker testing and fuel management practices and to make use of Neptune’s fuel quality intelligence when evaluating supply risks and preparing bunkering plans. Source: West of England

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/lat.text: Medium and heavy crude is the market’s real shortage Middle Eastern supply outages have pushed the global crude balance into a deficit of roughly 1 to 2 million b/d, with these outages driving down the availability of heavier grades in particular. Alternative sources of medium-density supply are increasingly scarce. Europe, which lacks domestic medium-density crude and is heavily import-dependent, is facing mounting challenges on this front: Johan Sverdrup, its largest medium-density field, has peaked and is expected to decline around 10% year on year in 2026, while Western sanctions continue to keep Russian medium crude largely out of the market. With these traditional sources constrained, the market has little slack to absorb outages, as seen in the recent disruption at Yanbu and the East-West pipeline. When such outages hit, refiners are left with two choices: pay up for alternative medium-to-heavy grades, or run lighter crude instead and sacrifice middle distillate yields. It’s this scarcity dynamic, not just the outage itself, that explains why Guyana’s medium-yielding barrels have been bid up so sharply recently, following the disruptions at the East-West pipeline, since they’re one of the few substitutes available. High middle distillate cracks are set to drive continued demand of heavier grades, a potential US diesel export ban, though dismissed as speculation by the US administration, would keep middle distillate cracks elevated outside the US regardless, further incentivizing refiners globally to ramp up consumption of medium crudes. Together, this is the backdrop that makes Latin America’s heavier grades, Venezuelan crude in particular, so relevant to refiners well beyond the region. Argentina and Guyana are pulling in opposite directions from Brazil Vaca Muerta’s growth has accelerated further in recent months, and the main constraint, pipeline capacity, is set to ease once YPF’s new pipeline comes online in late 2026 or early 2027, pushing supply above 1 million b/d. New licensing deals with US independents, new tax incentives and cheap associated gas are all pulling in fresh capital. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/rus.text: Russia could consider partially opening diesel exports once it returns to a production surplus, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told its Federation Council Oct. 2, describing the market as balanced and sufficiently supplied, local media reported. Traditionally the world’s number-two diesel exporter, Russia started shutting in its diesel production in July following persistent Ukrainian drone attacks on its refining sector, now extended until the end of October. For non-producers, which include traders and refineries with capacities of less than 1 million metric tons/year, the ban will remain in place until the end of January. The deputy prime minister added that given Russia produces more diesel than it consumes, it is necessary to avoid accumulating more stocks than the country has the capacity to store, which would force refineries to reduce throughput and affect the output of other products. Novak’s comments come a day after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said at the Valday Forum in Moscow that Russia had sufficient diesel but warned the fuel wouldn’t make it to international markets because of foreign sanctions. “We already have enough diesel fuel. But it won’t reach global markets because of the bans and sanctions against our oil and petroleum products,” Putin was reported to have said at the forum, according to the transcript posted on the Kremlin website. By the end of August, analysts at S&P Global Energy CERA estimated that almost half of Russia’s primary refining capacity was offline due to Ukrainian drone strikes, with persistent and targeted attacks often hitting the same sites repeatedly during the month. On Oct. 1, Putin estimated that Ukrainian strikes had shaved off about 1% of Russia’s GDP.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/dp-.text: DP World, the Ogun State Government and Ogun Deep Sea Port Company Ltd have signed two Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) to explore the development of a greenfield deep sea port and special economic zone in Ogun State, Nigeria. The MOUs were signed by His Excellency Prince Dapo Abiodun, Governor of Ogun State, and Yuvraj Narayan, Group Chief Executive Officer of DP World. His Excellency Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, attended the signing ceremony. The proposed development would bring together a deep-sea port and special economic zone across a 10,000-hectare site, creating a major new maritime and trade hub for Nigeria. Located along the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the development would connect industry and manufacturing with port infrastructure, logistics and global markets in one location. With one of Africa’s largest consumer markets and significant potential for industrial and manufacturing growth, Nigeria has an opportunity to further strengthen its position as a major hub for African trade and industry. Combining a deep-sea port with an adjacent economic zone would bring manufacturing, logistics and global connectivity together in one location, helping attract investment, support new industries and jobs, and give Nigerian businesses more efficient access to global markets. H.E. Prince Dapo Abiodun, Governor of Ogun State, said: “The agreements we have executed today for the Ogun Deep Sea Port and the Ogun State Blue Marine and Special Economic Zone formalise the beginning of two strategic projects that will reshape Nigeria’s economic landscape whilst providing over 50 000 direct employment opportunities.” Yuvraj Narayan, Group Chief Executive Officer, DP World, said: “Nigeria is a strategically important market for DP World and one where we have operated, invested and grown for more than a decade. The MOUs reflect our long-term commitment to Nigeria and our ambition to support its future trade and connectivity with infrastructure and logistics capabilities that help Nigerian businesses connect to global markets and grow.” Mohammed Akoojee, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, Africa, DP World, said: “This project creates a strategic new gateway for Nigerian trade, connecting businesses and industries more efficiently to markets across Africa and the world. By bringing together port infrastructure, logistics and an economic zone, we can create an environment that supports industry, attracts investment and helps Nigerian businesses compete globally.”

https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: The role of the ship manager is expanding at a time when owners are applying increased pressure on management fees. That tension should concern the whole European shipping industry. Shipmanagement should not only be viewed through the lens of the traditional ship manager. This term now refers to second and third-party management companies, like Columbia, and joint ventures between owners and managers. Whatever the set-up, the issues remain the same as many are being asked to take on more responsibility for a range of factors, from decarbonisation to complex regulations, crew welfare and increasingly sophisticated onboard technology. Too often, however, management services are still procured primarily on price. That model is becoming harder to sustain. Ship management is not simply an administrative function sitting behind the shipowner. It is the operating system of a vessel, the beating heart that connects owners, seafarers, suppliers, technology providers and regulators, and turning strategy into day-to-day performance on board. Europe therefore needs to think differently about what it wants from its ship management sector. It should not aim to be the cheapest. It should aim to be the safest, smartest and most trusted. If Europe allows its ship management capability to weaken, it risks losing far more than management contracts. Technical expertise, quality maritime jobs, operational knowledge and data move with those businesses, as a result, capital and ownership are also likely to gravitate towards the strongest management ecosystems. Shipping is also facing a shortage of experienced officers at the same time as ships are becoming more complex. AI-assisted decision-making and tighter environmental regulation are increasing the level of competence required, both at sea and ashore. The industry cannot solve the problem through recruitment alone, we need to retain and develop people throughout their careers. Reliable rotations, better connectivity, strong leadership, mental-health support and clearer pathways from sea to shore all have a role to play as well as a more focused approach on training for the next generation of seafarers. At the same time, Europe must remain international in its outlook. A strong European ship management sector does not mean relying exclusively on European seafarers. Its strength comes from combining European maritime expertise with talented people from across the world. This also relates to the increasing importance of technology in ship management.
