REUTERS/Chris Radburn SEOUL, Oct 11 (Reuters) – A South Korean container ship completed the country’s first commercial round trip to Europe via the Arctic on Sunday, as authorities bank on the route helping turn the port of Busan into a global maritime hub. The PanStar Acro docked in the southeastern port 50 days after setting sail on August 22. Authorities say the Arctic route could cut typical voyage times by around a third. President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping a priority, and officials hope to launch regular services by 2030. But the project risks friction with Western allies hoping to keep Russia isolated during its war in Ukraine. The route runs along Russia’s Arctic coast, and Seoul consulted with Moscow about the journey, including whether the ship needed ?help to tackle any problems, such as getting stuck in ice. On its outbound voyage, the vessel passed through Arctic waters and reached its first European port, Felixstowe in Britain, before calling at Rotterdam and Gdansk and returning home via the Arctic.

REUTERS/Hamad I Mohammed For a sign of just how extraordinary oil shipping costs have become, consider this: It’s now more expensive to hire a tanker from the US to China than to launch a rocket into space. That journey costs about $80 million, compared with $74 million for a standard SpaceX Falcon 9 launch, shipbroker Gibson said this week. The same amount of money could have bought a near-identical tanker outright earlier this year. The eye-watering prices are the result of a global tanker shortage that is getting worse with every additional barrel of oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. For weeks now, supertanker markets have been in the middle of a boom the likes of which industry veterans have never seen. Brokerage SSY says that, even after adjusting for inflation, rates are now the highest since the first supertankers hit the world’s oceans in the 1960s — surpassing the tanker wars of the 1980s, when Iran and Iraq attacked commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf. “There’s really not quite enough shipping to go around,” Russell Hardy, chief executive officer of Vitol Group, the world’s biggest independent oil trader, said at a conference this week. “We’ve had pretty parabolic pricing.” The surge is a fresh complication for an oil market that has spent months adapting to the historic disruption caused by the Iran war. Higher shipping costs are making crude more expensive for buyers, eating into refining margins and adding to inflationary pressures in energy markets.

The past fortnight has delivered a clear reminder that the industry’s regulatory problem is no longer a shortage of rules. It is the widening distance between what is agreed in London and Brussels and what can actually be demonstrated on deck, in the engine room and in a ship’s emissions data. Start with the audit evidence. The IMO has completed the first cycle of its mandatory Member State Audit Scheme, with 168 Member States audited since 2016. That is 94% of the membership, and one of the broadest assessments of maritime governance ever attempted. The organisation says the findings, corrective action plans and consolidated reports have exposed recurrent areas requiring attention, and their root causes. It has not published a league table, and it is unlikely to. The second cycle begins in July 2027 under a more risk-based, data-driven continuous monitoring mechanism. That diplomatic restraint is understandable. It is less helpful to owners, managers and charterers who must judge the real quality of oversight behind a flag and the recognised organisations acting on its behalf. A valid certificate confirms that a survey took place. It does not, on its own, confirm the condition of the ship on the day it matters. Port state control continues to fill that gap, and this autumn it is doing so with a sharp focus. The Paris and Tokyo MoUs are running a joint Concentrated Inspection Campaign on the securing of cargo units and cargo transport units, from 1 September to 30 November 2026. Inspectors are working through a standard questionnaire. Is there an approved Cargo Securing Manual aboard? Is it being complied with? Are sufficient approved portable securing devices carried, and are fixed and portable devices in good condition? Each ship faces one CIC inspection per MoU during the campaign. Outcomes range from a recorded deficiency to detention. The results will be analysed and presented to both MoUs’ governing bodies, with a view to later submission to the IMO, so the data gathered this autumn may well shape future rules. https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: There has been no appreciable change in the Royal Navy's dire financial situation, which has seen its capability sink below what is operationally necessary in several important areas. There had been some hope that the resignation of John Healey as Minister of Defense over the lack of commitment to raise UK defense spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 would finally bring about a commitment from the UK’s government to achieve the target. Hopes rose further when Healey was subsequently put in charge of the nation’s finances after new Prime Minister Andy Burnham appointed Healey as Chancellor of the Exchequer. But it now appears that the resignation of John Healey as Minister of Defense was less a matter of principle regarding defense spending and part instead of maneuvers to unseat Sir Keir Starmer as Prime Minister and replace him with Andy Burnham. There have been no additional funds allocated to defense since the government reshuffle, and a decision as to when spending should be increased to fund the 3% of GDP target by 2030 has apparently been further delayed, pushed from the budget and spending review this year into some time later next year. Furthermore, the new prime minister has made it clear that welfare spending is a higher priority than defense. Defense did not get a mention in the Prime Minister’s recent keynote political strategy speech at the annual convention of his party. The delay – if indeed it is a delay – has serious strategic implications, as it demonstrates to the UK’s adversaries that not only is there a continuing capability gap, but also a lack of resolve and will to put effective deterrence in place. In the short term, this increases the likelihood that the UK will be subject to incrementally-increasing hybrid attacks, which might expand from unattributable drone attacks on airbases in the UK to ballistic missile attacks on overseas bases such as RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Of all the services, the shortfall in current operational capability is being felt the hardest in the Royal Navy. The lack of immediate additional funding is lengthening the delay before equipment currently in the build pipeline will be delivered, extending the period before capability is restored to the bare minimum. The Ministry of Defence is already struggling to fund its existing program, leading to in-year cuts to training and ammunition expenditure.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: For the first time in weeks, U.S. forces have used kinetic methods to disable a ship in the Gulf of Oman for allegedly running the American blockade on Iran. On Saturday, an American fighter jet struck the stern of the freighter Ocean Molica. The crew were uninjured and the vessel was fully disabled, U.S. Central Command reported. The vessel had departed an Iranian port at some point prior to the strike and was moving through the Gulf of Oman, the command claimed in a statement. U.S. Forces Disable Cargo Vessel Attempting to Violate Blockade TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Oct. 10, after the ship’s crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran. A U.S. military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew. The large cargo vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after having previously departed an Iranian port. CENTCOM forces resumed America’s blockade against all ships entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14. Four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships have been turned around during three months of strict enforcement. Additionally, U.S. forces have destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' multibillion-dollar shadow network over the same period. All mariners are advised to heed blockade warnings from CENTCOM forces. Crews should also continue to monitor Notice to Mariners broadcasts and contact U.S. naval forces on bridge-to-bridge channel 16 when operating in the Gulf of Oman and Strait of Hormuz approaches. It was the fourth merchant ship that CENTCOM has disabled in connection with the ongoing blockade of Iranian ports, which resumed in its current form on July 14. The number does not count the 10 "head-for-an-eye" retaliatory strikes that the U.S. military conducted on Iranian tankers for each Iranian attack on GCC-linked tonnage. A residência oficial de Bocharov Ruchey, localizada em Sochi, já foi usada por líderes soviéticos como Nikita Khrushchev e Leonid Brezhnev e pelo primeiro presidente da Rússia após o fim da União Soviética, Boris Yeltsin. Putin se hospedou ali pela primeira vez antes de sua posse, em maio de 2000, e desde então passou a receber com frequência líderes estrangeiros no local. Em 2008, o imóvel passou a ser uma residência presidencial oficial. Isso significa que o chefe de Estado pode, ali, "se hospedar, trabalhar, morar e exercer todas as suas funções, inclusive a de comandante supremo das Forças Armadas", segundo Vladimir Kozhin, então chefe do Departamento de Administração de Propriedades da Presidência da Federação Russa. Putin esteve em Sochi 24 vezes em 2021, um ano antes da invasão em larga escala da Ucrânia, mas fez apenas duas visitas à cidade em 2024 e 2025, segundo o jornal britânico Financial Times. A redução das viagens de Putin à região do mar Negro coincidiu com o aumento do alcance dos drones ucranianos, que passaram a atingir com mais frequência a região costeira. Ainda assim, o governo não abandonou a residência oficial Bocharov Ruchey. Uma investigação da BBC News Rússia mostra que a residência está sendo reconstruída praticamente do zero, em escala muito maior e com um esquema de segurança mais rigoroso.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tan.text: According to Gibson, “the increase in attacks coincided with the breakdown of talks following the UN General Assembly in late September, suggesting that Iran is once again escalating attacks in the absence of any progress towards a diplomatic resolution. Surprisingly, the US is yet to publicly retaliate, as it did during early September when several tankers were sunk or disabled, though this could change after the midterm elections in early November. Remember “a tanker for a tanker”? With the rate of attacks high, vessel supply could tighten further as more vessels are removed from service pending repairs. Not all attacks are reported, and the common practice of having AIS turned off in the region makes it difficult to track the period following attacks. Many vessels remained dark following the incidents, making it hard to determine whether trading operations were impacted for a prolonged period, particularly for vessels controlled by national oil companies. However, evidence also suggests many vessels were patched up and quickly returned to service. Around a third of the vessels attacked had sufficient data to track downtime. On average, these vessels waited two months following the attack before loading their next cargo, though some required more extensive repairs in dry dock.” Meanwhile, according to Gibson, “the Middle East has not been the only region where tankers have been targeted. In the Black Sea, frequent attacks were seen over the summer against Suezmaxes and Aframaxes loading at the CPC terminal and other Russian ports. https://petronoticias.com.br/a-arabia-sa.text: A Arábia Saudita promete intensificar os ataques contra os terroristas houthis apoiados pelos iranianos após o ataque mortal no aeroporto de Riad, capital do país. O ataque, que representou uma escalada significativa na campanha dos houthis contra os sauditas e expôs a vulnerabilidade do reino a ataques contra infraestruturas civis. Bernard Haykel(foto principal), pesquisador sênior da Fundação para a Defesa das Democracias (FDD), afirmou que a Arábia Saudita já conhecia há tempos a capacidade dos houthis de realizar tais ataques, particularmente com o que ele descreveu como apoio do Irã e das milícias xiitas iraquianas. “A minha impressão é que eles não vão ceder. Eles não vão simplesmente se render aos Houthis por causa disso. É improvável que a Arábia Saudita recue diante dos houthis. O reino provavelmente intensificará sua campanha militar contra o grupo terrorista apoiado pelo Irã.” Haykel afirmou que Riade agora enfrenta uma escolha entre chegar a um acordo com os houthis ou intensificar sua campanha militar contra eles, acrescentando que espera que os sauditas sigam o segundo caminho e dependam mais das forças iemenitas que se opõem ao grupo. “Acho que eles vão intensificar os combates contra os Houthis ”, disse. O ataque ocorre num momento em que a Arábia Saudita enfrenta as consequências de um conflito regional mais amplo que Riad procurava evitar. Segundo Haykel, os líderes sauditas opuseram-se à guerra contra o Irã e fizeram esforços consideráveis ​​para impedi-la, mas agora reconhecem que terão de arcar com parte dos seus custos . “Eles percebem que terão que pagar um preço ”, disse ele. Michael Ratney(direita) , ex-embaixador dos EUA na Arábia Saudita e consultor sênior do Centro de Estudos Estratégicos e Internacionais (CSIS), disse que a dimensão e a audácia do ataque chocaram os sauditas, embora eles estivessem familiarizados com as capacidades militares dos houthis. Ratney observou que os houthis já haviam realizado diversos ataques contra aeroportos, inclusive em Riad, durante a semana anterior, sendo este último o mais grave desses incidentes. “ Acho que eles ficaram chocados, mas de certa forma entenderam que é isso que os houthis representam” , explicou Ratney. Ele identificou os ataques a aeroportos civis como uma escalada particularmente significativa. No passado, os terroristas geralmente se concentravam em instalações militares e infraestrutura energética, incluindo bases militares e instalações de energia sauditas. “O fato de eles atacarem aeroportos civis com a expectativa de causar baixas civis representa uma nova escalada para os houthis”, disse Ratney. Os ataques colocaram Riad numa posição difícil, já que o país busca atingir seus objetivos militares no Iêmen sem desencadear uma escalada mais ampla que possa expor outra

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/sto.text: Stolt-Nielsen’s 3Q26 core figures were in line with consensus but somewhat below our estimates, as higher bunker costs absorbed stronger spot rates. While the Middle East conflict has sent crude and product tanker earnings soaring, chemical tankers have captured only part of the momentum. Still, 4Q26 is expected to be modestly softer, but depleted chemical inventories point to a restocking cycle ahead. Despite slightly reducing our estimates, we reiterate Hold with a higher TP of NOK 405/sh. (385), supported by the improved debt profile. Adj. EBITDA of USD 184.4m was in line with consensus but 4.5% below our estimate. Stolt Tankers’ operating profit of USD 52.1m missed our USD 63m, as 40.5% higher spot rates were offset by bunker costs of USD 718/t (USD 500/t) and 22.1% lower spot volumes. Deep-sea TCE was USD 24,121/day (-2.9% YoY, +3.2% QoQ). New financing (a USD 165m newbuilding loan and a USD 370m RCF) further improved the debt profile. Disruptions around Hormuz and the Red Sea have pushed crude tanker earnings to all-time highs on longer ton-miles, risk premiums and firm sentiment. With roughly 70% of pre-war crude volumes now reaching the market via pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers, conventional tankers have been the clear winners. Chemical rates, however, have recovered only modestly, constrained by lost volumes, feedstock shortages and low production. Chemical volumes remain ~15% below pre-war levels. Feedstock shortages and elevated prices have drawn chemical inventories down to multi-year lows, particularly in Asia, so a prolonged restocking period will be required. Together with expected higher US exports, this should lift volumes and ton-miles. Meanwhile, strong product tanker markets should keep swing tonnage out of chemical trades well into 2027. The diversified business model continues to support the investment case: non-tanker segments contributed to ~50% of 3Q26 EBITDA. Overall financial performance is expected to be somewhat softer compared to 3Q26. Thus, despite slightly reducing our near-term estimates, we raise our TP to NOK 405/sh. (385), mainly driven by the improved debt profile, following the Avenir LNG deconsolidation. Source: Norne Research

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/pol.text: There have been two more pollution incidents arising from a similar arrangement. In both cases, an Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment (ODME) overboard discharge pipe was routed through a bunker fuel tank before terminating at the ship’s side. Although all three incidents involved tankers, the recurrence of this failure mode across unrelated vessels highlights a broader risk. The incidents demonstrate that seemingly isolated overboard piping can create a direct pathway between an oil-containing tank and the sea if the pipe loses integrity. ODME Overboard Pipe Failures In both recent cases, the section of ODME overboard discharge piping located within a bunker tank failed. Bunker fuel entered the pipe and escaped directly into the sea. Importantly, the discharge occurred despite the ODME overboard valve being closed and the removable spool piece having been removed inside the vessel. These measures effectively isolated the inboard ODME system but did not isolate the section of pipe extending through the bunker tank to the vessel’s side. The apparent causes of failure differed. In one case, corrosion and wastage were believed to be responsible. In the other, a crack developed along a welded seam from the vessel’s original construction. While the causes differed, the outcome was the same. Once the pipe wall lost integrity inside the bunker tank, the pipe became an uncontrolled pollution pathway allowing fuel oil to escape directly overboard. Why These Arrangements Warrant Attention An overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank can create a single-point failure with potentially significant pollution consequences.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/san.text: Between 1 August and 26 September we heard 10 listed ships switch to a Nicaraguan MMSI, and 8 of them were first heard on the new number in one box around the Strait of Hormuz. No other new flag comes close. None of the new numbers is one a list publishes. A ship’s MMSI is the nine-digit number her transponder broadcasts, and its first three digits name a country. Ports, insurers and cargo buyers check a ship against a sanctions list by that number, and every tracking map is keyed on it. Sanctioned ships change that number often, and each new flag has its own geography. We drew a box around the strait, from the waters off Dubai east into the Gulf of Oman, and counted the listed ships we heard take a new flag from 1 August to 26 September: None of the Nicaraguan numbers is one a list publishes for that ship. DANUTA I, for example, is on the US list under 511101556. We first heard her on 350641000 at 1:18 AM EDT on 26 September, 26 nm from the strait, broadcasting the name NAUTILUS I. That box is a saved report anyone can open: see it on HullCipher, no account needed. It lists every identity change first heard there in those eight weeks, 23 across 19 ships, new names as well as new numbers. Each ship has two marks on the map: a hollow ring where we last heard her old number, and a solid dot where we first heard the Nicaraguan one. Three switched without moving. PARVATI went quiet on 1 September and came back from the same spot three days later. SEA HERMES did the same over nearly a week. FENGSHUN, broadcasting XI WANG MU, came back from the same spot 16 hours later as HAIHE. ADA and DANUTA I have no ring: we last heard their old numbers off Malaysia, about 3,000 nm away. M K A last used hers 366 nm up the Gulf. Some numbers moved in pairs. The two Angolan numbers, 603921000 and 603925000, became 350626000 and 350641000. The two Madagascan ones, 647553028 and 647553055, became 350622000 and 350638000. Seven lookalike owners

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tt-.text: Members of the UK P&I Club, and the TT Club have voted strongly in favour of merging the two organisations to create the first transport mutual to span the entire cargo supply chain. Together, the group will cover maritime, logistics, ports and terminals industries. Approval was confirmed at the Clubs’ separate Special General Meetings held on 7th and 8th October, following a Member voting process that opened in September. The merger will take effect from 20th February 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. The vote is a significant milestone in the creation of a united group that is competitively distinct in the maritime and logistics insurance markets. It brings together the UK P&I Club, which insures more than 250 million tonnes of owned and chartered tonnage, and the TT Club, which insures 80% of the world’s container fleet and has an insurable interest in more than 70 of the world’s top 100 ports. The combined organisation will have annual premium income of around US$ 750 million and free reserves of around US$888 million. The operation is expected to generate a 5% overall improvement in the combined ratio. Against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty, rising claims costs, rapid technological change and intensifying competition for specialist skills, the merger uniquely positions the Clubs to support Members in navigating a risk landscape that is more complex and operationally connected than ever before. Merging the Clubs will create greater scale, financial strength and resilience to deliver long-term value for Members. They will benefit from market-leading technical expertise, greater access to specialist knowledge and technology, and a wider pool of resources and distribution networks across the transport chain. These will be backed by the Clubs’ combined depth in underwriting, claims and loss prevention. Both Clubs will retain their names, brands and market positions, and Members will continue to be supported by their existing underwriting, claims and service teams. Each Club will have its own Club Committee to provide focused, club-level oversight. Jan Valkier, Chairman, UK P&I Club, said: “Our Members have given a clear and resounding endorsement to this merger, and I thank them for their support. This is a landmark moment for both Clubs. Together we will create a group that is genuinely different from anything else in the market, with the scale, financial strength, insight and investment capacity to meet an increasingly complex and connected risk environment. Members will continue to work with the people they know and trust, and the UK P&I Club remains firmly committed to the International Group, which is a cornerstone of our identity.”

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/app.text: US crude exports remained elevated at 3.5 million b/d in September, edging up from 3.4 million b/d in August, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data, but well below the May peak of 4.4 million b/d. South Korea was the largest single destination at 568,600 b/d, followed by the Netherlands at 459,000 b/d, with Japan, France, Canada and the UK also among the top receivers. Volumes into Asia climbed across the region, including Northeast Asia, where US exports rose from 793,000 b/d in August to 1.1 million b/d. Exports into Southeast Asia climbed from 292,000 b/d to 528,000 b/d, while volumes into the Indian subcontinent climbed from 68,000 b/d to 220,000 b/d over the same period. Asian volumes in September largely reflect cargoes fixed before VLCC freight on USGC-Asia routes roughly doubled. The Hormuz disruption initially drove Asian refiners toward US crude as an alternative supply source, but its knock-on effect on tanker markets has since eroded the economics of those trade flows. Fixtures to Asia, including some UKC options, climbed to 7.8 million metric tons in September compared to 4.8 million in August. Surging tanker rates have effectively closed the spot eastbound arbitrage for US crude exports to Asia. Arbitrage calculations favor WTI Midland barrels going to Northwest Europe, where refining margins have strengthened and the freight burden remains comparatively manageable. The arbitrage for WTI MEH into Rotterdam was $19.99/b as of Oct. 8, while the equivalent incentive into Singapore had fallen to minus $17.01/b and into Northeast Asia at minus $19.77/b, according to S&P Global Energy CERA.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/d.text: The deal over supply of diesel between Presidents Trump and Putin this week has generated huge controversy. But from the perspective of the maritime community, the results could turn out rather differently than expected – giving the Russians more of what they have enough of already, namely money, and requiring them to ship to the United States what they are short of, namely diesel. Having exported 2.6 million tonnes of diesel per month prior to 2025, the Trump-Putin deal overturns a self-imposed export ban which Russia introduced on July 8, and which in theory is still in place. There are already widespread shortages of diesel at petrol pumps, and Russia has resorted to relaxing production standards and importing diesel from India, Korea, Morocco and Turkey. Ukraine, suffering an increase in civilian casualties, has signaled its intent to carry on with its targeted attacks on Russia’s diesel production system, so long as Russia continues its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Russia has 32 major refineries and historically used to refine about 6.5 million barrels per day. But diesel production is concentrated at six primary sites, all of which have been successfully targeted by Ukrainian long-range drone and cruise missile strikes, no doubt with the aid of precise American geolocation data. The Ukrainian strikes, at increasingly long range, have in particular targeted crude distillation units within refineries, where crude is initially processed. But catalytic and hydrocrackers where distillate is refined into diesel and hydro reformers have also been subject to special attention. Of the six diesel production sites, the Kirishi refinery 65 miles southeast of Leningrad was the biggest producer of diesel for exports, but was shut down completely after Ukrainian attacks on May 5 and August 30 and has not resumed production. The NORSI and the Volgograd refineries are operating at 25% capacity, after attacks in July. Crude distillation units at the Perm refinery were severely damaged in attacks in July and on August 21. Omsk refinery was attacked on July 7 and set ablaze once again on October 8, an attack carries out at a range of 1,860 miles and aided apparently by local insurgents. Taneco refinery in Tatarstan was hit twice in August at a range of 745 miles.

The world is recording a significant increase in electricity being generated by floating offshore wind farms, with a new report showing that operational capacity has increased by 38 percent over the past 12 months. Despite the offshore wind industry grappling with mounting challenges - including regulatory obstacles, soaring capital costs and supply chain bottlenecks among others - its costliest variant, floating turbine installations, is still making headway. The latest edition of RenewableUK’s EnergyPulse report now shows that the operational capacity from floating offshore wind increased from 277 MW to 382 MW over the 12-month period ending in October, representing a 38 percent increase. Europe continues to demonstrate its leadership in floating offshore wind, with Norway adding 97 MW to its grid, followed by France at 87 MW and the UK with 78 MW of new operational capacity. In Asia, China added 72 MW into its grid followed by Japan with 22 MW. Since the start of 2026 alone, a total of 109 MW in new capacity has gone operational, beating the previous record of 108 MW set in 2023. Two specific projects in France and Japan have added 30 MW and 17 MW respectively. Though the offshore wind industry is going through a tough period - particularly in the U.S., where the Trump administration has spent nearly $4 billion to buy back federal leases and halt major projects - the push for offshore wind remains unrelenting in other regions.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/u.text: The U.S. Coast Guard and its agency partners are working hard to bring ports back online in the wake of Hurricane Isaias, and they are getting quick results. The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida on Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane, weakening fast as it moved inland. At least three people were killed in storm-related accidents, and hundreds of thousands of people remained without power as of Saturday. Florida's utilities expect to fully restore power across the region for 95 percent of all customes by Monday, according to the governor's office. The recovery effort for regional seaports moved quickly. Gulfport, Mobile, and Pascagoula are already back up and running in normal mode, and other nearby ports are not far behind, the Coast Guard announced Saturday. “Our priority is to safely reopen the port and restore the flow of maritime commerce as quickly as conditions allow,” said Capt. Mike Vega, commanding officer of Coast Guard Sector Mobile. “Our crews are working across the affected region to assess critical infrastructure, restore communications and identify hazards to navigation." The most substantial assessment efforts were centered on Destin, Panama City and Pensacola, Florida, where the service kept traffic restricted while assessments continued. The effort is well-resourced: there are seven separate ATON teams looking at the condition of the aids to navigation around the region, plus five different teams assigned to assessing port infrastructure. Five more teams are assigned to reconstituting comms infrastructure and setting up temporary VHF radio coverage. Meanwhile, Coast Guard aircrews operating out of unaffected areas - notably a training airfield in Mobile - are conducting aerial assessments. The Trump administration has issued a disaster declaration for the state of Florida, and the National Guard is out in force to clear downed trees and restore road access.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/s.text: The Russian-flagged Ro-Ro cargo ship Lady Mariia (IMO 9220641) passed through the Strait of Gibraltar on August 29, possibly in company with the Iranian cargo ship Shabdis (IMO 9349588). After a cargo-handling stop in Oran, she was attacked on September 6 as she was sailing eastwards, in the sea area between SW Crete and the Libyan coast. Like the attack carried out on the Omani-flagged dark fleet tanker Qendil (IMO 9310525) in December last year, the Lady Mariia was attacked by bomb-dropping hexacopter drones, which launched a total of 12 munitions. Suspicions about who mounted these attacks focused on a Ukrainian intelligence unit supposedly based in Misrata, a semi-independent city-state in an area of Libya loosely controlled by the UN-recognized government based in Tripoli. The Lady Mariia escaped serious damage in the attack , which does not appear to have been designed to sink the ship. She maintained her course to the Port Said anchorage, where she weighed anchor late on September 8. She has remained at anchor there for 35 days, just outside Egyptian territorial waters, with her AIS system broadcasting her position. The Lady Mariia is well-known for shipping Russian military cargo and appears exclusively wet-leased from its legal owners, MG-Flot, for this purpose. MG-Flot was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury in June 2021, the Lady Mariia was sanctioned in May 2022, cited for handling stolen Ukrainian material and for running arms to Syria. MG-Flot is also heavily involved in shipments of arms between Iran and Russia across the Caspian Sea. The inactivity of the Lady Mariia , at anchor now for 35 days, is curious. A versatile vessel of this character, able to self-load and unload and with a ramped vehicle deck, could be chartered for about $15,000 per day, were it not sanctioned. The value of lost revenue is hence about half a million dollars so far. The ship must also pay dues for utilizing the Port Said Anchorage, at a rate past the initial gratis period of $2,155 per day. Taken together, the lost revenue to MG-Flot of parking their ship in the Port Said Anchorage is $514,650 per month, suggesting that there must be some purpose in the ship being where it is. What that purpose is remains unclear. Since Russia’s Mediterranean Flotilla left its Base 720 in Tartus, retaining only its visiting status, the Russian Navy has struggled to maintain a presence in the Mediterranean, and indeed has not had a ship in the Mediterranean for weeks at a time. The St Andrews Flag is not currently flying in the Mediterranean. When present, the Mediterranean Flotilla would have had a naval intelligence collection remit, so in the absence of warships, potentially the Lady Mariia is fulfilling this role.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/m.text: Morocco’s National Ports Agency (ANP) has reportedly cancelled the concession tender for Casablanca shipyard. ANP had launched the tender process in April last year seeking a private operator to upgrade and operate the yard for 30 years. Preliminary results for the tender were expected in July 2025. This was later delayed, with ANP saying the winner would be announced in August 2026, then delayed again until December 31. Now, after the 18-month delay, ANP has decided to cancel the tender and says it has adopted a new strategic direction for the yard. According to local media reports, the ANP board is said to have considered national sovereignty concerns. Other factors which were mentioned include a new focus towards national control of critical maritime assets, aligning with the vision of the Moroccan royal family. In a speech in 2023, King Mohammed VI directed for development of a “strong, competitive national commercial marine fleet.” In the same year, a Moroccan public think-tank - the Economic, Social and Environmental Council (CESE) - highlighted shipbuilding as a potential high-growth sector for the Moroccan economy. The Casablanca Shipyard was one of the designated shipbuilding zones. With a projected cost over $300 million, the shipyard would have been the largest in Africa if fully built. The yard was planned to cover a 21 hectare site with a 244-meter by 40-meter dry dock. ANP made its first attempt to concession the yard back in 2019 but failed to attract any bids. Around that time, ANP also tried to negotiate with France’s Naval Group to operate the yard without reaching an agreement. The tender re-launched in April last year has now ended with a cancellation. Sources within ANP quoted by local media indicated that the cancellation had nothing to do with the candidates or their offers. Notably, the tender round had attracted global shipbuilding giants. One bidding consortium was backed by Morocco’s Somagec, South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Turkey’s Kuzey Star Shipyard. The other consortium included Morocco’s Radi Holding, Spain’s Marina Meridional and the Chinese Ningbo Xinle Shipbuilding Group. In addition, Italian operator San Giorgio del Porto submitted an individual bid.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/g.text: The German Navy is expanding its footprint and its fleet with the addition of a new North Sea naval base and the acquisition of four more anti-submarine frigates, both positioned to offset the capabilities of the Russian Navy. On Thursday, the German government agreed to double its purchase of TKMS' MEKO A-200 DEU frigate design from four hulls to eight, exercising a previously-agreed contract option. The A-200 replaces the canceled F-126 Niedersachsen-class frigate program, which was beset by delays, reportedly caused by shipyard software compatibility issues. Instead of six F-126 hulls at a projected cost of as much as $21 billion - a massive overrun - Germany's Bundeswehr will receive eight A-200s at a combined cost of about $13 billion. The vessels will be built in Germany by TKMS - a major factor for Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, who has emphasized the value of performing the work at two established shipyards in Hamburg. Saab is providing the vessel's sensor arrays and combat management system, Kongsberg will supply the Naval Strike Missile for surface warfare, and Atlas Elektronik is building its critically-important towed sonar array for submarine hunting. The ships have a unique triple-screw design for a combination of high speed (when running a centerline turbine engine and waterjet) and low noise trolling (when running twin diesel engines port and starboard). Also on Thursday, Pistorius announced plans to build a new naval station at the port of Emden, a few miles from the Dutch border on Germany's North Sea coast. He emphasized its "quick access to the Atlantic Ocean and the far north," where the Russian submarine threat is concentrated. Germany's navy has not had an established presence at Emden since the 1990s, and its return will give the service a strategic alternative to its main frigate base at Wilhelmshaven, about 35 miles to the east. European members of the NATO alliance are concerned at heightened levels of Russian activity at critical subsea infrastructure sites in the Baltic, North Sea, Irish Sea and Barents Sea. Anticipating the possibility of a "deniable" attack on EU critical infrastructure on the seabed, the UK and the EU are investing in better protection to detect and deter interlopers under the surface - and ASW frigates are key for hunting subs. "This will enhance the deterrence capabilities of both Germany and NATO," Pistorius said in a press conference Thursday in Emden. "We currently have the smallest navy in the history of the German Armed Forces, yet simultaneously the largest and most comprehensive portfolio of tasks. Therefore, the navy must grow, and it will."

https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: A lot has been written about the Strait of Hormuz this year. It is a vital global energy choke point situated between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, bordered by Iran to the north and Oman and the United Arab Emirates to the south. In the oil and tanker markets it was well known as a potential risk factor because roughly 20% of the world’s seaborne oil trade (crude oil and refined products) passes through this 20-24-mile-wide passageway. However, after the start of the U.S. – Iran conflict on February 28 of this year, the Strait of Hormuz has also featured frequently in the mainstream press, and it has become a household name. Shortly after the start of the conflict, Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz “closed”, wreaking havoc in the oil markets. Ever since, there has been a tug of war between the United States and Iran about control of this waterway. In the early stages of the war, Iran seemed to have the upper hand in the Strait of Hormuz. Immediately following the US strikes, Iran effectively closed the Strait. Traffic through the waterway plummeted by over 95%, leaving hundreds of tankers (and other ships) stranded and causing historic disruptions to global energy supplies. Iran used its control over the Strait of Hormuz to choke of Persian Gulf exports from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, while – at least initially – being able to maintain its own exports. There was a big difference in dropoff between the countries that have access to bypass pipelines (Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates), and the ones that do not (Iraq and Kuwait). For example, between February and March 2026, Saudi Arabia’s exports fell from 7.35 Mb/d to 4.57 Mb/d (-38%), while the UAE dropped from 3.47 Mb/d to 2.08 Mb/d (-40%). The Saudis expanded the use of the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, while the UAE had access to the Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline. Contrast this with the dropoff in exports from Iraq (-82%), Kuwait (-81%) and Qatar (-80%). During the same period, Iran was able to maintain its exports at around 2.0 Mb/d. Exports from the region (including Iran) continued to fall through April and May, especially after the United States implemented a naval blockade on Iranian ports and coastal areas to prevent Iranian oil exports. There was a brief recovery in flows after the U.S. and Iran signed a Memorandum of Understanding (June 17), which established an immediate 60-day ceasefire and a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. However, this MOU collapsed in July following renewed clashes and retaliatory strikes. On July 14, President Trump reinstated the naval blockade on Iran, which remains in place until today. By the end of July, the Houthis got involved in the conflict by announcing a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, forcing Yanbu

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543609-tg.text: Energy data company TGS has signed a framework agreement with newly established Galdor Exploration to use artificial intelligence (AI) and integrated subsurface data to identify exploration opportunities on the Norwegian Continental Shelf and across the wider North Sea region. Under the agreement, Galdor will gain access to TGS' integrated energy data and technology solutions, while the companies will work together to implement AI-enabled exploration workflows. The collaboration will include the use of TGS' proprietary Seismic Foundation Model, alongside advanced machine learning techniques intended to support the identification and evaluation of exploration prospects. Galdor Exploration, established on July 19, 2026, is pursuing a data-driven exploration strategy combining AI-based workflows with the experience of its exploration team. The company aims to identify and mature exploration opportunities that may have been overlooked or underestimated using conventional exploration methods. “Galdor’s strategy is built on a conviction that the future of exploration lies in a modern exploration organization, where we combine deep exploration experience with premium subsurface data and next-generation AI-enabled workflows,” said Ørjan Gjerde, CEO and Founder of Galdor Exploration.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543610-oe.text: OEG has been awarded a contract by Ørsted to supply temporary power for the construction of the Hornsea 3 offshore wind farm, covering offshore converter station commissioning and wind turbine installation and commissioning activities. Under the contract, OEG will provide temporary power aboard a jack-up vessel during offshore converter station commissioning works, using five 200 kVA generators and two 300 kVA generators operating in synchronization. The configuration is designed to deliver temporary power of up to 1,400 kVA to the offshore converter station. For the turbine installation and commissioning phase, OEG will supply 150 kVA generators paired with specially designed 3,000-litre mountable fuel tanks. The modular equipment arrangement is intended to maximize available power while reducing the footprint of the equipment on turbine transition pieces, where installation space is limited. “We have been working closely with the Ørsted construction management team over the last few months to ensure we provide the correct bespoke technical solutions in support of this exciting new project. We look forward to continuing this close collaboration and supporting the project through to completion,” said Rob Williams, Technical Manager for OEG's temporary power team.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543602-al.text: The US Interior Department proposed on Friday to hold an offshore oil and gas lease sale in Alaska's Cook Inlet early next year, offering about 1.05 million acres (425,000 hectares) for drilling as part of a congressionally mandated leasing program. The proposed sale, known as Big Beautiful Cook Inlet 2, would make 224 blocks available for leasing and is scheduled for March 3, 2027. The proposal follows a Cook Inlet sale in March that attracted no industry interest despite the Trump administration's efforts to boost oil and gas development. No bids were submitted for the acreage offered. The Marine Minerals Administration said the sale is required under US President Donald Trump's 2025 tax bill, which mandates annual Cook Inlet lease sales from 2026 through 2028 and again from 2030 through 2032.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543608-rs.text: Saab UK has received an order from Ørsted for a Seaeye Cougar XT Compact remotely operated vehicle (ROV), expanding the offshore wind company's fleet of Saab Seaeye Cougar systems to three units. The electric ROV will support inspection and maintenance activities across Ørsted's offshore wind portfolio, including subsea infrastructure such as foundations, cables and other submerged assets. The Cougar XT Compact combines a compact design with electric propulsion and control systems intended to provide maneuverability and precision during subsea inspection and intervention operations. The vehicle will be used to support the monitoring and maintenance of offshore wind infrastructure, helping Ørsted assess the condition of submerged assets and maintain operational availability. “We are delighted to receive this order from Ørsted. Expanding its Saab Seaeye fleet with a third Cougar system reflects the confidence the company has in our technology and its ability to support inspection and maintenance operations across offshore wind assets,” said Jon Robertson, Seaeye Managing Director at Saab UK.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543604-oi.text: Oil prices oscillated on Monday as the market considered possible further supplies after US President Donald Trump hailed fresh Russian diesel exports against supply-constricting signals after major attacks on Saudi Arabia. Retracing earlier losses, Brent crude futures LCOc1 rose 69 cents or 0.7%, to $105.41 a barrel by 0923 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude CLc1 was at $92.42 a barrel, up 57 cents, or 0.6%. The Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Further attacks happened on Sunday. In addition, more attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported this month, threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September. https://www.oedigital.com/news/543605-bi.text: Bibby Marine has launched its new battery-first electric commissioning service operation vessel (eCSOV) at Armon Shipyard in Vigo, Spain, ahead of its planned delivery in 2027. The vessel, which will carry the name Staffordshire, entered the water on October 10 and will undergo further outfitting at the shipyard over the coming months, including the installation of its battery systems. Unlike conventional hybrid-assist designs, the eCSOV is designed to use its energy storage system as the primary source of power rather than as a supplementary propulsion system. Bibby Marine has partnered with Kongsberg and Corvus Energy on the vessel's propulsion and battery systems, while working with Stillstrom to develop compatibility with offshore charging infrastructure. The company estimates that the battery-first configuration could reduce vessel operating costs by more than 40% in self-charging mode, with potential savings rising to around 70% when operating solely on offshore charging. The new eCSOV has been designed to revolutionize wind farm operations, according to Bibby Marine, supporting offshore operations with modern capabilities, efficiency and comfort for those working on board.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543606-rs.text: Ørsted has exercised a buyback right to acquire the remaining 49.9% stake in the Gunfleet Sands 1 & 2 offshore wind farm in the UK from its investment partners, paving the way for full ownership of the 172 MW asset. The company currently holds a 50.1% interest in the wind farm, located seven kilometres off the Essex coast, with partners JERA Nex BP and the Development Bank of Japan holding 24.95% stakes each. The transaction, estimated at $19.8 million (£15 million), is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to be completed in November, after which Ørsted will own and operate the entire project. The acquisition follows the exercise of a long-standing buyback right established under the original partnership agreements. According to Ørsted, taking full ownership will provide greater flexibility in managing the wind farm and evaluating late-life options, including a potential extension of its operational lifetime. “Gunfleet Sands 1 & 2 has been part of the UK’s renewable energy story since 2010, and we’re proud of the contribution it continues to make. Taking full ownership gives us greater flexibility to shape the site’s future and build on the value of an asset we know well,” said Richard Bodal Hansen, Ørsted's UK Country Manager.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543607-ed.text: RWE has completed the sale of its 33.33% stake in the 1.1 GW Five Estuaries offshore wind farm project in the U.K. to EDF power solutions UK and Ireland, with EDF taking over responsibility for leading the development on behalf of the joint venture partners. The project, an extension to the operational Galloper Wind Farm, is planned for construction in the southern North Sea across two seabed areas covering approximately 128 square kilometres. Five Estuaries received development consent from the UK's Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero on December 17, 2025. The consent allows for the installation of up to 79 wind turbines, with a maximum tip height of 370 meters, along with their foundations. Once operational, the offshore wind farm is expected to be able to supply electricity to approximately one million average UK households. Before the transaction, Five Estuaries was owned by RWE with 33.33%, a Macquarie-led consortium with 25%, ESB with 20.83% and Sumitomo Corporation with 20.83%.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543603-en.text: Eni has signed two binding agreements to sell 10% interests in seven production sharing contracts (PSCs) in Indonesia to Pertamina and Medco, covering assets operated by its joint venture with Petronas. Under the first agreement, Eni will sell its 10% interests in the East Sepinggan, North Ganal and Rapak PSCs to Pertamina, Indonesia's national energy company. The assets include the producing Merakes and East Merakes gas fields, as well as the Geng North and Gehem gas discoveries, which are being developed through the North Hub gas project. Under the second agreement, Eni will sell its 10% interests in the West Ganal, East Ganal, Ganal and Muara Bakau PSCs to Medco. These assets include the producing Jangkrik field, the Maha, Gendalo and Gandang gas projects being executed as part of the South Hub project, and the recently announced Geliga gas discovery. The assets are operated by Searah, an independent joint venture established by Eni and Petronas, with each company holding a 50% interest.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543601-ri.text: Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organizers released early Monday. “To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday’s session of the gathering for energy policy and industry. “You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.” Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious". The strikes are a blow to Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's multi-billion-dollar program to diversify the economy away from oil, modernize society and position the kingdom as an investment and tourism hub.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543600-ir.text: Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday. Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. After a June interim ceasefire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a US response. But the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying on Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations. A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway. Regarding the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, an Iranian ally, Baghaei reiterated Tehran's openness to help resolve the crisis through dialogue. "The issue of Yemen should have been resolved a long time ago with the (UN) roadmap and we had said we would support any agreement reached by Yemenis and Saudis ... Our request is that this situation be resolved through dialogue."

https://www.rigzone.com/news/energy_mark.text: That’s what Standard Chartered Bank Energy Research Head Emily Ashford said in a report sent to Rigzone recently, which outlined that the system “can move barrels, but at a great cost and logistical complexity”. “Gulf crude oil export volumes have recovered as increasingly expensive and fragile workarounds are functioning, while policy makers are using inventories and keeping trade open to manage the downstream consequences,” Ashford noted in the report. The Energy Research Head highlighted that normal Gulf export volumes do not mean normal flows. “Gulf crude exports have recovered strongly, returning towards pre-conflict volumes on several days in September,” Ashford said. “However, focusing on headline volumes misses how complex the process to get those barrels moving has become, including ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman and naval escorts,” Ashford added. “This has worked to restore export capacity, but at the cost of additional vessels, longer journey times, higher freight and insurance costs, and continued exposure to attack,” Ashford warned.

https://safety4sea.com/itf-launches-glob.text: The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has launched Mind At Sea, a global mental health and suicide prevention campaign aimed at improving seafarers’ access to support and making wellbeing discussions a routine part of ship visits. L aunched on 10 October, World Mental Health Day, in Sydney, Australia, the campaign carries the message “It’s ok not to be ok” and will run across multiple countries and continents until early December. The ITF plans to run the campaign annually, with the longer-term goal of integrating mental health and wellbeing discussions into routine ship visits conducted by all ITF inspectors. During participating visits, inspectors will be encouraged to hold informal 10-15-minute conversations covering stress, fatigue, sleep and isolation, while directing seafarers to relevant support services. The initiative will also promote the ITF Seafarers’ App, mental health helplines and welfare services. Built around four actions, reflect, recognise, respond and reach out, it aims to encourage open conversations and help seafarers identify when they or a colleague may need support. ITF-affiliated unions will also be encouraged to develop peer support initiatives and share resources with seafarers’ families. Life at sea can put enormous strain on seafarers, and too many still feel they have to keep that to themselves … commented Dr Asif Altaf, the ITF’s Wellbeing Programme Coordinator, adding that the campaign aims to help seafarers understand where to seek assistance.

https://safety4sea.com/fire-aboard-hmm-p.text: A container fire aboard HMM’s HMM PLATINUM in the Indian Ocean has prompted a salvage response and forced the vessel to divert from its scheduled voyage from India to Brazil, with an alternative port of refuge now reportedly under consideration. A ccording to Dolphin Maritime and Aviation Services, the fire broke out in a container while the vessel was sailing off the southern coast of Madagascar. The ship was en route from Kattupalli, India, to Santos, Brazil, when the incident occurred. The vessel was reportedly carrying approximately 2,300 containers at the time of the fire. However, the extent of damage to the ship and its cargo remains unknown, with further assessments expected once the vessel reaches a suitable port. Initial reports indicated that the HMM PLATINUM was heading to Durban, South Africa, to seek refuge. Subsequent information, however, suggests that an alternative destination is being considered, with Gqeberha, formerly known as Port Elizabeth, among the ports under consideration. Furthermore, professional salvors SMIT have reportedly been appointed under Lloyd’s Open Form (LOF) terms to respond to the incident. The LOF is a widely used salvage agreement that allows salvage operations to begin without the parties having to agree on a fixed remuneration in advance. Salvage remuneration is generally determined later, in accordance with the agreement’s terms and the circumstances of the operation.

https://safety4sea.com/lessons-learned-f.text: A routine moment in a vessel’s changing room resulted in a serious finger injury after a crew member’s hand became trapped in a rapidly closing engine room fire door. T he incident, detailed in a Marine Safety Forum safety alert, highlights how an everyday movement can lead to a lost-time injury when unsafe layout arrangements, inadequately controlled door mechanisms and reduced situational awareness coincide. Beyond the immediate circumstances, the case raises a wider question for ship operators: are familiar onboard hazards being actively controlled, or have they simply become part of daily life? According to the Marine Safety Forum, the injured person had finished his working day and was in the changing room next to the engine room access door. He was standing in the narrow space between the lockers and the door, which opened inwards towards his position. While balancing himself and looking down, he inadvertently placed his right hand against the door frame, with his middle finger overlapping the gap between the frame and the door. At almost the same time, the third engineer opened the engine room door and released it. The door’s self-closing mechanism brought it shut rapidly, trapping the crew member’s middle finger and causing a severe injury.

https://safety4sea.com/iran-says-us-resp.text: Efforts to restore normal maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remain uncertain after Iran described the United States’ response to its seven-point proposal for reopening the strategic waterway as “insufficient” , signalling continued obstacles to a potential agreement. M ohsen Rezaei, Iran’s security chief and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, was quoted by Iranian state media on 11 October as saying that Washington must clarify outstanding issues before Tehran would consider further progress, Reuters reports. He added that Iran would not reopen the strait to the United States or engage in negotiations until its conditions had been met. Iran presented its proposal during the United Nations General Assembly, outlining conditions under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and normal maritime passage resume within seven days. The United States subsequently responded through Qatari intermediaries, although Tehran maintains that the reply failed to address its concerns adequately. The latest developments follow remarks made by US President Donald Trump at the White House on 26 September, when he said Tehran had proposed reopening the strait immediately as part of a broader agreement. Trump said he had rejected the proposal. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi subsequently acknowledged the US president’s remarks but said Tehran was awaiting an official response through mediators before determining its position. According to Reuters, Iran said in late September that it had received an official US response to its latest proposal that had previously collapsed. The response came days after Trump publicly stated that he had rejected the proposal.

https://safety4sea.com/baltic-states-urg.text: The leaders of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia have called on the European Union to prohibit the transit of Russian grain, arguing that European transport infrastructure should not be used to support Moscow. I n a joint letter sent on 9 October to European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the three leaders urged the EU to tighten restrictions on Russian agricultural exports while strengthening transport links to help Ukrainian goods reach international markets. Latvian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Russia was attacking Ukrainian ports and obstructing the country’s grain exports while continuing to transport its own agricultural products through European infrastructure. “Our infrastructure must not help Russia finance its war,” Michal said, adding that further pressure should be placed on Moscow while Ukraine’s access to global markets is protected. In their letter, the three leaders argued that Russian attacks on Ukrainian cargo ships, railways and other critical trade routes are aimed at undermining Ukraine’s economy and restricting its ability to export goods. The situation in the Black Sea is particularly concerning. Russia’s attacks have severely disrupted the movement of grain to global markets. While undermining Ukraine’s ability to export grain, Russia is actively seeking alternative routes for its own grain exports through the EU, including via the Baltic Sea.

https://safety4sea.com/cm-expert-thinkin.text: Observed every year on October 10, World Mental Health Day brings global attention to mental health, encourages open conversation and reinforces the need to challenge stigma and strengthen support. This year’s theme, “Lived experiences heard: Real voices, real change,” set by the World Federation for Mental Health (WFMH), places lived experience at the heart of that effort. It calls for people who have experienced mental health challenges not simply to be part of the conversation, but to help shape the policies, services and decisions intended to support them. Meanwhile, mental-health contacts to SeafarerHelp rose by 35.9% year-on-year to a record high , while another industry study found that 27% of seafarers had no access to free mental-health support or confidential counselling and a further 17% would not feel safe using the support available to them. Other indicators reinforce the concern. Seafarer happiness declined from 7.18 in Q1 to 6.87 in Q2 2026 , while only 49% of seafarers surveyed said crewing levels were sufficient to work safely without excessive fatigue. These figures point to a persistent gap between recognizing mental health as an industry priority and ensuring that effective, trusted support reaches people at sea. Listening, therefore, is only the starting point. The real challenge is to turn seafarers’ experiences into action – into safer working environments, stronger support systems and a culture in which seeking help is both accessible and accepted.

https://safety4sea.com/imo-assesses-digi.text: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is supporting Senegal’s efforts to digitalize port procedures through a needs assessment to guide the establishment of a maritime single window (MSW) at the Port of Dakar. C onducted from 5 to 9 October, the assessment examined existing port processes and institutional frameworks to identify the requirements for implementing the system. An MSW is a one-stop digital platform that streamlines the exchange of information required for ships’ arrival, stay and departure from ports. By simplifying information exchange between ships and public authorities, the system can reduce duplication, improve coordination and cut the time and costs associated with port clearance. Since 1 January 2024, all IMO Member States have been required to establish, maintain and use MSWs in ports. During the mission, IMO consultants engaged with Senegal’s National Agency of Maritime Affairs (ANAM), the port administration, relevant ministries and public agencies, including customs, port health, border police and immigration services. Consultations also involved private-sector stakeholders, including shipping lines, shipping agents and terminal operators. A comprehensive mission report will outline a roadmap for developing the MSW at the Port of Dakar. It will identify key stakeholders and their responsibilities, assess institutional and operational needs, and provide practical recommendations for deploying the system. The recommendations will align with IMO principles and guidance and address the development of supporting digital tools.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/tan.text: A Tanker Is Struck Off Qatar as Gulf Attacks Surge An unnamed tanker was struck by multiple projectiles 51 nautical miles off Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, according to an October 7 report from UK Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO has reported 16 attacks on ships in the Middle East Gulf in the past 10 days, and this is the first outside the Strait of Hormuz since September 9. Windward has identified and confirmed 12 of the vessels, noting all were using the U.S. military-assisted southern corridor and transiting dark, and 11 were tankers. National Oil Companies Pay Unprecedented Sums to Keep Crude Moving Maritime security is now at its most perilous in the region since the early days of the conflict, lifting freight costs to unprecedented levels and driving steep discounts on oil prices offered by national oil companies in order to secure sales. National oil companies are paying tankers $50 million per transit to ship crude to ship-to-ship transfer areas off Fujairah and Oman, with discounts now at $35/barrel of the OSP (official sale price), Windward has been told. The benchmark rate to ship crude on a VLCC to China from Saudi Arabia has surpassed $1.3 million per day; the Iran attacks intensify pressure on the logistics chain already under severe pressure to find tankers willing to undertake risky transits. The freight component of crude shipped from the Middle East Gulf now exceeds 25-30% of the cost of the commodity. In normal market conditions, this is between 1-3%.

https://splash247.com/misc-lines-up-five.text: Malaysian shipping group MISC is preparing another five LNG carrier newbuildings in China after securing a fresh long-term charter award from compatriot Petronas. The Bursa Malaysia-listed owner has accepted a letter of award from Petronas LNG, covering five new LNG carriers on firm 20-year charters. MISC said it would enter into shipbuilding contracts with Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding, part of China State Shipbuilding Corporation, to construct the vessels. The latest award comes on top of a separate five-vessel programme agreed earlier this year . MISC initially contracted three 174,000 cu m LNG carriers at Hudong-Zhonghua, adding another two in February. Petronas subsequently confirmed a 20-year charter agreement for all five, with employment scheduled to begin between 2029 and 2030. MISC has steadily expanded its gas carrier orderbook through long-term employment agreements with the Malaysian energy group.
