https://www.rigzone.com/news/wire/eu_pol.text: The European Union looks to be relaxing its opposition to oil and gas production in polar areas, while still calling for all fossil fuels to be kept in the ground in its forthcoming Arctic strategy. A draft of the strategy, seen by Bloomberg, contains no references to a moratorium on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, marking a shift in wording from the EU's 2021 stance. The wording has been a topic of intense discussions between the trade bloc and Norway, which has lobbied hard for the EU to abandon its climate-based opposition to oil and gas exploration in the high north. The Nordic nation awarded five oil and gas exploration licenses in the Barents Sea, which is part of the Arctic, in last year's licensing round and opened up 38 blocks in 2026 for applications. Norway supplied almost a third of EU's gas imports last year, including a small part from those fields. The petroleum industry's fear was that the EU would pledge not to buy oil and gas from Norway's new Arctic fields. Instead, the draft says the union will "prioritize" renewable energy sources and hydrocarbons produced outside the Arctic. The European Commission also says it will work toward an international commitment to prevent further development of Arctic oil and gas resources, or purchases from them, when such activity "poses a threat to the Arctic ecosystem." In 2021, the EU had said that "building on the partial moratoriums on hydrocarbons exploration in the Arctic" in parts of the US, Canada and Greenland, "the EU is committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions" and that it would work toward "a multilateral legal obligation not to allow any further hydrocarbon reserve development in the Arctic or contiguous regions, nor to purchase such hydrocarbons if they were to be produced." The latest draft also reiterates the EU's broader commitment to work toward keeping coal, oil and gas in the ground, including in the Arctic, in line with its climate targets. The bloc has set a legally binding goal of cutting net greenhouse gas emissions by 90 percent by 2040 from the 1990 level.

https://safety4sea.com/northstandard-war.text: NorthStandard has published a safety alert following a container fire involving UN 3378 Sodium Carbonate Peroxyhydrate (sodium percarbonate), urging caution when accepting shipments of the substance, particularly from the Chinese ports of Qingdao and Lianyungang. I n its latest alert, issued on 16 October, NorthStandard reported receiving information about a further container fire involving the cargo under circumstances similar to those previously identified. The update follows an initial alert issued on 7 October, when NorthStandard reported multiple container fires involving UN 3378 cargoes loaded at Qingdao and Lianyungang. Importantly, NorthStandard confirmed that the cargo had been correctly declared in each of the initially reported incidents, indicating that the warnings were not based on identified cargo misdeclaration. Following the additional incident, NorthStandard reiterated its recommendation for extreme caution when accepting bookings for this substance from the two ports and increased vigilance where such cargo is already onboard. Sodium percarbonate is an oxidising substance that can release heat and oxygen during decomposition, potentially intensifying a fire. NorthStandard also highlights concerns that a developing fire could affect other dangerous goods stowed nearby, increasing the potential consequences of an incident. Under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code, UN 3378 may be stowed either on deck or under deck. This means affected containers could be located in areas where access and firefighting operations are more challenging.

https://safety4sea.com/vehicle-carrier-f.text: The Vehicle Carrier Safety Forum (VCSF) has published Fire Drill Guidelines for Vehicle Carrying Vessels, outlining practical measures to strengthen fire response preparedness through rapid intervention, safe crew deployment, effective use of fixed firefighting systems and coordinated emergency response. T he guidelines provide a structured framework for realistic, scenario-based drills at sea and in port, focusing on the decisions and actions required to contain fires before they escalate. Designed to supplement the VCSF’s Fire Response – High Level Guidelines, the document is principle-based rather than prescriptive, allowing operators to adapt exercises to individual vessel designs, firefighting equipment, cargo configurations and operational conditions. A central recommendation is the early and correct deployment of fixed firefighting systems (FFS), which VCSF identifies as critical to preventing fire escalation on vehicle carrying vessels. For initial-response drills, the guidelines establish an objective of deploying fixed firefighting systems as soon as reasonably practicable, targeting deployment within 15 minutes of the fire alarm. The 15-minute target is a recommended drill objective, rather than a new mandatory regulatory requirement. Its operational significance lies in encouraging crews to practise the sequence of actions needed for timely fire suppression while maintaining personnel safety.

https://safety4sea.com/imo-net-zero-fram.text: A new analysis by Opportunity Green warns that Japan’s proposed amendments to the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) could undermine shipping’s decarbonisation objectives and weaken financial support for climate-vulnerable developing countries. I n its briefing, “Attempt to weaken the IMO Net-Zero Framework”, Opportunity Green argues that Japan’s latest proposal would significantly change the framework agreed in principle at MEPC 83 in April 2025, potentially weakening its ability to support the greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction objectives of the IMO’s 2023 Revised GHG Strategy. According to the organisation, the proposal represents an insufficient compromise for countries seeking ambitious emissions reductions and equitable financial support, particularly Small Island Developing States (SIDS) and Least Developed Countries (LDCs). Under the NZF approved in April 2025, ships that fail to meet greenhouse gas fuel intensity requirements would be required to address compliance deficits through the purchase of Remedial Units (RUs) or, under specified conditions, the use of Surplus Units (SUs). Revenue from the framework’s emissions pricing mechanism would be channelled into a dedicated IMO Net-Zero Fund to support zero- and near-zero-emission (ZNZ) fuels and technologies, as well as measures supporting a just and equitable transition. Japan’s proposal would remove the Fund and make the purchase of Surplus Units the primary mechanism for addressing compliance deficits. Where insufficient units are available, shipping companies could instead make direct contributions to IMO-approved projects.

https://safety4sea.com/philippines-ferry.text: Fire Chief Superintendent Wilberto Rico Neil Ang Kwan Tiu/Credit: Philippine Presidential Communications Office Philippine authorities are investigating possible failures in dangerous cargo handling, stowage and vessel inspections following the fire aboard MV June Aster , which killed 77 people, injured 43 and left eight missing on 9 September 2026. A ccording to a 16 October update by the Philippine Presidential Communications Office, the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) is examining potential criminal charges against the vessel’s crew, owners, cargo handlers and government personnel following the incident. The passenger roll-on/roll-off vessel was travelling from Batangas to Coron, Palawan, when the fire broke out. Investigators are examining potential violations involving the loading and declaration of dangerous cargo, particularly asphalt and calcium hypochlorite, a chemical commonly used in swimming pool disinfectants. Fire Chief Superintendent Wilberto Rico Neil Ang Kwan Tiu, head of the BFP, said the substances were reportedly stored near the vessel’s engine exhaust, where elevated temperatures may have contributed to ignition. Rough sea conditions may also have caused the cargo to shift, potentially allowing the substances to mix and contributing to the fire.

https://safety4sea.com/northern-sea-rout.text: Commercial transits through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) have exceeded the full-year 2025 total, with increased tanker, bulk carrier and container ship activity highlighting growing use of the Arctic corridor. A ccording to the Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL), 104 confirmed transit voyages were recorded along the Northern Sea Route by 30 September 2026, exceeding the 103 voyages registered during the entire 2025 navigation season. Estimated cargo volumes reached 3.7 million tonnes, while the combined deadweight of vessels increased by 26% to 7.8 million DWT. The figures come as the European Union seeks to maintain international access to Arctic shipping routes and strengthen its focus on maritime security, surveillance and infrastructure protection in the region. According to CHNL’s analysis of AIS data from MarineTraffic by Kpler, oil tankers accounted for a substantial share of NSR cargo movements during the 2026 navigation season. The data identified 22 eastbound tanker voyages carrying an estimated 2.1 million tonnes, primarily crude oil. Bulk carriers also contributed to transit activity, with 13 eastbound cargo voyages and 27 westbound voyages recorded by the end of September. Container shipping activity increased, with 13 transits recorded during the same period. These included four international Asia–Europe container voyages without Russian endpoints, compared with one during the entire 2025 season.

https://safety4sea.com/intermanager-encl.text: InterManager has called for urgent action to prevent enclosed space deaths onboard ships, warning that persistent shortcomings in safety procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention continue to put seafarers at risk. A ccording to its latest research, InterManager has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents between 1996 and 2026 , involving tankers, bulk carriers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. A recent survey of more than 900 seafarers identified a persistent gap between established safety procedures and operational realities onboard. Respondents highlighted overly complex paperwork, inadequate time and manpower, commercial pressures, insufficient practical training and a reluctance to address the underlying causes of accidents. The findings also raised concerns that inspections often prioritise procedural compliance rather than assessing whether safety measures are effective in practice. https://safety4sea.com/imo-uncertainty-s.text: Demand for lower-carbon marine fuels has weakened this year as uncertainty over the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) proposed net-zero framework continues to weigh on shipowners’ investment and fuel purchasing decisions. A ccording to Reuters, industry executives say the lack of regulatory clarity, alongside growing reliance on carbon credits under existing emissions schemes, is slowing the uptake of marine biofuels despite continued efforts to decarbonise shipping. IMO member states are expected to reconvene by early November to consider the formal adoption of the organisation’s net-zero framework, following a decision last year to postpone the process. The outcome is seen as an important factor in determining how quickly shipowners commit to alternative fuels and the investments needed to support the transition towards net-zero emissions by 2050. The slowdown is already evident in Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering hub, where sales of marine biofuels have fallen sharply. Government data showed that Singapore sold approximately 603,000 tonnes of marine biofuel between January and September, representing a 47% decline compared with the same period in 2025. This follows a strong increase in demand last year, when total annual volumes more than doubled from 2024. Jens Maul Jorgensen, a director at dry bulk shipowner Oldendorff Carriers, said he did not expect biofuel demand to increase significantly until the IMO reached a decision on its proposed framework.

https://safety4sea.com/china-identifies-.text: China’s Ministry of Transport has outlined 22 priority artificial intelligence (AI) application scenarios for the water transport sector , focusing on safety improvement, operational efficiency and green transformation. T he Guidelines for the Application Scenarios of Artificial Intelligence in the Water Transport Sector, issued by the General Office of the Ministry of Transport, aim to accelerate AI adoption across the industry and support the development of a modern water transport system. The guidelines identify three main areas for AI deployment, with applications intended to strengthen risk prevention, improve transport services and support sustainable development. Nine priority scenarios focus on strengthening safety through AI, including intelligent port safety risk prevention and control, waterway operational safety, shipping operational risk management, water traffic safety monitoring and maritime search and rescue. These applications aim to improve risk prediction, enable dynamic risk prevention and control, and strengthen safety assurance and emergency response capabilities. A further 10 scenarios target improvements in operational efficiency and service quality. These cover automated terminal operations, intelligent coordination of port logistics, waterway operational services and digitalised shipping operations.

https://safety4sea.com/kr-launches-cyber.text: Korean Register (KR) has launched a pilot service for its new Cyber Resilience Platform (KR-CRP), designed to help shipowners and shipyards manage cybersecurity documentation and meet the requirements of the International Association of Classification Societies’ (IACS) Unified Requirement (UR) E26. T he development reflects the growing need to integrate cybersecurity considerations into ship design, classification and operational management. As ships become increasingly connected and reliant on digital systems, effective cyber resilience requires more than technical protection alone. The launch comes as cybersecurity becomes an increasingly important part of ship design, classification and operational safety, with the industry facing growing demands to strengthen the resilience of onboard systems against cyber threats. KR-CRP provides a digital environment for preparing and managing the design documentation required under IACS UR E26, which addresses the cyber resilience of ships. The platform is integrated with KR’s drawing approval and classification survey processes, with the aim of reducing administrative work for shipowners and shipyards while making compliance more efficient. During the launch event, KR outlined how the platform could support the management of cybersecurity requirements throughout the relevant approval and survey processes. A demonstration also showed how KR-CRP can use data from existing onboard security monitoring systems developed and installed by third-party providers.

https://safety4sea.com/japan-turns-to-ai.text: Japanese maritime AI startup Noahlogy has secured a contract from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) to study how artificial intelligence can support expert decision-making in ship inspections, as authorities explore ways to improve efficiency while maintaining safety and regulatory compliance. T he project, titled Study on Advanced Support for Expert Judgment in Ship Inspections Utilising AI, will examine how AI could assist with inspection-related tasks, including the review of technical drawings and documentation. The study is scheduled to run from August 2026 to March 2027. Based in Tokyo, Noahlogy is a University of Tokyo spin-off specialising in artificial intelligence and digital transformation for the maritime sector. The company said it would draw on its AI capabilities and industry-specific expertise to assess where the technology could provide practical support to government-administered ship inspections. Ship inspections require specialised technical assessments to verify that vessels comply with applicable regulations and safety requirements. These assessments include reviewing drawings and calculation sheets, as well as conducting onboard checks of structures and equipment. However, the complexity of these tasks, combined with the need to maintain inspection quality, has increased the focus on improving productivity across inspection operations. Under the MLIT contract, Noahlogy will first examine existing workflows for drawing reviews and other ship inspection activities. The study will then identify tasks where AI assistance could be feasible and define the requirements for introducing the technology.

https://www.marinelog.com/news/intermana.text: Captain Kuba Szymanski, Secretary General of InterManager: “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades.” Ship management trade association InterManager i s calling for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety. The association’s latest research highlights persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organization has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, in tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades,” says InterManager Secretary General Captain Kuba Szymanski. “The industry does not need more paperwork for the sake of paperwork, it needs practical measures that work onboard. If a procedure cannot realistically be completed with the time, people and equipment available, then we need to question the system, not blame the seafarer.” “We already know many of the factors behind these accidents,” says Syzmanksi. “What is missing is consistent action. The priority now must be simpler procedures, better training, stronger leadership, improved ship design and far greater sharing of accident data. Enclosed space deaths are not inevitable. The industry has the knowledge to prevent them so why isn’t it doing it already?” InterManager’s latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. Over 900 respondents highlighted overly complex paperwork, inadequate time and manpower, commercial pressure, insufficient practical training and a reluctance to address underlying causes. The survey also highlights concerns that inspections can focus on superficial compliance rather than the effectiveness of actual safety practices. It also identifies opportunities to make greater use of real-time gas sensors, wearable technology, digital permits, hands-free communications and unmanned inspection tools to reduce human exposure.

https://www.marinelink.com/news/sse-pick.text: SSE Renewables has selected Subsea7's Seaway7 as preferred supplier for offshore wind turbine foundations and subsea inter-array cables at its 1.4 GW Berwick Bank B offshore wind project in Scotland, under an agreement expected to support 465 UK jobs. The preferred supplier agreement covers engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) of approximately 90 fixed-bottom turbine foundations, as well as the design, supply and installation of inter-array cables. The project is planned for the outer Firth of Forth, approximately 38 kilometers off the Scottish Borders coastline, with water depths averaging 52 meters and reaching up to 59.7 meters. According to SSE, Berwick Bank B would become the world's deepest fixed-bottom offshore wind farm upon completion. Seaway7 plans to deploy three installation vessels for the offshore campaign: Seaway Alfa Lift, Seaway Strashnov and Seaway Phoenix. The appointment remains subject to a final contract award and a final investment decision (FID) by SSE, expected in late 2027.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/oil.text: Oil prices held near a five-month high on Tuesday, as traders assessed reports of fresh attacks on vessels and Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure. As of 04:15 ET (08:15 GMT), benchmark Brent crude futures had risen 0.8% to $110.48 a barrel, whileU.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 1.3% to $105.02 a barrel. Brent settled within touching distance of a five-month high on Monday, even though it had fallen earlier in the session on reports that the U.S. and Iran may have reached a breakthrough in mediated negotiations. However, that decline was short-lived, analysts at Deutsche Bank said in a note. Oil prices surged once again after Iran’s First Vice President said the country had “no choice but to exercise sovereignty” over the Strait of Hormuz, exacerbating worries over crude supply disruptions in the critical chokepoint. Recent strikes on vessels near Hormuz have slowed the flow of oil through the waterway. Hormuz has been largely shuttered since after the start of a joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February, although reported shipping figures have indicated that supplies showed signs of recovery last month. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright also suggested that Gulf crude flows had recovered to about 80% of pre-war levels, although refined-product shipments remained constrained. In a note, ANZ analysts warned that the rebound in oil flows was now under threat, with preliminary data pointing to another slowdown due to intensifying attacks on ships in the Gulf.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/the.text: The recent decision in Olam International Ltd v Pacific Basin Supramax Ltd (The Grande Island) [2026] EWHC 2136 (Comm) concerned a familiar feature of charter partynegotiations where standard wording had been incorporated but parts of it deliberately deleted. The question was what those deletions meant for the provisions left behind. Background The Grande Island was chartered under an amended NYPE form for a trip from Ghent to Nigeria. The charter party incorporated the BIMCO Piracy Clause for Time Charter Parties 2013, but sub-clauses 81(a) and (b) were expressly deleted. Had it remained, Clause 81(a) would have given Owners a broad right, based on the reasonable judgement of Owners or the Master, to refuse to proceed to or through an area considered dangerous because of piracy, or to leave such an area. Clause 81 (b) dealt with the alternative orders to be given by Charterers following the exercise of that right. Furthermore, Clause 81(c) was retained, and it allowed Owners, where the vessel proceeded to or through an area exposed to piracy risk, to take reasonable preventative measures to protect the vessel, crew and cargo. The clause gave examples of such measures, including re-routing, proceeding in convoy and adjusting speed or course, but this list was not exhaustive. After arriving off Warri, the vessel was unable to berth. Considering the background of piracy risk in the area, she left Warri and returned towards Lagos, before returning to Warri around three days later. The dispute was whether that temporary departure was permitted under Clause 81(c) and therefore whether the vessel remained on hire. Charterers’ case Charterers’ position centred on the parties’ decision to delete Clause 81(a) and (b). In their view, this was important because Clause 81(a) contained their express right for Owners to leave an area on account of piracy risk. Having specifically removed that right, Charterers argued that the more general wording of Clause 81(c) should not be interpreted as giving it back.

https://splash247.com/us-moves-to-legiti.text: The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at a Citadel Securities event in New York, Wright said the government was developing an approval process for formerly blacklisted vessels to trade under recognised owners, carrying only non-sanctioned oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” he said. Wright insisted the move was not a blanket lifting of sanctions on Iranian or Russian oil, describing it instead as the conversion of ships into legitimate assets. He put the global dark fleet at around 1,600 tankers and suggested “dozens” or possibly “hundreds” might eventually re-enter compliant trading. Tanker owners’ association INTERTANKO has pushed back hard, warning that legalising a vessel does not automatically address its condition, ownership or insurance. “If additional tanker capacity is required, policy should encourage cargoes towards the quality, compliant fleet,” the association said.

https://splash247.com/dutch-inland-shipp.text: Dutch inland shipping companies Amer Shipping and Van de Graaf & Meeusen have joined forces to establish a new chartering business in Antwerp, backed by a fresh dry cargo newbuilding order at Concordia Damen. The two family-owned operators have launched TriBarge to target Belgian and French shippers, combining their existing networks and vessel capacity with plans for joint fleet investment. The new company will handle dry cargo, general cargo and breakbulk movements across the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region, German canals, the Moselle and inland waterways reaching Basel. Through its partnership with Stream Shipping, an existing venture between Amer Shipping and German cooperative MSG eG, TriBarge will also be able to serve destinations as far as the Black Sea. The partners have already contracted an 85 m dry cargo vessel at Concordia Damen. The newbuilding, to be named Porta Sud , is scheduled to enter service in the second half of 2027 and will be designed to access smaller inland ports, tributaries and canals as well as major rivers. The move comes just weeks after Amer Shipping returned to Concordia Damen for another two 110 m CDS Dry Cargo newbuildings, lifting its programme of shallow-draught vessels to six.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543788-ja.text: DNV has become the first non-Japanese recognized organization authorized by Japan's Flag Administration to apply floating offshore wind classification rules in the country. The authorization allows DNV to apply its floating offshore wind rules within Japan's regulatory framework, supporting the classification and technical assessment of floating wind installations. The rules cover floating substructures, mooring and station-keeping systems, as well as associated safety and utility systems. DNV said the approval strengthens its ability to provide technical expertise, risk management, independent assurance and certification services to companies developing floating offshore wind projects in Japan. "We greatly appreciate the constructive cooperation with the Japanese authorities throughout the process. It reflects our long-term commitment to Japanese maritime and offshore industries and strengthens our ability to contribute independent expertise and assurance as the market develops. We see increasing interest in floating offshore wind globally, and trusted technical frameworks will play an important role as projects progress,” said Cristina Saenz de Santa Maria, CEO Maritime at DNV. The authorization follows cooperation between DNV's Japanese operations, its international technical specialists and Japanese authorities during the approval process.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543784-su.text: Sunda Energy has secured a 12-month extension to the current phase of its Chuditch gas licence offshore Timor-Leste, following an earlier warning from the country's upstream regulator that the production sharing contract (PSC) could be terminated over unmet drilling obligations. The extension was granted by Timor-Leste's Autoridade Nacional do Petróleo (ANP) to Sunda's wholly owned subsidiary SundaGas Banda Unipessoal, which operates PSC TL-SO-19-16 in partnership with state-owned TIMOR GAP. The license contains the Chuditch gas field, where the partners have been preparing to drill the Chuditch-2 appraisal well. ANP issued a notice of intention to terminate the PSC on June 19, 2026, citing the joint venture's failure to meet its minimum exploration work commitment to drill Chuditch-2 by June 18. The regulator gave the partners 120 days to submit written representations before it could proceed with termination. Since receiving the notice, SundaGas and TIMOR GAP have been holding discussions with ANP over arrangements to advance the appraisal drilling program.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543787-de.text: Saitec Offshore Technologies and Japan's Kansai Electric Power Company (KEPCO) have agreed to extend operations at the 2 MW DemoSATH floating offshore wind demonstrator in Spain through 2027, with Japanese construction company Kumagai Gumi joining the project as a new partner. The three companies have signed a cooperation agreement to continue operating the floating wind turbine at the BiMEP open-sea test site off the Basque coast, shifting the project's focus towards research, technology optimization and testing for future commercial developments. Kumagai Gumi will contribute expertise in construction, focusing on improving future decommissioning methods and evaluating construction processes suitable for mass production of floating wind structures. The agreement comes three years after DemoSATH began operations in 2023, becoming Spain's first grid-connected floating offshore wind turbine. The demonstrator consists of a 2 MW turbine mounted on Saitec's concrete twin-hull SATH floating foundation, installed approximately 3.2 kilometers offshore Armintza, in water depths of around 85 meters. The structure was built and assembled at the Port of Bilbao before being towed to its offshore location.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543786-un.text: Union Vega Offshore has ordered two battery-hybrid platform supply vessels (PSVs) from Fujian Mawei Shipyard, with options for four additional vessels, under a design contract awarded to Breeze Ship Design. The vessels will be based on Breeze Ship Design's next-generation Z 4409 PSV design, with delivery of the first vessel scheduled for 2028. Each vessel will measure 84 meters in length and feature 900 square meters of deck space, battery-hybrid propulsion, a moonpool and accommodation for up to 44 personnel. The design also allows for the future installation of a 50-tonne active heave compensated (AHC) crane, expanding the vessels' potential offshore capabilities. In addition to conventional platform supply operations, the Z 4409 design is intended to support light offshore construction, geophysical surveys and seismic support activities. Breeze Ship Design said the contract builds on its existing relationship with Fujian Mawei Shipyard and will involve cooperation with Union Vega Offshore on the newbuilding program.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543785-oi.text: Oil majors are set to post a big jump in third-quarter profit as the US-Israeli war on Iran has boosted refining and trading results, while investors will monitor how wisely they use their cash piles and whether they resist a spending spree. The severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli airstrikes began the war in February has pushed energy prices to multi-year highs, allowing trading desks to profit from the volatility. In a sector notorious in the past for boom and bust, the majors have all promised this time to refrain from losing control of costs in what is one of the highest-earning years for global oil producers in recent memory. Shell, BP and TotalEnergies all expect refining margins to increase three- to fourfold in the third quarter from a year ago, with Shell guiding for a record high of $42 a barrel. TotalEnergies expects cash flow from its refining and chemicals business to double to around $4 billion from the previous quarter. Exxon signalled higher refining margins in the quarter could boost downstream profit by $4.5 billion versus the previous quarter. As majors report third-quarter results at the end of the month, investors are asking whether they will stick to their existing spending plans in times of exceptional earnings, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Biraj Borkhataria in a research note.

https://www.oedigital.com/news/543783-fi.text: Finder Energy has signed a contract worth an estimated $42.3 million with Eneos Drilling for the Hakuryu-5 semi-submersible rig to drill three development wells at the Kuda Tasi and Jahal (KTJ) offshore oil project in Timor-Leste. The agreement covers the provision of the rig, associated equipment and personnel for a firm three-well campaign, with options for two additional wells, Finder said in an October 15 announcement. The contract has a minimum commitment of 140 days, while the three-well drilling and completion program is expected to take approximately 150 days. The estimated $42.3 million contract value represents the gross joint venture cost, with the final amount dependent on the actual duration of operations and applicable contractual rates. Drilling is scheduled to begin from December 1, 2027, with a contractual commencement window extending to March 15, 2028. The agreement remains conditional on obtaining the required KTJ joint venture, government and Finder board approvals by December 31, 2026, as well as Eneos parent company and board approvals by November 16, 2026.

https://www.tecnologistica.com.br/notici.text: A DP World abriu uma nova edição do programa Elas na Operação , que oferece capacitação gratuita para mulheres interessadas em trabalhar na operação de carretas de movimentação interna de contêineres (ITV) no setor portuário . A operadora de terminais portuários afirma que o objetivo é contribuir para que mais mulheres estejam preparadas e confiantes para conquistar espaços nas operações portuárias, desenvolvendo as competências necessárias para disputar oportunidades em um setor que ainda tem muito espaço para avançar em diversidade. "A primeira turma foi um sucesso e, desta vez, damos continuidade a um trabalho que aproxima qualificação profissional, inclusão e geração de oportunidades para a comunidade", afirma Daniela Biscaro, supervisora de sustentabilidade da DP World no Brasil . Desde 2021, o número de mulheres no terminal da companhia em Santos cresceu mais de 220%. Atualmente, aproximadamente 53% das mulheres que trabalham na unidade atuam em funções operacionais, e mais de 100 delas operam equipamentos. O programa terá carga horária de 30 horas, distribuídas ao longo de duas semanas, com atividades de formação técnica e comportamental. A capacitação incluirá conhecimentos sobre a operação de equipamentos portuários, desenvolvimento profissional e preparação para processos seletivos e entrevistas de emprego. Parte das atividades será realizada em um simulador do Senai, enquanto os demais módulos ocorrerão no terminal da DP World, em Santos (SP). A formação será conduzida por profissionais da companhia, e as participantes que concluírem o programa receberão certificado.

A Águia Branca Encomendas , empresa do Grupo Águia Branca especializada no transporte de mercadorias por meio de bagageiros de ônibus, ampliou sua área de atendimento para 19 cidades do Norte e Noroeste Fluminense. A operação conecta empresas desses municípios a mercados como São Paulo e Vitória, com embarques no mesmo dia para encomendas coletadas até as 18h e prazos de entrega que variam conforme o trecho, podendo chegar a 24 horas. No Norte Fluminense, a cobertura inclui São Fidélis, Cardoso Moreira, São Francisco de Itabapoana, São João da Barra, Quissamã, Carapebus e Conceição de Macabu. Já no Noroeste, abrange Bom Jesus do Itabapoana, Italva, Laje do Muriaé, Natividade, Porciúncula, Varre-Sai, Aperibé, Cambuci, Itaocara, Miracema, Santo Antônio de Pádua e São José de Ubá. Com a expansão, a empresa passa a atender 80 municípios fluminenses e mantém uma rede nacional presente em 18 estados e no Distrito Federal. O serviço utiliza o bagageiro de ônibus de empresas parceiras para transportar cargas fracionadas, sem a necessidade de aguardar a formação de grandes volumes para o embarque. Segundo a companhia, a frequência das viagens permite o envio regular de mercadorias para reposição de estoques, abastecimento de operações e distribuição de produtos. Na nova área de cobertura, o atendimento ocorre por meio de agências credenciadas, responsáveis por receber as encomendas e orientar os clientes sobre as modalidades disponíveis. As opções de coleta e entrega, incluindo o serviço porta a porta, variam conforme a disponibilidade em cada município. A operação atende empresas de diferentes segmentos, como os setores de peças, médico-hospitalar, óptico, gráfico, industrial, têxtil, de tecnologia e agropecuário, além de negócios de embalagens, importação e exportação, autopeças, cosméticos, confecções e produtos para os mercados pet e veterinário. “A expansão amplia as alternativas logísticas para as empresas da região, que passam a contar com transporte de cargas fracionadas, rastreamento e opções de coleta e entrega porta a porta, conforme a disponibilidade em cada município”, afirma Marcos Reetz, gerente comercial da Águia Branca Encomendas. A empresa realiza mais de 720 viagens diárias e conta com cerca de 200 agências em sua rede.

https://safety4sea.com/cm-book-review-ma.text: What happens when a ship no longer needs a person on board to navigate it? Who is responsible when an AI system makes a decision at sea? And can maritime law keep pace with technologies developing faster than the rules governing them? T hese questions sit at the heart of Marine Technology, Ocean Development and the Law of the Sea, edited by James Kraska, US Naval War College and Dr. Khanssa Lagdami, World Maritime University. Autonomous shipping is a natural starting point of the book, with the authors examining port State jurisdiction over remotely controlled vessels, the impact of autonomy on time charterparties and whether the actions of a MASS shipmaster can be attributed to the flag State. The book also considers what AI and automation could mean for seafarers and the protections provided under the Maritime Labour Convention. The discussion then moves from autonomous ships to two other major challenges facing shipping: decarbonization and cybersecurity. The authors look at whether the transition to lower-carbon shipping can be legally just and equitable, while chapters on jamming and spoofing highlight the new vulnerabilities created by increasingly connected vessels. The scope then extends beyond shipping, exploring how technology is changing the use of ocean space through seabed mining, SMART submarine cables, marine scientific research and underwater archaeology. These developments raise familiar questions around precaution, jurisdiction and competing interests, but in increasingly unfamiliar technological settings. Ultimately, the book shows that the challenge is not simply whether technology can change what happens at sea, but whether the law can adapt quickly enough to determine who is responsible, what is permitted and how new activities should be governed.

https://safety4sea.com/chief-officer-los.text: A chief officer was lost overboard during an operation to rescue 28 seafarers from the burning containership Espirito Santo Express in the South Atlantic on 15 October, according to Portugal’s Maritime Accident Investigation Office (GAMA). A s of the latest update, the officer was serving aboard the Portuguese-flagged bulk carrier Aeolian Arrow, which had responded to the emergency involving the containership and successfully recovered all 28 crew members. GAMA has now launched a safety investigation into the incident, classified as a very serious maritime casualty. The rescue followed a fire aboard Espirito Santo Express on 15 October 2026 while the containership was sailing through the South Atlantic en route from Singapore to Santos, Brazil. The vessel was reportedly fully laden and sailing from Singapore to Santos, Brazil, when the fire broke out. On 17 October, Hapag-Lloyd, the vessel’s charterer, confirmed that it had been informed of the incident by the ship’s owner, Seaspan. Although all 28 seafarers from the containership were successfully rescued, the subsequent loss of the bulk carrier’s chief officer has added a fatal dimension to the emergency response. According to GAMA, the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) in Rio de Janeiro appointed Aeolian Arrow as the On-Scene Coordinator for the rescue operation. The bulk carrier’s crew recovered 19 seafarers from a lifeboat and another nine from a liferaft after they abandoned Espirito Santo Express following the onboard fire.

https://gcaptain.com/maersk-and-hateco-p.text: FILE PHOTO: A truck transports a Maersk container at APM Terminals at the Port of Los Angeles, California, U.S., March 4, 2026. REUTERS/Mike Blake/File Photo Oct 20, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S, the world’s No. 2 container carrier, signed an agreement with Vietnamese conglomerate Hateco to develop a railway freight terminal network in Vietnam during President To Lam’s official visit to Denmark. APM Terminals, the port operating unit of A.P. Moller-Maersk, inked a memorandum of understanding with Hateco in Copenhagen on Tuesday to develop a container terminal system with total investment estimated up to $3.5 billion, according to a statement from Hateco . The proposed network, which will include a rail freight terminal in Haiphong and three container facilities across northern provinces, “aims to connect industrial parks, logistics hubs and production zones with major transport hubs,” it said. President Lam also met other business leaders in the Danish capital, including executives from Lego Group, Carlsberg and Pandora, as Vietnam seeks to attract more investment, technology and expertise, according to the government website . https://splash247.com/marinakis-tanker-v.text: Greek shipowner Capital Tankers has lined up $930.3m in financing for 11 VLCC newbuildings under construction in China and South Korea, making further headway in funding its expanding crude tanker fleet. The Evangelos Marinakis-backed company has signed four financing arrangements since late September, covering vessels booked at Hanwha Ocean, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Co (DSIC) and Hengli Shipbuilding. The largest portion, totalling $450.6m, covers five 307,000 dwt VLCCs at DSIC. Three vessels are being financed at between $89.6m and $90.9m each under an October agreement, with another two securing $89.6m apiece. Capital Tankers has also arranged $241.8m for three 320,000 dwt LNG dual-fuel-ready VLCCs at South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean, alongside $237.9m for three 306,000 dwt vessels at Hengli in China. The Hanwha financing carries a five-year repayment schedule, while the Chinese yard packages are structured over ten years. All include substantial balloon payments at maturity, ranging from $39.7m to $60.9m per vessel. Separately, Capital Tankers has disclosed a $64.5m sale-and-leaseback arrangement for its newly delivered 155,348 dwt LNG dual-fuel suezmax Amor , built at New Times Shipbuilding in China. The financing, arranged earlier this year, runs to October 2033, with a $40m final payment.

https://www.marinelink.com/news/union-ve.text: Union Vega Offshore has ordered two battery-hybrid platform supply vessels (PSVs) from Fujian Mawei Shipyard, with options for four additional vessels, under a design contract awarded to Breeze Ship Design. The vessels will be based on Breeze Ship Design's next-generation Z 4409 PSV design, with delivery of the first vessel scheduled for 2028. Each vessel will measure 84 meters in length and feature 900 square meters of deck space, battery-hybrid propulsion, a moonpool and accommodation for up to 44 personnel. The design also allows for the future installation of a 50-tonne active heave compensated (AHC) crane, expanding the vessels' potential offshore capabilities. In addition to conventional platform supply operations, the Z 4409 design is intended to support light offshore construction, geophysical surveys and seismic support activities. Breeze Ship Design said the contract builds on its existing relationship with Fujian Mawei Shipyard and will involve cooperation with Union Vega Offshore on the newbuilding program.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/h.text: The orderbook for new containerships continues to set records, with HMM becoming the latest to place a sizable order. It is part of the carrier’s strategy to expand its container capacity toward a goal of 1.5 million TEU of capacity while it also pursues a “hub & spoke” strategy for containers as well as expansion in other segments, including dry bulk and tankers. Last week, HMM reported its board had authorized a further shipbuilding order as well as additional vessel purchases. It moved quickly, reporting today, October 20, that it has placed a newbuilding order with HD Hyundai for eight 13,000 TEU vessels. Due starting in 2029, the vessels will be deployed on one of its flagship routes, sailing between the Far East, India, and the Mediterranean. HD Hyundai reported the order is valued at $1.42 billion, with two of the ships to be built at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries’ yard in Ulsan and six at HD Hyundai Samho’s Yeongam shipyard. The vessels will measure 337 meters (1,105 feet) in length and be outfitted with dual-fuel propulsion engines using both LNG and conventional marine fuel. At the same time, HMM reports it concluded a deal to acquire four feeder vessels (three with 2,800 TEU capacity and one with 1,700 TEU capacity) as part of its regional feeder network strategy. The company recently said it would be focusing on mid-sized and smaller vessels as opposed to ultra-large containerships in the next phase of its growth strategy. HMM is targeting expanding its capacity to approximately 1.5 million TEU. When it launched the growth strategy, the carrier was below 1 million TEU, but it has now exceeded that benchmark with 1.034 million TEU based on Alphaliner’s calculation, with a total of 97 vessels (72 owned/25 chartered). Overall, the company reports it has invested approximately $4.5 billion this year in fleet expansion, logistics, infrastructure, and future technologies. With this order, along with a recent order from MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company for 20 ultra-large 24,000 TEU ships, the analysts at Linerlytica noted that the containership orderbook ”has jumped to a post-2009 peak of 46.5 percent." They report the orderbook capacity has reached 16.2 million TEU, despite an apparent peak in spot market freight rates.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/b.text: A Japanese-owned bulker docking at a private port facility in Vietnam hit the dock on Sunday, causing significant damage to the vessel and the structure. Officials are demanding a plan for the vessel and have posted new safety regulations after the incident. The Aquacharm (182,000 dwt) arrived at the Dung Quat port in Central Vietnam near Da Nang on October 14 after a trip from Australia. The vessel, which was built in 2022 and is registered in the Marshall Islands, was transporting over 170,000 tons of iron ore. The vessel is 292 meters (958 feet) in length. The ship has a crew of 22. The ship held off the port, waiting for dock space, and took a pilot aboard on Sunday afternoon, October 18. The pilot had notified port officials that they were getting underway around 4:45 pm that afternoon and that they would be proceeding to Berth 10 at the Hoa Phat Dung Quat Iron and Steel Complex. About one hour later, as the vessel was maneuvering into the berth, the large bulker struck a section of the pier that was under construction. It berthed at about 6:30 p.m., and regional officials were on hand to inspect the damage. A preliminary inspection revealed a significant 5-meter tear across the bow of the ship. The damage extended to both sides of the ship but was well above the waterline. There was no tank damage, release of pollution, or injuries reported to the crew. A large section of the new berth extension was also heavily damaged. The allision occurred on an extension of the pier running between berth 10 and 11, spanning approximately 50 meters (164 feet).

https://maritime-executive.com/article/e.text: The EU has revised its strategy document for the Arctic, with major changes to its posture on foreign presence and a new emphasis on geopolitics and sovereignty. Left unchanged is its commitment to avoid carbon-based energy extraction in Arctic environments. EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen told AFP that Arctic carbon remains off-limits - despite heavy lobbying from Norway, which envisions a future for its energy industry in the offshore resources of the Barents Sea. "[The EU position] on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground," Jorgensen said. The document also includes support for IMO-led binding regulation of black carbon emissions from shipping in the Arctic, including adjacent areas as far south as 60 degrees north. Black carbon is a major risk factor for accelerated ice melting in a region where ice thickness, average age and coverage extent have been falling. "With a proposal for mandatory regulation for ‘polar fuels’ - currently on the table at the IMO - the EU ambition to cut black carbon from Arctic shipping comes at the perfect moment," said Dr Sian Prior, Lead Advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance. "The polar fuels proposal led by Denmark . . . would ensure that ships will be restricted to using cleaner fuels while sailing in Arctic waters." But the main thrust of the strategy centers on geopolitical influence and defending Europe's interests in the Arctic. This includes an expanded European icebreaker fleet; a new "Maritime Security Hub" for information-sharing on shipping activity and shadow fleet movements in Arctic regions; and an "Arctic Cable Hub" to detect cable threats and coordinate submarine cable repairs, a direct response to Russian subsea espionage capabilities. Economic sovereignty measures will include better integration of the EU's ports and rail connections with Arctic traffic; expanding European Transport Corridor designations for Arctic routes; support for a Pan-Arctic Cable to link Greenland to the European mainland, augmenting the connection that runs through Iceland; a commitment to Arctic satellite connectivity; and development of critical mineral resources.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/f.text: The first Maersk container vessel arrived in India for scheduled maintenance, marking another milestone in the efforts to expand India’s shipbuilding and repair capabilities internationally. The Maersk Chattogram (37,157 dwt) will undergo a full drydocking and overhaul starting on October 20 at India’s L&T (Larsen & Toubro) shipyard located in Kattupalli near Chennai. The vessel, which was built in 2016, has been sailing for Maersk since 2022 and is registered in Singapore. It is 186 meters (610 feet) in length with a capacity of 2,754 TEU. According to the companies, the ship will be using India’s largest shiplift system for drydocking and maintenance. The normal lifecycle work includes its scheduled special survey, along with maintenance and overhaul work covering the hull and structure, machinery, equipment, and propulsion system. “The project is expected to bring together Maersk's fleet and technical teams with L&T, Indian subcontractors, suppliers, and maritime service providers,” highlighted Arun Ramchandani, Head – Precision Engineering & Systems for L&T. The company is one of the largest shipyards in India and is developing its repair business, including having overhauled vessels for the United States’ Military Sealift Command and the UK’s Royal Fleet Auxiliary. The assignment follows through on a commitment Maersk made to India as part of the country’s goals to grow its merchant marine and shipbuilding industries. Maersk signed MOUs with both Larsen & Toubro and Cochin Shipyard to explore ship repair, maintenance, and shipbuilding. Maersk has already, in October 2025, reflagged two container vessels, Maersk Vigo and Maersk Vilnius, to the Indian registry. The move helped the company meet India’s new cabotage restrictions but was also seen as a step toward growing operations in the region.

https://maritime-executive.com/editorial.text: The Dossier Center, an investigative organization funded by the Russian billionaire exile Mikhail Khodorkovsky, has published the results of an investigation into suspicious passengers being carried aboard a fleet of civilian Russian-flagged cargo ships that move Russian military exports to countries in Africa. Besides transporting military cargos, these ships - once unloaded - have increasingly been seen at anchor off sensitive coastlines, often for months, and for no apparent purpose; the Lady Mariia (IMO 9220641) is currently anchored off Port Said, the Yuriy Arshenevskiy (IMO 8406705) is reportedly still dallying in the Dardanelles and the Lady D (IMO 9349289) spent months loitering off Famagusta. There is a very well established pattern of movements of Russian cargo ships used to ship military equipment to Africa, primarily for use by the state-sponsored Africa Corps mercenary organization. Ships typically load in the naval port of Baltiysk in the Russian Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, and have made cargo runs in recent years to Conakry in Guinea, Bata in Equatorial Guinea, Lomé in Togo, Madagascar and to Tobruk in Libya. Cargoes unloaded in these coastal states are sometimes then run through to land-locked countries in Africa serviced by the Africa Corps, namely Burkina Faso, the Central African Republic, Niger and Mali, most of which used to host French garrisons. All of the Russian-flagged ships identified as being involved in this military cargo trade are now sanctioned, and most belong to Astrakhan-based MG-Flot, including the Adler (IMO 9179854), Anastasiia (IMO 9349291), Ascalon (IMO 9198226), Baltic Leader (IMO 9220639), the Lady D and the Lady Mariia. Two other companies are also involved, the Moscow-based Oboronlogistika LLC operating the Ro-Ro cargo vessel Sparta (IMO 9268710), and the St Petersburg-based Baltic Freight Group operating the Yuriy Arshenevskiy. The Dossier Center has identified 28 passengers who embarked at Kaliningrad, but were not apparently on board when the ship concerned returned to the Baltic. These passengers are ‘ghosts’ in that they have false names, which do not appear on common and easily-accessed databases in Russia, such as those storing driving license details, voter records or telephone directories. These passports were issued by offices previously known to have prepared Russian Military Intelligence (GRU) documents, likely printed in an older format that lacks a biometric chip, and are numbered sequentially - as if produced in a batch. The passports have never been tracked again, for example through international Advance Passenger Information (API) systems, after having been used one time on the ship’s outward journey.

https://maritime-executive.com/article/b.text: Salvage efforts are continuing after the series of vessel attacks off the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea. Officials are now reporting that drone fragments have been recovered from one of the vessels, which should confirm the origins of the attack, but a second one of the vessels that was attacked is believed to have sunk overnight. Bulgarian forces mounted a salvage operation, which they estimate cost the country as much as €200,000, but they were able to secure one of the attacked vessels, Chelsea-3 (5,827 dwt), and tow it to an anchorage in Burgas. Teams inspecting the vessel located the fragments, which are currently undergoing chemical analyses that will tell them the type of explosives that were used and identify the drone. The vessel, which is owned by Ukrainian interests and registered in Malta, was attacked approximately 17 miles east of Byala on October 13. It was sailing only with ballast, and the 15 crewmembers were evacuated. Bulgarian officials refused to speculate on the origins of the attack but noted it was not likely that Ukraine would attack one of its own ships. Bulgarian forces conducted the first visual inspection on October 15, reporting the vessel was drifting southward, but bad weather and heavy seas prevented efforts to secure the vessel. By October 16, the vessel was 10.7 nautical miles east of Lozenets, but it appeared that its anchor was holding the ship. Teams were able to tow the vessel to Burgas on October 17. The inspection revealed three large holes, including one in the portside stern and another midships. No ammunition or military supplies were found on the vessel. Officials said that international assistance was available if needed to identify the drone fragments and the explosive. Overnight between October 19 and 20, officials also reported another one of the attacked vessels, the Palau-registered Able disappeared from radar, and they believe it has finally sunk. The ship was attacked on October 6 in Bulgaria’s EEZ about 70 nautical miles from Byala. Air Force and Navy teams inspected the ship on October 9 and reported extensive damage from a fire and that the engine room was flooded. The ship, which was 5,985 tons, was loaded with barley from Romania bound for Turkey. The inspection failed to find any drone fragments.

https://gcaptain.com/iran-claims-more-ta.text: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed Tuesday that a supertanker caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a series of similar claims that have yet to be independently substantiated. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the tanker was violating Iranian transit regulations when it struck a mine, according to Reuters. In another statement carried by Iranian media Tuesday , the Guards said two tankers had been set ablaze and disabled by mines along a route south of the strait that Tehran considers unauthorized. Neither statement identified the vessels or provided independently verifiable evidence of the reported strikes. The Guards also did not make clear when the two tankers were allegedly hit, leaving open whether the latest announcements describe new incidents or repeat earlier claims. The reports follow several similar announcements in recent months, many involving unnamed tankers said to have exploded or caught fire while attempting to use shipping routes not authorized by Iran. But assessments from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) and the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) have repeatedly questioned those accounts.

https://gcaptain.com/after-354-accidents.text: A new survey of more than 900 seafarers has exposed a persistent gap between safety procedures and the realities of working aboard ships, prompting renewed calls for action to prevent deaths in enclosed spaces. Ship management association InterManager says it has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents between 1996 and 2026, involving tankers, bulk carriers, containerships, passenger vessels and other ship types. Despite decades of safety campaigns, training requirements and regulatory attention, the association says many of the same problems continue to put seafarers at risk. The latest survey found that crews often struggle with overly complicated procedures, insufficient time and manpower, commercial pressure and inadequate practical training. Respondents also raised concerns that inspections sometimes place more emphasis on paperwork than whether safety measures actually work onboard. “Enclosed spaces have been killing seafarers for decades,” said Captain Kuba Szymanski, InterManager’s secretary general. “The industry does not need more paperwork for the sake of paperwork, it needs practical measures that work onboard.” “If a procedure cannot realistically be completed with the time, people and equipment available, then we need to question the system, not blame the seafarer.”

https://gcaptain.com/iran-strikes-more-s.text: Drone view of oil tanker HELGA berthed at one of Iraq's southern offshore oil terminals near Basra as it prepares to load crude oil, becoming the second vessel to arrive since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, April 24, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty (Bloomberg) — Iranian attacks in the Persian Gulf are striking more ships and causing more severe damage than earlier in the conflict , bringing fresh risks to energy flows from the region. At least 23 incidents involving ships attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz were logged in the first two weeks of October, with at least five reporting impacts to their engine rooms, according to data from naval groups in the region and alerts from security consultants. Direct hits on engine rooms can cause fires and leave ships without power or propulsion, taking vessels out of service for months and leading to costly repairs. Middle Eastern producers have shown a willingness to keep supplying oil in the face of Iranian attacks — preliminary data from trade intelligence company Kpler put the seven-day average of Middle East oil exports fractionally above prewar levels. But the intensifying strikes threaten to worsen one of the biggest constraints in the global oil market: the number of available ships. Several shipping and maritime security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the topic, said they were seeing increased levels of engine-room damage from attacks, as well as a larger volume of incidents in general, but that it was hard to say if Iran was deliberately targeting ship engines. “What we’re seeing is an increase in the frequency of attacks, and therefore, more damage in engine rooms and disabling fire,” said Phillip Belcher, marine director at Intertanko, the world’s main trade group for the tanker industry.

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/sed.text: From HSFO and VLSFO to LNG and biofuel, chartering and operations teams can now check today’s bunker prices without leaving Sedna. Sedna, the Intelligent Operating System for Shipping, has partnered with Nereus, the intelligence platform for bunker and lubricants procurement, to bring bunker market prices into the conversations behind voyage decisions. The Nereus Bunker Indication Prices app, now live on the Sedna Certified App Marketplace, gives chartering, operations, and bunker procurement teams daily indication prices for more than 450 ports and six fuel grades, directly in Sedna Email. Bunker prices shape the economics of every voyage. A change in price can shift a voyage’s profitability, which employment a vessel takes next and where it bunkers. Until now, chartering and operations teams have had to get those prices separately, from a broker, a supplier or a market intelligence service, and bring them back into the email conversations where voyages are discussed and negotiated. The Sedna and Nereus integration closes that gap. Nereus covers the full bunker procurement lifecycle, from market research and inquiry management to negotiation and post-fixture execution. Through the integration, Nereus updates its bunker indication prices every day and sends them to Sedna Email automatically. Users see today’s indication price at each port for HSFO, VLSFO, LSMGO, ULSFO, LNG, and biofuel, with each grade shown at the ports where it is available. Chartering, operations and bunker teams work from one shared set of prices, without opening a second system. Sedna Founder and CEO Bill Dobie said: “Shipping decisions are made under time pressure, with information spread across inboxes, spreadsheets and specialist tools. We bring critical context to teams at the moment they need it. Nereus is a good example: trusted bunker market data, inside the conversations where fixtures and voyages are discussed, so teams spend less time gathering information and more time acting on it.” – View daily bunker indication prices for more than 450 ports worldwide – Check prices for high sulphur fuel oil (HSFO), very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO), low sulphur marine gas oil (LSMGO), ultra low sulphur fuel oil (ULSFO), liquefied natural gas (LNG), and biofuel – See which fuel grades are available at each port – Receive updated prices every day, sent from Nereus to Sedna automatically – See prices for alternative bunker ports in one place – Work from one shared set of prices across chartering, operations and bunker procurement teams

https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/jap.text: A new analysis by Opportunity Green warns governments of the wide-ranging risks posed by Japan’s proposal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), ahead of adoption negotiations on the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) this November and December in London. Japan’s latest proposal for changes to the NZF would significantly alter the agreed policy architecture, undermining even further the chances of making the 2023 Revised Strategy a reality. The primary changes involve: removing the Net-Zero Fund, the key pillar of “economic measure”; making the purchase of Surplus Units (SUs) the primary mechanism for addressing compliance deficits; and introducing an industry-led “direct contribution” as a global financing mechanism. Opportunity Green highlights four interconnected risks for IMO member states in this scenario: 1. Scrapping a just and equitable transition: A global IMO Fund is the tool to ensure climate vulnerable developing countries are supported in shipping’s clean transition, which countries committed to under the Revised Strategy. As it stands, the NZF would generate $10-15bn in additional, predictable compliance revenue to help countries meet their needs: investments in zero-emission ship technologies and energy and more resilient trade infrastructure. Removing the Fund also means losing the enforcement mechanism for the Framework. 2. Depriving countries of the power to shape the maritime transition: Replacing the Fund with “direct contributions”, a system where companies are in charge of deciding where revenues are directed, effectively transfers decision-making power to companies. It could result in larger fleet owners paying compliance revenues back into their own supply chains and infrastructure, as opposed towards the needs of the global sector or climate vulnerable developing countries. 3. Weakening incentives for zero-emission energy: Using SUs for compliance would undermine incentives for early uptake of zero-emission energy and fuels, allowing companies to effectively pay to pollute instead of investing in their transition. 4. Undermining emission reduction: Weak incentives for zero-emission energy and fuels would also mean prolonged use of high-emitting fuels such as fossil-based liquefied natural gas (LNG) and biofuels in the industry. This would mean shipping cannot meet the emission reduction targets countries have committed to. At the upcoming round of negotiations in November and December, countries are urged to retain key principles of the NZF and adopt the agreement in its current form to keep a fighting chance of meeting the IMO Revised Strategy and support states in meeting their international legal obligations on climate change. https://petronoticias.com.br/a-maersk-re.text: A Maersk anunciou hoje (20) que o abastecimento de etanol no navio Maersk Halifax, o primeiro de propulsão dual fuel adaptado da companhia, em Singapura, foi muito bem sucedido. A operação marca a primeira vez que o composto foi utilizado como combustível em um navio desta categoria da frota da Maersk e representa mais um marco importante nos esforços da empresa para explorar múltiplos caminhos de combustíveis para o futuro da navegação descarbonizada. Realizada em colaboração com a Autoridade Marítima e Portuária de Singapura (MPA) e outros parceiros, a operação envolveu o abastecimento de aproximadamente 5.000 toneladas métricas de bioetanol com certificação ISCC, proporcionando experiência operacional valiosa e insights sobre a infraestrutura, o fornecimento, a prontidão da cadeia de suprimentos e as operações de navios relacionadas ao uso do etanol como combustível marítimo. A operação, disse a empresa, reforça o compromisso de longa data da Maersk com a busca por múltiplos caminhos de combustíveis e tecnologias que apoiem a transição da indústria marítima rumo à descarbonização do transporte oceânico. O etanol vem se destacando como um combustível promissor de transição devido à sua disponibilidade global, às redes de produção e distribuição já estabelecidas e à compatibilidade com tecnologias de motores movidos a álcool. Quando certificado e obtido a partir de rotas de baixo carbono, o etanol pode proporcionar reduções significativas de emissões de gases de efeito estufa em comparação com combustíveis marítimos convencionais. “A transição energética exige que exploremos e ampliemos soluções capazes de gerar impacto real. Na Maersk, seguimos com uma estratégia multicombustível porque reconhecemos que nenhum caminho de combustível pode descarbonizar sozinho o transporte marítimo global. No início deste ano, a Maersk conduziu uma série de testes bem-sucedidos com etanol nos navios de propulsão dual fuel Laura Maersk, Antonia Maersk e Tangier Maersk “, afirma Emma Mazhari , Diretora de Mercados de Energia. © 2026 Petronotícias.
